Its ability to analyze various isotopes using the same setup is unique because the experiment utilizes a $^{116}$Xe-based target located within the European Spallation Facility's active beam area, allowing for the natural production of low-weight dark matter particles. By combining different measurement methods in time and spatial dimensions, the experiment effectively rules out false signals and minimizes contamination from neutron-based reactions. Following improvements to the calorimeter's detection setup, including the replacement of amorphous silicon photodetectors with crystalline ones, CRESST's sensitivity for dark matter interactions with electrons and neutrons has reached levels comparable to the best results from other experiments. Notably, CRESST's detection setup is capable of identifying dark matter particles generated by isotopes other than those directly interacting with the target material. For instance, the experiment can utilize a $^{130}$Te-based target located outside the active beam area to detect weightless dark matter particles weighing up to 100 MeV/c$^2$. Furthermore, CRESST is planning to implement novel detection techniques to expand its detection capabilities.

Blind Image deblurring attempts to estimate a latent image's sharpness and a blurred image, an ill-posed problem, resolved by restricting either the image or a blur kernel representing blur. Differing from prior research, this study regulates the structure of the blur kernel. The kernel mixture concept utilizes Gaussian kernels with enhanced scale and center configurations, producing a nearly non-parametric blur shape representation. The decision of the base kernel count becomes more flexible due to a data-driven method. This strategy is successfully tested in a satellite imaging scenario where it outperforms current standards regulating latent images in favour of the kernel's structural adjustment.

This paper introduces a new concept called associative BiHom-Yang-Baxter pair with weight (λ,γ) which can be used to solve the double curved Rota-Baxter BiHom-system. Furthermore, we establish equivalent definitions of covariant BiHom-Yang-Baxter systems of weight (λ,γ) and of BiHom-pre-Yang-Baxter systems of weight (λ,γ), and prove their correspondence with the associative BiHom-Yang-Baxter pair. We also show that the BiHom-pre-Yang-Baxter pair of weight (λ,γ) can be used to solve the double curved Rota-Baxter BiHom-system. In addition, we define the notion of weakly BiHom-pre-Yang-Baxter pair of weight (λ,γ) and demonstrate its equivalence to the associative BiHom-Yang-Baxter pair, as well as its equivalence to the BiHom-pre-Yang-Baxter pair. Finally, we provide examples of weakly BiHom-pre-Yang-Baxter pairs of weight (λ,γ) and show that the BiHom-pre-Yang-Baxter pair of weight (λ,γ) can be used to solve the double curved Rota-Baxter BiHom-system.

Formal verification offers critical correctness assurances for software,
particularly vital in systems requiring safety and security assurances.
Hoare logic serves as a widely employed formal methodology for thoroughly
examining software adherence to specifications through precondition/postcondition
declarations. The improvement of semantic parsing methods and increasing
computational capabilities enable higher-quality formal verification of software,
motivating the integration of Hoare logic within a compiler. This compiler
component, referred to as a Hoare solver, determines and enforces Hoare validity
on given source code and specifications. We introduce a novel, efficient method
for inserting Hoare assertions as invariants into C code and demonstrate the
satisfaction of formal specifications by using this method in compiled examples. 
Furthermore, this approach not only enforces correctness but also enhances performance 
through side-effect elimination during Hoare verification. The combination of formal
verification and program transformation leads to notable speed-ups in typical parallel
program benchmarks, verified with an automated reasoning tool and validated with 45 test
cases.

Distributed consensus is crucial for various distributed systems, such as distributed databases and blockchains, to function correctly. The Canopus protocol efficiently manages large-scale distributed consensus without the need for a single leader, achieving this through a virtual tree structure that limits network traffic and hardware redundancies within the network. The existing Canopus protocol excels at performance, however, struggles when dealing with failures that don't directly affect performance, leading to the development of RCanopus. RCanopus enhances Canopus to not only tolerate various types of failures but also to guarantee the accurate detection and recovery of failures and protect against malicious attacks, all while maintaining agreement among live nodes.

A recent study employs coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations to analyze the mechanical properties of lipid bilayers composed of dioleoyl-phosphatidylserine (DOPS) and cholesterol (CHOL). By examining various cholesterol concentrations within DOPS bilayers, the study quantifies the effects of cholesterol on modulating lipid membrane stiffness. The research utilizes primary simulation data to compare with existing theoretical models, revealing an initially increased stiffness in cholesterol-rich membranes, which however exceeds expected notions. Notably, the study discovers that incorporating cholesterol significantly reduces the bending rigidity of lipid bilayers, suggesting an increased fluctuation in membrane dynamics. The research explores potential applications of these findings in understanding and predicting various biological processes, like non-linear sound wave propagation in tissue and the force behind cellular membrane bending during endocytosis.

This paper examines the loop quantum cosmological model generated from the ADM Hamiltonian. It looks at a spatially homogeneous, flat FRW model and finds that its modified Friedmann equation is analogous to that of the APS LQC model. Notably, the model's critical matter density at which quantum gravity effects set in is significantly lower than in the APS LQC model, resulting in a much earlier onset of these effects. Additionally, the research presents an approach to solving the LQC model's evolution equation without invoking the effective field theory framework.

The Pierre Auger Observatory catalog details 100 extensive air-showers 
recorded between 2004 and 2020 for high-energy particles, spanning a specific
energy range from 78 to 166 EeV. This comprehensive dataset is made available 
for close examination, alongside nine events used to establish the energy scale 
for each detected primary particle. An accompanying plot displays the locations 
where these energetic particles entered Earth's atmosphere, leaving their data unanalyzed.

Incorporating deep neural networks into robotic systems poses a significant problem: deep neural networks generate unpredictable outputs. Novel approaches aim to develop robotics-friendly neural networks that yield measurable outputs, optimized for control precision. Nevertheless, existing methods require extensive fine-tuning after integration into a robotic system, which compromises their performance. This study investigates a novel neural network architecture, the measurable output network (MeaNU), designed to produce measurable outputs. MeaNU incorporates a measure constraint in a single training stage, adhering strictly to output constraints immediately prior to control, while its generalization capabilities are assessed in a simulation-based environment. The MeaNU's performance is further compared with cutting-edge neural network architectures optimized for control precision in various experiments.

The integration of advanced traffic forecasting technology significantly affects urban transportation systems.
The traffic4cast competition pushed the limits of short-term traffic prediction, utilizing high-resolution traffic data.
In this paper, we address a related challenge involving predicting traffic volumes using a conditional variational autoencoder on single camera images.
Initially, we tested the efficacy of dividing test images into smaller patches to enhance prediction accuracy and robustness against unexpected scenes.
However, this method proved vulnerable to outliers.
As an alternative solution, we developed multiple approaches to combine the predictions of individually processed patches, particularly tailoring them to applications where predictions are highly dependent on surrounding environment context.
The evaluation showed that our proposed method consistently outperformed the accuracy achieved in the traffic4cast competition.
The source code is available for reference at https://github.com/traffic4cast/traffic4cast2022-solution-jk.

In recent years, rewriting theory has been used to create systematic introductions for various types of higher categories. This approach is based on the observation that the limitations of strict categories can be overcome by considering them as specific types of Gray categories, which in turn can be seen as a particular type of tricategory. Building on this idea, we present a unified framework for a broad range of higher categories, demonstrating that each one corresponds to a distinct subtype of the fundamental taut monoidal double category. This work is inspired by the concept of the taut preorder from rewriting theory, allowing for the clear interpretation of various higher category structures as subtypes of the double category framework.

Automatic hippocampus segmentation on magnetic resonance imaging is a critical factor in diagnosing and treating neuropsychiatric disorders. Current deep learning-based methods primarily utilize data from patients with healthy or Alzheimer's disease. This raises concerns about their performance in other domains, such as patients with epilepsy and hippocampal resections. We have developed and evaluated a novel deep learning-based approach that integrates information from multiple datasets with varying levels of annotation. By leveraging a self-supervised segmentation framework and adapting the consistency loss to the Epilepsy-Hippocampus Dataset, our method demonstrates better performance compared to existing approaches. When applied to partially annotated data from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative dataset, our method enables state-of-the-art performance without requiring additional resources. Furthermore, our method provides insights into performance gaps between datasets, such as the difficulties encountered in processing resected hippocampus data. This highlights the potential for novel imaging biomarkers to study epilepsy-related hippocampus changes, such as the development of cavity shapes and patterns.

Quantum nonlocality is demonstrated using the collective resource of entanglement on the basis of the scenario of three parties simultaneously occupying two possible paths without any two occupying the same path. This setup shows quantum properties such as path information cannot be shared and entanglement cannot be divided, with numerical analysis confirming highly secure quantum key exchange is achievable. Additionally, experimental implementation is proposed using a setup consisting of a single photon source, beam splitters, and for the collection of emitted photons a system of collection lenses and single photon detectors.

Our research identifies the cosmic ray nucleon collision as the primary driver of proton radiation belt formation at lower energy levels ($\sim$10 MeV), specifically within the innermost region of Earth's atmosphere. Previous studies on proton belt formation have predominantly focused on higher energy levels ($\sim$GeV) and the effects of electromagnetic forces during the proton's scattering process. In contrast, at energy levels below $\sim$100 MeV, proton belts are influenced by electromagnetic forces during the cosmic ray nucleon collision, resulting in the filling of proton radiation belts within the 0-64 km altitude range. By utilizing Monte Carlo simulations based on GEANT4's electromagnetic cross-section models, our findings validate that proton radiation belts within this range contain both H and H2 ions. Our work, however, reveals that proton radiation belts are mainly composed of non-energetic protons, which lose their energy below 10 MeV in the lowermost layer of Earth's atmosphere before being replaced by H2 ions at lower energies, thereby indicating that proton radiation belts are primarily generated by proton loss while also undergoing the co-formation of H2 ions filling the belts. Furthermore, proton radiation belts exhibit seasonal fluctuations caused by variations in the atmospheric density at night due to the atmospheric tides. In particular, proton radiation belt variations are most pronounced in the 0-20 km altitude range and demonstrate positive correlations with the atmospheric density fluctuations at an amplitude of $\sim$10%. A pressing issue for the practical implementation of deep neural networks (DNNs) concerns their expressivity limits, especially in light of recent findings suggesting that with increasing complexity, most DNNs struggle to surpass certain performance barriers. In this study, we investigate how the expressivity of DNNs influences their inherent performance limitations, using a established framework that demonstrates how the architecture's internal workings affect its output. Additionally, we employ a new method for systematically evaluating expressivity in DNNs, providing insight into its connection with classification capabilities. Ultimately, our findings indicate that the performance outcomes of DNNs are often determined by their inability to overcome fundamental obstacles, underscoring the need for novel architectures that can surpass the current theoretical boundaries.

To protect user data in low-rank matrix completion tasks, we develop a novel
noise-based method ensuring differential privacy. This method incorporates
noise with characteristics inspired by the Huber loss function in robust
statistics, and is termed as the Huber mechanism. By demonstrating that both
interpolated and iterative implementations of the Huber mechanism meet
differential privacy requirements, and establishing connections to well-known
measures like Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms, we establish the theoretical
foundation for achieving differential privacy in this application. 
Furthermore, we show that using the Huber mechanism yields superior performance
over its interpolative counterpart with smaller additive constant and reduced
practical applicability. This method is also shown to outperform traditional
Gaussian mechanism-based approaches in terms of both performance and statistical
efficiency. To showcase its practical utility, we apply the Huber mechanism
to handle the challenges associated with analyzing noisy multivariate data.

We propose a novel approach to modelling interstellar dust where larger grains are comprised of a uniform material, referred to as 'astrodust', and tiny particles, known as PAHs, come in various distinct forms. The evidence suggests that a uniform grain composition is most consistent with the observed patterns of infrared polarization, and the established ratio between optical and infrared polarization. A detailed analysis reveals that a combination of astrodust and PAHs accurately replicates the properties of galactic extinction and emission from interstellar dust while adhering to existing constraints on dust abundance. The associated data and software have been made publicly accessible for further research.

Research on the formation of planets around low-mass stars with masses similar to those of Jupiter's counterparts, known as brown dwarfs, is an area of ongoing study. Despite several planets being discovered around nearby stars with masses below 0.2 times the mass of the sun, many questions regarding planet formation in such environments still persist. Notably, the minimum mass required for a planet to be stable is an unresolved question.  We conducted an extensive study to determine the lower mass limit for a planet that can orbit its host robustly.  To achieve this, we observed 15 brown dwarf binaries with close orbital distances using ALMA's 870 $\mu$m band and searched for millisecond-scale variations in the radial velocities of their components.  As a result of this study, we were unable to detect any velocity changes larger than 0.3 km/s.  From this data, we calculated the minimum mass required for a planet to be stable, which we found to be between 0.5 and 6 times the mass of the earth, assuming an idealized exoplanetary equilibrium shape.  Based on these findings, we estimated the timescales over which such a planet would be able to stabilize its host's orbital motion, which would range between 10 and 500 years, assuming an earth-like mass ratio between the planet and its host. The original Lights Out game is played on a $n \times m$ grid where players make combinations of lights to turn off all the lights. This graph theory variation of the game considers any connected graph $G$ with vertices representing lights and edges representing the possible light combinations. A successful strategy in this game involves making combinations of light switches until all lights go off. A configuration of lights is considered solvable if there exists a successful strategy, and the game is solvable on a graph $G$ if all its solvable configurations share a common starting point. This paper explores the concept of solvability on graphs and introduces the concept of distance-light graphs based on a new concept called distance-lightness. An investigation into the game's solvability on specific graph types such as strong graphs, hypercubes, and grid graphs follows.

This paper presents a novel, multi-stage image segmentation model, combining the techniques of image restoration and image segmentation. The integration of image restoration aspects enables the proposed model to effectively handle images corrupted by noise, blurriness, missing pixels, and varied color schemes. Specifically, this approach extends the influential Mumford-Shah model, allowing for improved segmentation of gray-scale and vector-valued images affected by noise, blurriness, or missing data. Our paper devises a specialized, multi-stage algorithm to address this challenge, utilizing a primal-dual interior-point method, and demonstrates the efficacy of this model through comprehensive numerical case studies.

Program analysis through Abstract Interpretation involves simulating the behavior of a program in a simplified environment to approximate its true behavior. This simulation traditionally has two steps: the upward phase uses approximation to ensure the analysis stops, followed by the downward phase which uses interpolation to mitigate the loss of accuracy resulting from approximations. This paper suggests an alternative by temporarily switching from an initial approximation to a more precise one, before interpolating to make the analysis more accurate. The proposed approach is theoretically justified and tested on a simple case study, which revealed significant gains in precision compared to the standard technique.

A wide range of topological phonons has been discovered in various compounds, 
including BiTeI, PbTe, and Skutterudites. These phonons exhibit intriguing 
properties such as non-linear wave propagation and potential for quantized thermal 
conductance. To date, topological phonons have been poorly characterized in 
semimetallic materials. Our study reveals that a newly discovered semimetal from 
MoTe$_{4}$Se$_{3}$ family indeed hosts topological phonons, as characterized by 
a phonon-folding topological Brillouin zone, non-trivial phonon band structure, 
and localized high-frequency phonons. These topological phonons are stable and resistant 
to anharmonic effects. Moreover, the material is versatile for various applications 
due to its modifiable band gap and versatile crystal structure through molecular design.

Unsupervised outlier detection methods that rely on distances are versatile and may be applied to any type of data without preconditions regarding its distribution. Nevertheless, the original distance-based outlier detection methods could be computationally impractical when dealing with large data sets due to their inefficiency. To mitigate this limitation, the enhanced distance-based outlier detection methods aimed to overcome the computational drawbacks while preserving the flexibility and unsupervised nature of their predecessors. Specifically, the proposed approaches involve incorporating neighborhood sets and leveraging previous results to achieve improved time complexity, thus making the distance-based outlier detection processes more efficient.

The probability of (de-)excitation and photon emission is evaluated for a non-relativistic, moving atom interacting with a quantum electromagnetic field near a stationary, perfectly conducting plane. These findings expand upon previous scalar model outcomes where the atom was represented by a scalar variable coupled to a scalar field with either Dirichlet or Neumann conditions applied on the boundary. This assessment considers how spontaneous emission is influenced by various factors, such as motion atom's position, velocity, and orientation, as well as electromagnetic field characteristics. Reduced atom-field coupling coefficients are derived for general cases in a Cartesian coordinate system. For simplicity, we present a few representative numerical results, although a comprehensive analysis of these values is beyond the scope of this paper.

As applications relying on graph representations grow, the focus has shifted from global fairness to incorporating fairness at the node level, considering that Graph Neural Network (GNN)-based models primarily operate within local neighborhoods. To address this gap, we propose a framework that captures the concept of Neighborhood Fairness (NF), quantifying fairness based on the characteristics of each node's surrounding environment. Experimental results demonstrate NF's utility and reveal a correlation between its violation and adverse outcomes in real-world scenarios. To mitigate NF violations, we design two optimization techniques - Reclustering Learning (RL) and Graph Self-Improvement (GI) - both of which incorporate NF constraints. GI employs a novel algorithm to identify and modify critical graph edges, prioritizing improvements in areas with the highest fairness concerns. Our experiments confirm the efficacy of these algorithms and provide insights into key hyperparameters' behavior.

This study focuses on kinetic models for reversible enzyme reactions and evaluates the effectiveness of two analytical techniques in obtaining approximate solutions to these models. We apply and compare the Homotopy Perturbation Method and the Simple Iteration Method to derive approximate analytical solutions to non-linear equations describing reversible enzyme reactions. The resulting approximations are then compared with exact solutions in both spatially homogeneous and homogeneous systems. For systems where the conversion rates of substrates and products are similar, the Homotrubbery Method yields superior results. Conversely, the Simple Iteration Method provides more accurate solutions when substrate and product conversion rates exhibit distinct differences.

Theoretical models predicting the existence of supersymmetry anticipate that the LHC will detect squarks and gluinos in the near future. The squarks and gluinos decompose into three-body components consisting of a lightest neutralino, a quark, and a gluon. This process allows the creation of final states containing a single jet and missing energy, which serves as the signature for detecting squark and gluino particles when they have masses in the 1-2 TeV range. The detection of squark and gluino particles can be enhanced by searching for three jets and missing energy, particularly when virtual squarks and gluinos, with masses up to 4 TeV, decompose into final states containing two jets and a neutrino. This method offers the possibility of probing gluinos with masses close to 4 TeV when they decompose into quarks and missing energy. The LHC detection of squark and gluino particles in the near future will largely depend on the signature associated with the three-body decay products, which will also offer the possibility of setting limits on the theoretical models predicting the existence of supersymmetry.

Two proposed expectation models for temporary financial bubbles, involving individuals with varied predictions and positive influence, show that bubble collapse can happen suddenly.
Even with rapid information spread at infinite speed, the bubbles might not always fall if assumed to grow steadily.
Key factors affecting the bubble's emergence and longevity include low to varying expectations, strong to varying confidence levels, and the level of information available to all agents.
In cases where expectations differ, the bubble's survival chances depend on variations in positive influence among agents.
These models can also explain market over-shooting after a temporary bubble collapse, revealing a complex mechanism leading to deeper market depressions.

Quantum harmonic oscillators were numerically simulated in their ground state using a lattice-based approach. This involved coupling nearest-neighbor sites with a potential that mimics a mass on a massless spring. Quantum coherence was introduced using complex-valued wave oscillations in the lattice. Constant forces and coherent oscillations were applied to the oscillators, resulting in a comparison of their effects on coherent oscillations. Applying a uniform force across multiple oscillators caused a shift in the average position of the lattice sites but did not affect the quantum oscillations within the lattice. In contrast, adding random forces led to diffusion among the lattice sites, revealing a relationship between transport and the quantum oscillation length. This diffusion was compared with the predictions of the quantum master equation for coherent states.

Recent research has shown significant progress in improving recommender system performance through leveraging reviews for predicting ratings, however the current methods have several limitations. The existing techniques often use complex neural networks, which make it challenging to easily understand reviewer sentiments when making predictions. Moreover, the available datasets are relatively small when compared to the vast amount of reviews generated daily. To overcome these challenges, this paper introduces a lightweight end-to-end learning framework, which incorporates sentiment analysis to guide review representation in rating prediction. The proposed method also addresses issues like review spam and noise, which are not typically handled by the existing methods. The framework achieves better performance in rating prediction compared to the state-of-the-art techniques on real-world datasets, which is backed by experimental results.

Developing CS NLP systems is obstructed by the scarcity of CS data. This study delves into utilizing data augmentation to create Dialectal Arabic-English CS text, utilizing a novel CS metric and initial benchmarks for CS word-level translation and translation tasks. It presents a novel, state-of-the-art CS translation model that outperforms existing models and offers potential applications for other CS languages. This study also presents a new CS metric that can identify the level of CS usage in texts, offering a unique way to analyze CS languages. It proposes an approach to create quality CS data utilizing a novel CS metric and a representation technique. This study achieves state-of-the-art results in translation and data augmentation tasks, providing a new approach for CS translation and data augmentation. It showcases the effectiveness of the new approach through state-of-the-art results on two datasets and outperforms existing models in word-level translation and translation tasks. This study's findings show that the new CS metric can perform well in CS translation tasks and can be competitive with other metrics. It presents a new approach for CS translation tasks and can be used in other CS languages and can be extended to other CS metrics. This study's approach can be used for CS translation and data augmentation and can be used in other CS languages and can be extended to other CS types. It can be used in many CS translation and data augmentation tasks and can be used in other CS languages and can be used in other dialects and can be used in other tasks.

We show that any subgroup of homeomorphisms of a compact surface that fix the boundary, whose action within the surface's interior is highly transitive, cannot be topologically compact when using the compact-open topology. Additionally, by combining this result with a prior finding that a compact surface's automorphism group is always compact-open topologically, it follows that the homeomorphism group of a compact surface is also compact-open topologically. This enables the establishment of a compact-open compactification for the homeomorphism group of a compact surface, enabling a compactification for the surface's automorphism group, which in turn enables a compactification for the surface itself.

We're investigating integrable boundary conditions that can be geometrically interpreted as D-branes within specific theoretical models based on conformal field theory in both two-dimensional spaces (2D) and the target space. Our focus involves boundary conditions related to Gepner points, as well as those associated with Wilson-'t Hooft line and boundary insertions in Lee-Weinberg-Caldwell models. We're analyzing these boundary conditions by looking at their effects on the relevant F-theory backgrounds. We're also explaining how known brane configurations in both 4D and 6D supergravity theories relate to the aforementioned integrable boundary conditions, and discussing potential connections between brane arrangements, boundary conditions, and certain classical background solutions.

As tasks increasingly rely on computer execution, the demand for reliable solutions is rising across domains, including engineering and computer graphics. A fundamental concept in addressing these challenges is the mesh, a composite of basic elements where hexahedral units offer distinct advantages compared to other shapes, especially when spatial constraints are involved. Although hexahedral meshes are less frequently utilized than their tetrahedral or prismatic counterparts, they remain a preferred choice in specific scenarios. The development of efficient algorithms for packing these elements is a crucial challenge, particularly in situations where hexahedral solids must fit within tightly bounded regions. In this study, the hexahedral folding algorithm previously presented by Kharaibah et al. has been adapted and extended to accommodate multiple starting hexahedra. However, when a single initial hexahedron is insufficient for packing the remaining elements, the study introduces a novel solution that seeks an acceptable initial placement for the first hexahedron through a random search within a predefined radius. Following this procedure, the proposed method employs the previously described algorithm to refine the mesh. The algorithm's feasibility and efficiency in solving two-dimensional and three-dimensional packing problems were validated through numerous case studies and real-world applications. Notably, the study successfully addressed a novel problem related to the compact rendering of characters in a 3D environment using hexahedral meshes.

The tasks of relation extraction and knowledge graph link prediction share a
common link in their objectives, allowing them to complement each other within a
shared framework. Specifically, relation extraction serves as a crucial component
in extracting knowledge graph facts, and by pairing it with knowledge graph link
prediction, we can verify the accuracy of extracted relationships. Through this
synergistic approach, we can improve both relation extraction and knowledge graph
link prediction performance, and ultimately contribute to the development of an
end-to-end system that combines both processes.

This study introduces an innovative analytical delay model specifically tailored for the deep submicron CMOS inverters used in 0.18 $\mu$m CMOS technology. Developed based on the static early voltage and the static delay of a transistor, this new model accurately takes into consideration the impact of leakage current, incorporating it into the existing model for enhanced precision. Derived equations encompass various parameters like drive current, transition time, rise/fall time, and static delay, with the latter defined as the time required for the output voltage to reach 90% of the final value. Verification is performed through the proposed model, comparing its predictions with actual HSPICE simulation results for the mentioned technology.

Making optimal decisions in complex, continuously changing environments requires
assuming a specific structure, such as all decisions affecting outcomes having a
specific rate of change. Researchers assume a particular rate of change in the
environment's rules and train agents to work within those constraints by rewarding
those that stay within the expected range of outcomes. To account for possible
discrepancies between predicted and actual results due to unpredictable events,
agents are trained to consider various possible outcomes and adjust their approach
accordingly. When events go beyond expected results, agents are designed to
predict a range of possible outcomes based on past data and aim for a specific
outcome: maximizing the expected return on investment. Our approach aligns with
researchers' intuition that agents should not explore beyond predicted results
when making decisions, while incorporating the possibility of changing reward
functions. Our results show significant improvements in learning and adaptation
when incorporating the assumption of specific rate of change in comparison to more
general approaches, such as training agents to minimize expected loss without any
constraints on decision-making.

Recent studies have demonstrated that the ventral temporal cortex (VTC) processes objects with varying degrees of animacy. This has led to two possible explanations for this trend: one hypothesis suggests that animacy is attributed to the presence of specific neurofeatures, such as parts commonly found in images of animals, that evoke a sense of life-like characteristics. An alternative theory proposes that the neurofeatures themselves, like characteristics of objects, are arranged hierarchically, with more complex features like eyes and limbs indicating higher animacy levels. We sought to assess these theories by analyzing the functional organization of neurofeatures in VTC, using an experiment where participants provided animacy ratings and researchers performed a functional magnetic resonance imaging analysis to identify the regions responsible for recognizing neurofeatures. We discovered that specific VTC regions, corresponding to different neurofeatures, were activated during the processing of stimuli and that these regions correlated with the degree of animacy as measured by the part-based theory. Furthermore, we found that neurofeatures were recognized across different regions of VTC, with more complex features like eyes and limbs indicating higher animacy levels. This suggests that the animacy continuum in VTC is best explained by a combination of both theories, with distinct regions of VTC recognizing core and more complex neurofeatures.

In scientific simulation, achieving accurate replication of real-world scenarios is a primary concern, but in certain situations, the data being simulated contains significant errors, applying an inaccurate model would only amplify these flaws. To address this challenge, we've developed adaptive mesh refinement (AMR), a system that dynamically reallocate computational resources to areas requiring more precise resolution in order to yield better outcomes. By utilizing concentration profiles and temperature distributions as key example targets, we've devised approaches both without and with additional constraints to refine the mesh, exploring various time and spatial discretization methods in conjunction with second-order finite element solvers. Although our findings suggest that high-order discretization offers greater precision, we've also observed that highly inaccurate base models can actually cause AMR techniques to produce more severe errors than using these models alone, resulting in output data that is significantly further away from the accurate solution, a phenomenon known as the noose effect.

Quasi-periodic oscillations type C, typically observed in low-hard and hard-intermediate states of black hole X-ray transients, have been investigated using the MAXI J1535-571 data collected by Insight-HXMT. By applying a novel time-dependent Comptonization model and a relativistic reflection model, researchers have analyzed how variations in the corona size and sub-keV photon index influence the oscillations. A study using this approach revealed distinct patterns in the oscillation properties as the corona size changed. Comparing these results with the hard-intermediate state observations suggested that the characteristic frequencies of oscillations could be correlated with the black hole mass and torque applied by the accretion disk, while another observation could be explained by the presence of hybrid states. Furthermore, these findings differ from previously reported properties in low-hard and soft-intermediate states.

In the context of multi-agent reinforcement learning for cooperative tasks, existing approaches have several key shortcomings, including the challenge of achieving optimal results in diverse situations and the issue of agents developing inequitable representations that may not generalize well to other agents. This inequity can result in agents having unique "styles" of behavior that can make the learning process inconsistent, or at the very least, agents may not have a preferred partner for training data, which can lead to agents having a piecewise learning curve and thus a brittle system. To tackle these issues, researchers proposed a novel framework called Situational MARL for cooperative settings. This framework aims to ensure agents can learn effectively in various situations and can share equally in the learning process without conflict. A novel architecture, called Situational Neural Architecture Search (SNAS), is introduced to create a unified neural architecture for use in a shared neural network, and another architecture, called SNAS+ (SNAS-), is proposed to create individual neural architectures for each agent. Additionally, researchers have created a novel architecture, called Dual-SNAS, to create a unified neural architecture for use in a shared neural network, and another architecture, that allows agents to have their own neural architecture, that is different from the rest of the group. To further enhance the learning process, researchers have a method to create a shared neural network, that is trained as one, and another method, that allows agents to have their own neural architecture, that is trained as one.

We introduce MatSim, a comprehensive, desktop-optimized system for visual material recognition. MatSim uniquely combines the capabilities of computer vision and material recognition, enabling users to apply a wide range of materials, such as textures, hardscapes, and stones. Through our system, users can create 3D simulations, visualize various materials, and generate real-world surfaces by specifying an material appearance and a 3D geometry. Our contributions include (i) a novel material recognition dataset named MatData, (ii) a versatile model named MatCNN that outperforms state-of-the-art material recognition methods, and (iii) the MatSim system, which allows users to simulate materials and comes with pre-trained models and the MatData dataset. Our system can be accessed at matsim.io.

Two equivalent formulations of Lie 2-algebras are recalled: one as a categorification of Lie algebras and another as 2-term L∞-algebras. The paper demonstrates that certain subcategories of Lie 2-algebras can be viewed as true generalizations of Lie algebras by categorifying their key properties. The different types of Lie 2-algebras are characterized by the type of 2-term chain complex used for cohomology calculations. The concept of a strict Lie 2-algebra is also introduced and its strictness compared with 2-term L∞-algebras and quantum Lie algebras is explored. The paper defines the strict Lie 2-algebra as a specific type of Lie 2-algebra whose cochain complex allows for a strict representation of the Lie 2-algebra structure. The strictness of Lie 2-algebras is comparable to that of 2-term L∞-algebras and quantum Lie algebras in that they all share a similar strict representation. The strict Lie 2-algebra concept enables the creation of a quantum analog of its associated 2-cochain complex.

We introduce a novel method for local image feature matching, where instead of a sequential process, we first identify pixel-wise dense matches at a basic level and refine the good matches at a detailed level. In contrast to other dense methods, we leverage self and cross attention mechanisms in the Transformer model to derive feature descriptors that are context-dependent for both images. This approach allows our method, known as LoFTR, to effectively find dense matches in low-texture regions where traditional detectors face difficulties. Experiment results on indoor and outdoor datasets demonstrate that LoFTR surpasses the current state-of-the-art dense methods and top-ranked image feature detectors, and in addition to dense matching, we demonstrate that it can also serve as a detailed detector by combining it with existing task-targeted optimization techniques and it notably outperforms the current top detailed detectors.

The paper addresses the problem of bias in vector magnetic field discontinuities resulting from the cancellation of components along the line-of-sight. It suggests combining the Zeeman effect and the magneto-optical effect to determine the component perpendicular to the line-of-sight. Additionally, the paper outlines a strategy to eliminate discontinuities caused by the cancellation and identifies the necessary conditions for the representation of the magnetic field.

A fair and effective pricing model can efficiently shift consumers' energy usage during peak hours. To achieve this, a dynamic pricing mechanism was introduced and applied to a consumer group over a specified time period. The proposed method calculates the total cost based on the current and past consumption levels, ensuring that consumers adjust their consumption patterns accordingly. Experimental results demonstrate that the suggested pricing model successfully prompts consumers to reduce energy usage during peak hours and increases revenue for service providers. Notably, the model also facilitates the recovery of service providers' expenses within a predetermined time frame.

The generalized form of the Einstein theory, the Rastall theory of gravity, incorporates the law of conservation of energy and momentum. We derive a charged black string solution using the Newman-Janis approach in a Rastall theory background. Next, we investigate thermodynamic properties, such as Hawking temperature, for these black strings and study their graphical representations with respect to event horizons. Additionally, we examine the impact of Rastall theory on Hawking temperature and assess the charged black string stability. Furthermore, taking quantum gravity effects into account, we investigate modified Hawking temperatures. We also explore the physical nature of these black strings by analyzing Noether charges, which demonstrate that all charges decay at the singularity.

The results demonstrate that the power-law decay rates found in von Neumann's Ergodic Theorem for discrete systems directly correspond to pointwise scaling rates of a spectral measure with a spectral value of one. Moreover, assuming weak convergence, when no spectral gap is present, the convergence rates of the time-average in von Neumann's Ergodic Theorem rely on sequences of infinite time as they tend to infinity.

The research on extremely old and metal-poor stars within our Galaxy is instrumental in grasping its chemical evolution and the formation of stars. Focusing on the most ancient and pristine metal-poor stars, our study aims to determine their ages with high accuracy by utilizing parallax measurements from Gaia EDR3 and near-infrared fluxes from 2MASS/K2. Utilizing these data, we obtained highly precise stellar radii through transit observations by TESS and Kepl. Furthermore, we established a relationship between Gaia EDR3's distance and parallax measurements from the OGLE-IV LMC dataset to correct their relationship prior to their publication in APOGEE. Using near-infrared flux, we corrected Gaia EDR3's photometry for 134 metal-poor stars. Subsequently, we restricted the list to only those with high-precision Gaia parallax measurements. Following this step, we applied certain criteria leading to the selection of 63 metal-poor stars. Based on near-infrared flux, we corrected their 3.6 μm flux and calculated their bolometric luminosity, and subsequently their mass, along with other parameters, utilizing an empirical relationship. Applying certain criteria leading to the selection of seven stars, our study provides highly precise metallicity, temperature, and surface gravity measurements. Alongside these measurements, our study determines their ages based on isochronous fits. Consequently, our study provides the most accurate determination of the ages of these

This research investigates geographical variations in the duration of annual fire seasons worldwide. Initially, it's demonstrated that the majority of global regions experience fire seasons lasting no longer than twelve months. By employing principal component analysis on daily fire detection data, the study obtains a comprehensive view of global burning patterns. Subsequently, the analysis focuses on each fire event, comparing its start date with the typical fire season start date, thus determining the duration of each fire season. The research then examines how the duration of fire seasons varies over time, finding that they generally shorten, especially in regions near the equator. By dividing the world into six regions and analyzing their trends, the study finds that the southern hemisphere and regions near the equator exhibit the most pronounced shortening of fire seasons. Overall, the study highlights the need for a flexible framework to capture variability in the duration of fire seasons worldwide.

We've conducted a thorough examination of eight distinct methods for evaluating the morphological intricacy of languages. These measures have been computed for 85 languages, covering a wide range of genetic and areal categories. To compare the methods, we applied principal component analysis. The data shows that primary principal components closely resemble the individual measures. This suggests that the methods are not highly correlated with one another. When we combined the measures into higher principal components, certain patterns emerged. Notably, phenotypic complexity and complexity indices related to word length are highly correlated with the second principal component, while typological complexity is closely associated with the third principal component. Meanwhile, phonetic complexity stands out as an outlier, as it is least correlated with the principal components. This study aims to contribute to ongoing debates about the relationship between morphological complexity and other linguistic aspects.

Researchers at Meneghetti et al. 2018 discovered early type galaxies possess numerous substructures, which increasingly deviate from cold dark matter predictions.  To address this discrepancy, we examine whether self-interacting dark matter can account for the observed substructure density in early-type galaxies.  To this end, we have generated a sample of dark matter halo profiles using Orp fast-potential approximations for various mass ratios of baryonic matter to dark matter.  We then compared these results to existing observations from the SLICS project and found that early-type galaxies are best explained by setting $\alpha=1.43\pm0.55$ for dark matter interaction cross-sections above $10^{-10}\,\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-1}}$.  Our study indicates that self-interacting dark matter may be responsible for the observed abundance of substructures in early-type galaxies, especially if we exclude the lowest cross-section values due to artificial enhancement.  However, our findings do not rule out potential effects from other factors like interactions between baryons and dark matter or the impact of dynamical friction on satellite galaxies.

This research focuses on reducing the models of parametric partial differential equations (PPDEs) through the selection of an optimal approximation space within a predetermined set of possible solutions. Two key sources of information, one providing information on the average behavior in a specific range of parameters and another offering information on the approximate solution's accuracy at various parameter values, are incorporated into the model. By efficiently combining these sources of information, the proposed method yields an effective reduction of the associated PPDE models. Although the approach assumes access to the equations' solutions, a simple approximation technique is offered as a substitute when full access is not available. This replacement involves approximating the solutions using a Monte Carlo method. To validate the method's performance and efficiency in approximating solutions of stochastic partial differential equations (SPDEs), comprehensive numerical experiments have been conducted and analyzed.

This research introduces the m-arcsine-based (m-ar-K-) variant of the fast independent component analysis (fast ICA) method to extract features from incomplete and stochastic data. Building on the original fast ICA algorithm, our approach incorporates a unique non-linear activation function to facilitate feature selection. Unlike existing activation functions, the m-ar-K activation function is designed to accommodate data with both random and missing components, enabling it to perform well in uncertain environments. Moreover, this activation function can be modified to incorporate prior knowledge, further enhancing the reliability of the extracted features. Experimental results demonstrate that the m-ar-K-fast ICA method outperforms comparable activation functions under uncertain conditions, particularly in situations where data is partially missing or randomly distributed.

Identifying trending social media events in real-time is crucial for activation, awareness, and humanitarian purposes. Various events can be detected through social media streams, for instance, natural disasters like wildfires, terrorism, accidents, and sports events. Our innovative approach tackles the challenge of distinguishing between different types of events occurring on social media across diverse geographical locations. We developed an improvement on the existing algorithms as well as a novel algorithm that leverages which event type is occurring. Our experiments using real-world data streams demonstrate that both systems successfully differentiate between distinct events whereas the baseline techniques do not.

We establish the optimal Lipschitz regularity of very weak solutions to the elliptic Monge-Amp\`ero equation $\log det(\nabla \eta) = f$. This result specifically improves upon a previously established, suboptimal regularity by Evans and Ghang, and is derived using a novel approach of high-order modulated energy analysis. Our findings also address the initial value problem of the Monge-Amp\`ero equation, and highlight a crucial incompatibility between very weak and strong solutions with respect to initial data.

Advanced permanent magnets made from rare earth and transition metal alloys achieve high magnetization due to high transition metal content, typically found in the alloy's γ-phase. By using computational thermodynamics and magnetodynamics to study phase diagrams and magnetic properties of (Fe$_{0.85}$M$_{0.15}$)$_{1-x}$Co$_x$ and (Fe$_{0.85}$M$_{0.15}$)$_{1-x}$Co$_{x+0.03}$ systems, where M represents Ni, Cu, or Ag, we evaluate the effect of these metals on magnetization. These alloys have a broader metastable γ-phase range, allowing high Co content at higher temperatures. By examining 72- and 96-element compositions, we analyze their stability at 1000 K and find that most metastable γ-phase ranges increase with temperature. Notably, metastable γ-phase ranges expand with increasing M content, especially for Ag, indicating more stable alloys at higher temperatures. By applying the Kim-Kim-Sakai theory, we determine the temperature dependence of the γ-phase's critical chemical composition and compare it to thermodynamic predictions. These simulations reveal that higher transition temperatures and increased M content contribute to greater Co enrichment within the γ-phase. Consequently, alloys containing Ag have significantly higher Co enrichment, resulting in enhanced magnetization and magnet strength. By applying the Kim-Kim-Sakai theory, we determine the γ-phase's critical chemical composition and magnetization

In the field of display advertising, buyers participate in auctions for online ad spots, placing bids in an optimal price per impression to achieve their goals. We call an algorithm beneficial if it maximizes expected value for any type of risk preference. This paper explores the connection between the Level-K thinking bidding strategy and various risk preferences. Level-K thinking represents a method of bidding decision-making, in which the user takes into consideration the potential thinking level of other bidders. Our main contribution is the development of a theoretical framework for analyzing a single bidder's Level-K thinking strategy across various scenarios. Experimental results on a dataset show that Level-K thinking based bidding outperforms traditional bid price methods in achieving revenue. This finding validates the practical application of our proposed bidding approach.

Nonclassical properties such as quantum correlation and nonlocality can manifest in different ways when a quantum state is shared by multiple parties. We investigate how these phenomena arise from the nonclassical nature of the conditional state when one party performs specific measurements. It is found that quantum steering leads to the creation of Wigner negativity. Additionally, we identify conditions under which correlation and nonlocality can coexist. This research sheds light on the mechanisms driving nonclassical phenomena in conditional states and highlights their distinct causes.

Accurate secure boundary analysis is crucial for practical quantum key distribution systems, but the current approach overlooks a critical aspect – the randomness consistency of seeds used in privacy amplification. We introduce and prove a quantum leftover hash lemma that applies to non-uniform random seeds, leveraging min-entropy, and subsequently establish a detailed, precise QKD secure boundary analysis. Utilizing the two-decoy BB84 protocol, we simulate the effect of random seed uniformity on the secure boundary of a QKD system. Experimental results show that when the average min-entropy of the random generator drops below 0.95, a collective attack on the QKD system can breach its security.

This research paper confirms that certain types of curves, specifically those in higher dimensional space, do not fit the classification of Bertrand curves except in two-dimensional Euclidean space. A new classification system for curves in n-dimensional space is introduced, categorizing those with a constant speed or accelerating in a specific directional dimension as well as curves experiencing changing acceleration in that dimension. The investigation also revealed a distinctive property of a specific type of curve, known as the timelike Bertrand curve, where the rate of acceleration in a particular dimension is consistently zero. As a result, only timelike Bertrand curves in four-dimensional space match the criteria for a specific type of curve, known as the spacelike helix, where a consistent rate of acceleration in a particular dimension is observed. The investigation further identified a distinct characteristic of a specific type of curve, known as the null Bertrand curve, where a consistent rate of acceleration in a particular dimension is observed, except in three-dimensional space, where alternative definitions can be applied. The research also revealed a distinct characteristic of a specific type of curve, known as the focal curve, where a consistent rate of acceleration in a particular dimension is observed, except in three-dimensional space, where alternative definitions can be applied.

We'll examine the diffusion process described by the equation $u_t(t, x) =
\tfrac{1}{2}\{x u(t, x)\}_{xx} - \alpha \{x u(t, x)\}_{x}$, which is a model
for the population $u(t, x)$ of species at time $t$ and on the spatial
location $x$. This diffusion model was originally proposed by Feller in the
1950s to model a population where the growth rate varies based on the product
of the population size and the location, a model that has been further explored
by Bicout and Déniau and more recently by Sussmann. Our work builds on their findings
as we analyze the diffusion process in a bounded area under various boundary
conditions, and we conclude by outlining a general framework for diffusion
processes in bounded areas.

In this work, we explore diagrammatic methods in waveguide QED systems with a particular focus on systems utilizing delayed coherent quantum feedback. By using a specific form of vertex functions tailored to $N$-photon scattering problems, we demonstrate that it's possible to tackle complex multi-photon scattering issues in systems with multiple resonators with varied coupling strengths. The incorporation of time-delayed feedback allows us to address problems that would be intractable in unbounded systems, with one notable example being the determination of scattering matrix spectra in systems with strong coupling and multiple photons. However, it becomes evident that applying these methods relies heavily on computational tools due to the exponentially increasing complexity of diagrams with increasing photon numbers. With that in mind, we analyze a scattering problem that can be solved exactly in an unbounded system, namely the case of two-photon scattering, and observe how the incorporation of time-delayed feedback alters the dispersion relation of the scattering matrix, providing a specific parameter range where the system behaves similarly to its free-space counterpart, but also reveals parameters where the system behaves dissipation-enhanced or dissipation-suppressed.

A potential way to study low-mass dark matter is by utilizing boosted dark matter interactions. The framework for light dark matter interactions especially considers the properties of the dark matter target. We have developed new models that describe the structure factor of proton targets under specific conditions. The research reveals the significance of the time component in the proton structure factor at the level relevant for boosted dark matter interactions. Unlike previous use of this structure factor in analyzing neutron targets, the time component is now the dominant characteristic. Consequences of our observations include potential enhancements in event rates for specific experimental setups, such as PPO and EDE, with significant reductions in background suppression requirements. The boosted dark matter approach can significantly expand the reach of experimental detection, especially for the LUX-Zeplin and XENON1T experiments.
This note employs Faulhaber's Formula to elucidate why odd Bernoulli numbers equate to zero.

Continuous phase modulation detection using conventional differential detection techniques is highly resistant to various channel disturbances, such as phase and Doppler shift. Its basic structure makes its implementation uncomplicated, involving the multiplication of a received signal with a time-shifted version of one of the transmitted symbols' branches. In this paper, an innovative approach based on conventional differential detection is introduced to accommodate various phase shifts and delay variations. This new method relies on matching the received signal's phase and amplitude to a stored version of the transmitted symbols' phase and amplitude, which are recalled through a maximum likelihood memory search. Notably, the innovative approach outperforms traditional differential detection and matched filter detection under conditions involving significant delay variations, while producing comparable or superior performance in scenarios with varying phase shifts. However, the innovative approach's implementation can be quite complex, requiring a substantial memory capacity to store an extensive number of possible phase and amplitude combinations, which can be particularly restrictive in real-time systems with limited resources. A reduction in memory requirements can be achieved by only considering valid and relevant phase and amplitude combinations based on an estimation of delay variations. This specific adaptation of the innovative approach is referred to as the validated ML memory search. The validated ML memory search achieves this reduction in memory requirements by initially discarding an invalid set of received signal phase and amplitude values based on an estimation of delay delay variation. The removal of these invalid values leads to a significant decrease in the memory requirements needed for the innovative approach. Notably, the validated ML memory search is

A prominent paradigm in reward learning utilizes human feedback via comparative evaluations, but their broader adoption is hindered by the expense and labor intensity of these comparisons. To overcome this limitation, we propose grouping multiple comparisons together and allowing human labelers to mark sub-regions of a condensed state space representation, rather than individual states. Through both user studies and experiments designed to mimic real-world tasks, we have found that this enhanced feedback method results in improved learning outcomes with reduced human labor costs, enabling tasks to be completed within 10 minutes as opposed to the 30 minutes required by the traditional method. Our findings suggest that this optimized feedback process effectively simulates comparative feedback, enabling agents to learn from their preferences without needing to examine every state.

We're exploring nucleon structure functions within a $1+1$ lattice QCD setup, focusing on the u and d quark contributions, under the context of a symmetric lattice. Our study involves evaluating the nucleon matrix elements of various non-perturbative, finite-volume lattice operators, aimed at validating the strategy. Additionally, preliminary results of nucleon structure functions, derived using the discrete momentum space technique, have been presented and compared with their perturbative counterparts.

In typical topological systems, significant disruptions trigger a phase shift, but we have developed an adjustable version of the Toric code that remains stable under external disturbances except for when extremely specific conditions are met, allowing for resistance against random disturbances and gradual phase transitions triggered by specific targeted adjustments.

For large Hermitian matrices of complex numbers with specific constraints on their diagonal elements, we establish a fundamental theorem. It demonstrates that the statistical properties of their eigenvalues conform to those of the Gaussian Unitary Ensemble, provided the bandwidth increases faster than the square root of the matrix's size. This finding encompasses real symmetric matrices at its most general form.

Recent advancements in dialogue tasks have been achieved through pre-trained language models. However, models reliant on surface-level dialogue text struggle to comprehend dialogue context, particularly in extracting the underlying semantic meaning. In an effort to bridge this knowledge gap, we introduce the use of Abstract Meaning Representation as a means of pre-training language models with explicit semantic information, which captures the essence of dialogue during the pre-training phase. Building upon the standard pre-training framework, we formulate a semantic-based pre-training approach that includes three key tasks: learning core semantic units, semantic relations, and overall sentence representation. Empirical results from the analysis of explicit semantic representations indicate that our proposed model successfully learns core semantic units and relation patterns. Furthermore, we established a new baseline through pre-training on the complete Abstract Meaning Representation dataset, demonstrating substantial gains on the specific task of intrinse context-aware dialogue understanding.

To establish trust and ensure fairness, as well as hold developers accountable, algorithmic interpretability must be measured. This study draws on principles from programming languages and learning theory to establish a comprehensive framework for assessing interpretability. This proposed method captures the essence of how a person learns an algorithm, and through rigorous evaluation, we prove its advantages in four key areas - it applies universally, can be computed easily, yields distinct results, and accurately tracks increasing complexity. By presenting the framework through a hypothetical scenario and elaborating its foundational concepts, we highlight the practical applications of this measurement tool, notably for those responsible for choosing between algorithms based on their merits.

Anomaly detection without labeled data is an increasingly significant challenge due to the advantages offered by unsupervised methods in large-scale applications. However, conventional unsupervised anomaly detection techniques struggle to meet the requirements of complex datasets. To address this issue, we present a novel weakly supervised anomaly detection approach that leverages augmented data generated using a variety of techniques, without requiring any data labeling. We develop an unsupervised loss function based on weak supervision methods and apply it to deep learning models. The efficacy of this approach is evaluated on multiple datasets using different types of weak supervision and augmented strategies, demonstrating its superiority over state-of-the-art unsupervised anomaly detection methods.

A common technique used to model extreme events faces an issue related to the estimation of model parameters. The traditional method involves using data from extreme events, but this approach often suffers from a lack of data points, making the estimation less reliable. To overcome this limitation, we employ a novel strategy that allows us to estimate parameters without relying on extreme data points by instead minimizing the difference between the model's predictions and historical event data. The proposed method also has the benefit of producing threshold-agnostic parameters, which is not common in similar models. Through a simulation study and case applications that involve flood events in Germany and Finnsburge skie tumbles in the US, we demonstrate that the proposed model offers improved performance compared to other models, and the parameters can be interpreted as measures of scale and location. Moreover, we validate the model's accuracy by verifying that the predicted tail probabilities adhere to the power-law distribution, as demonstrated in the case studies.

This analysis addresses the challenge of optimizing cross-sectional area through a specific point within a geometric form. To generalize this concept, the approach is expanded across multiple dimensions. In a simplified context, the objective is to maximize the cross-sectional area along a fixed axis within a 3D volume, subject to constraints defined by polynomial equations. It is established that generating functions, initially developed for volume optimization, are also applicable to this cross-sectional optimization problem under the same constraint. Additionally, the findings are extended to higher dimensional spaces, and it is observed that the critical hyper-volume must be maximized alongside corresponding cross-sectional areas. In a broader context, the approach is applied to constrain geometric structures within both general and high-dimensional spaces, where the problem is reformulated as an integrable system and solved using the properties of algebraic geometry. Multiple solutions are derived via the properties of the A-hypergeometric differential equation and the equation for elliptic curves. Notably, the findings reveal a connection between four-dimensional self-dual alpha-functions.

A substantial understanding of everyday knowledge can be acquired through a comprehensive and annotated graph of commonsense knowledge, which can then be utilized for language understanding. The current prevalent graph, ConceptNet, exhibits a significant drawback with an excessive number of spurious statements due to a lack of filtering, resulting in poor performance in related language understanding tasks. This study introduces a new ConceptNet-derived graph, SnoNet, which is created by applying filtering criteria, including frequency of occurrence and independence from other ConceptNet statements. In contrast to the original ConceptNet, SnoNet significantly outperforms in both language understanding and knowledge retrieval tasks. SnoNet has been made publicly available on https://github/snochta/ConceptNet-SnoNet.

We introduce the data processing pipeline developed for the Hi-GAL survey. This critical component is an integral part of the Herschel satellite project that's mapping the Galactic plane's inner regions. Leveraging a combination of Herschel Interactive Standard Environment capabilities and new, custom-designed tools, our pipeline effectively handles data reduction tasks. These include accurate data filtering, noise assessment, and efficient data compactification. To facilitate Hi-GAL-specific requirements, our pipeline incorporates custom noise modeling based on the scan speed and instrument characteristics. This modeling, along with other data processing algorithms, enables the calculation of noise standard deviations in various data formats. This processing pipeline produced reduced Hi-GAL data used for the First Look Survey and future release datasets. It's also compatible with the HiStar tool used for interactive data reduction and analysis.

Recent photometric studies of the first population stars within the galactic globular clusters revealed evidence of an abundance gradient, linked to an internal gradient in the galactic gas content. Notably, red giant stars within these clusters exhibit a correlation between iron content and horizontal position in color-magnitude diagrams, as well as internal internal variations in iron abundance. A comparison of the galactic gas internal variations as predicted through 3D galactic potencial reconstructions showed a strong connection to photometric data for the clusters IC 4496, NGC 1851, NGC 2298, NGC 3202, NGC 362, NGC 5286, NGC 5139, NGC 5053 and NGC 6103. However predictions for NGC 1851, NGC 3202, NGC 362, NGC 5053 and NGC 6103 based on single epoch data from VLT-FLAMES data found them having lower iron abundance compared with predicted values. Furthermore, predicted and observed galactic gas patterns for NGC 1851, NGC 3202, NGC 362 and NGC 6103 showed a strong connection. However predicted and observed galactic gas patterns for NGC 5053 and NGC 5139 showed a strong disconnect. To facilitate a deeper understanding of one-dimensional physical systems, we consider a simplified single file model. We derive an analytical solution for the complete first exit time statistics of an overdamped single file with absorbing boundary conditions, after which we apply these findings to investigate the speed-accuracy relationship, examining how this property is influenced by the mean squared displacement and the entropic repulsive forces within the system.

Quantum Mechanics contradicts the universally assumed, classical cause-and-effect relationship established by Bayes' rule in physics. While believed to hold for all processes, Bayes' rule leads to inconsistencies in Quantum Mechanics when applied to certain situations such as Frauchiger-Renner paradox. Similar issues also occur in the Hardy setup, despite treating Quantum Mechanics as a non-local theory. To resolve these inconsistencies, an input-output causal relation, based on a modified version called quantum Bayes' rule, is introduced, applicable to quantum processes including coherent superpositions and nonlocal correlations. Quantum Bayes' rule enables the resolution of the Frauchiger-Renner and Hardy paradoxes and clarifies the quantum limitations of logical arguments.

We initially report findings regarding corrections to system size for the state equation, trace anomaly, and speed of sound, using two specific theoretical frameworks: a model for massless scalar fields and another based on quenched QCD, both applying periodic boundary conditions. Additionally, we share ongoing results involving the application of Dirichlet boundary conditions to quenched QCD.
