As the information and communication technologies advance, security and trust become crucial for seamless data exchange between devices. With a massive number of participating devices, conventional security methods used in the Internet of Things are inconsistent, which raises security and privacy concerns. To address this issue, a novel conventional, lightweight, efficient, secure, reliable, and transparent multi-factor authentication algorithm for smart devices has been introduced. This approach uses shared keys to ensure secure communication. Performance evaluation through computational metrics showed that this algorithm outperforms existing similar algorithms.

The Ramsey sequence serves as a prime illustration of quantum phase measurement for a spin qubit under a time-varying, single-tone magnetic field.  Despite being a foundational tool in atomic spectroscopy, the efficiency of measurements can be optimized through analysis of post-measurement state collapse.  By developing an analytical model of the Ramsey measurement, including state collapse following projective measurement at arbitrary time t < T, researchers can identify the optimal measurement time, leading to enhanced fidelity.  Employing spin qubits in different materials proves to be beneficial, with results indicating that measuring at the correct Ramsey point can yield significant gains in F_ramsey, up to 20% for phosphorus qubits compared to 12% for quantum dots in semiconductor materials.  The research further reveals that making use of a Bell Stern-Gerlach measurement prior to projection can achieve an extra 5% gain in F_ramsey for qubits in GaAs, while offering non-trivial noise robustness due to its insensitivity to local noise.

Network centrality metrics quantify node importance using various geometric and diffusive characteristics, focusing on distinct scales. From a geometric perspective, a multi-scale centrality is defined by a node's tendency to lie close to shortest paths within its surrounding area. The Gromov centrality metric measures importance at different network scales based on the size of the neighborhood and recovers well-known metrics as limiting cases. It is demonstrated that the Gromov centrality is sensitive to geometric and boundary constraints of the network, reflecting the excess relative to the triangle inequality. Additionally, a multi-scale centrality for communities within a network is proposed, aiming to contribute to the understanding of geometric and diffusive characteristics. The Gromov centrality for communities focuses on their geometric properties, aiming to capture various diffusion-based centrality metrics. It is shown that the community-based Gromov centrality captures effective geometric properties of the modularity matrix and the scaling behavior near the transition point between community structures and ergodicity. The proposed approach facilitates a geometric interpretation of centrality metrics and diffusion-based systems, providing a novel understanding of static and dynamic characteristics.

A closed form expression for the orbital elements of an imaginary system consisting of two bodies linked by a common axis has been derived using Lagrange's formalism. This new finding provides a direct link between the characteristics of a spinning (rotating) planet and the orbital behavior of its companion, potentially offering an explanation for the equatorial bulge observed in Mercury and other planets. Significantly, this new formulation allows a straightforward calculation of key parameters such as the orbital distance, eccentricity, and mass ratio for systems influenced by a spinning (rotating) planet. To validate this new model, a comprehensive analysis was conducted to determine its resilience in the face of varying parameters. This new formulation has been engineered to be compatible with a range of scenarios, including cases where the parameters of the system may not adhere to conventional requirements. Specifically, this new formulation allows a straightforward adaptation to systems where the masses of the bodies may differ significantly from one another, yet still display symmetrical behavior.

Sets of matrix pencils sharing the same Kronecker canonical form are classified under strict equivalence into infinite groups called bundles. Introduced in the 1990s, this concept is an extension of the earlier idea by Arnold in 1971, relating to matrices under similarity transformations. Despite substantial research on the topology of bundles of matrix pencils, some key challenges persist when dealing with bundles of matrix polynomials. Recent breakthroughs, particularly in [Kostov2021], have successfully transposed the theory of bundles of matrix pencils to complex bundles of matrix polynomials under symbolic equivalence, leading to the development of a coherent methodology for studying such complex bundles. This paper demonstrates that this methodology is applicable to more general bundles formed from matrix polynomials under strict equivalence, and that the basic properties of bundles with trivial components have been preserved in this generalized context.

The $C^*$-algebra formalism of topological T-duality developed by Mathai and Rosenberg is applied to a broad class of topological spaces that can be modeled on certain almost abelian solvmanifolds, ultimately providing a commutative $C^*$-algebra description that facilitates T-duality. A commutative algebra description is presented that incorporates the T-duality transformation in a compactified form, effectively eliminating duality invertibility issues encountered with the original $C^*$-algebra description of non-compact manifolds. A compact, formal Duke-algebra description of non-compact solvmanifolds is established, demonstrating that the T-duality transformation in a solvmanifold can be expressed through a sequence of algebra operations. These findings are further supported by the construction of non-trivial elements within the dual algebra representing the T-duality transformation. A comprehensive study of the invertibility of the T-duality transformation in solvmanifolds is provided, ultimately revealing that specific conditions regarding the compactness of the manifold and its geometric properties are required to ensure the invertibility of the transformation. These conditions are found to be met in a broad class of torus bundles, ultimately leading to the establishment of T-duality invariant characteristics based on the $C^*$-algebra description. These findings are further validated by the construction of non-trivial $C^*$-algebras representing the T-duality transformation in these solv

The Steiner tree orientation conjecture proposed by Robert and Thurston remains unproven. A prior research led by Champy and A. Gyárfás introduced an embedding method that yields a treewidth-bound, specifically O(1.3^d) in d dimensions, for graphs lacking minors. Our research endeavors have resulted in a more efficient embedding technique with a significantly improved treewidth-bound of O(2^{d/2} \log 2^{d/2}) in d dimensions. This finding has further enabled us to demonstrate that minor-free graphs with a constant tree-decomposability width possess a bounded treewidth of at most 2^{\Omega(d)} in d dimensions, thereby refuting a long-standing hypothesis proposed by Dujmović et al. Our research has also led to new insights into the set cover and the oriented coloring number in minor-free graphs, allowing us to demonstrate that the oriented coloring number is bounded by 2^{\Omega(d)}, thereby disproving another long-standing hypothesis proposed by Dujmović et al. Our research has further led to the development of a new algorithm to solve the parameterized Steiner tree orientation problem in polynomial time for graphs with a constant tree-decomposability width, thereby extending the findings of Marx and Schaudt. Our parameterized Steiner tree orientation algorithm has also enabled us to develop the Steiner orientability theorem, allowing us to decrease the complexity of the tree-decomposability parameter and the size

For C1-smooth discrete-time systems exhibiting strong monotonicity, the prevailing long-term behavior of linearly stable cycles is established in a probabilistic framework. This research then extends to periodic parabolic equations and reveals new findings regarding the ubiquity of periodic solution convergence. Notably, in Neumann-bound equations defined on convex domains, the set of initial conditions corresponding to homogeneous periodic solutions is shown to be prevalent, while in radially symmetric domains, the set of radially symmetric periodic solution trajectories exhibits prevalence among initial values.

The potential of using noisy intermediate-scale quantum computers with the variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) lies in molecular simulations, where accurately generating quantum states corresponding to the molecular Hamiltonian is crucial. Since chemistry-related molecules are generally spinnless, employing fermionic-excitation evolutions over qubit-excitation evolutions may lead to more efficient state preparations. However, fermionic-excitation evolutions are based on the.engelbrecht protocol and utilize long sequences of multi-qubit gates that are highly prone to errors. In this research, the efficacy of qubit-excitation evolutions combined with the sequential substitution of fermionic-excitation gates using the.adaptive_ee protocol and the $\text Z_2\text S$ method has been evaluated in various scenarios, and it has been observed that this strategy consistently results in more precise state preparations than fermionic-excitation evolutions. Moreover, it has been observed that the efficiency of state preparations using qubit-excitation evolutions can significantly be enhanced by incorporating the $\text Z_2\text S$ method. Consequently, preparing the initial quantum state corresponding to the molecular Hamiltonian using qubit-excitation evolutions and the combined strategies turns out to be resilient to noise. Furthermore, noise resilience has been observed in the VQE algorithm when computing eigenvalues of molecules, and it has been found that using qubit-excitation evolutions in state preparations can lead to more accurate results.

A key characteristic of deep generative models is the interaction of representation, its distribution, and a neural network mapping, with techniques like variational autoencoders (VAEs) often applied, but posing significant optimization challenges. Specifically, the inclusion of an encoder introduces complexity, particularly in terms of the amortization gap and the uncertainty of the variational approximation. To address these issues, a new model, the Deep Generative Decoder (DGD), is presented, featuring a single neural network for variational approximation, thus eliminating the need for an encoder, and facilitating end-to-end training. DGD is further enhanced through the integration of a Wasserstein autoencoder (WAE)-inspired variational loss and a maximum-likelihood and maximum-variational lower bound (MML-MCL) objective, thus allowing for the utilization of standard optimization techniques. Comparative evaluations demonstrate the efficacy of DGD against VAEs and WAEs on various datasets, while the incorporation of DGD tends to enhance the performance of variational autoencoders and Wasserstein autoencoders.

The detection of a primordial stochastic gravitational-wave background (SGWB) is a key focus of the Cosmic Explorer project, an advanced gravitational-wave detector that will investigate the universe's expansion history, resolving its mysteries, and supplementing existing astronomical research. By modeling the 100-MHz SGWB's amplitude, this study utilizes the uncertainty principle to calculate the 95% confidence interval for the Cosmic Explorer's frequency-dependent strain sensitivity, and finds that the new detector will be capable of making a significant first detection of a cosmological scale SGWB, and that this will occur earlier than the detector's optimal observation period. Furthermore, with existing detector data excluded from consideration, this study assumes that the LIGO/Virgo Collaboration's O3 dataset serves as the current best estimate for the SGWB, and finds that the Cosmic Explorer will be capable of providing significant improvements in parameter estimation for binary black hole and binary neutron star mergers at higher redshifts, and that this will occur at more than two orders of magnitude lower luminosity values. Notably, with its improved sensitivity and resulting signal collection time, the Cosmic Explorer will be capable of providing a "detection quality" comparable to 20 years of LIGO's observing time at optimal settings, and will be capable of detecting signals from binary mergers out to 500 Mpc, and will be capable of detecting signals from binary mergers out to 500 Mpc.

Our study employs high-resolution spectroscopy to analyze the molecular composition within a comet's inner atmosphere. We measured the emission lines of H2O, CO, CH4, CH3OH, HCN, and NH3 originating from the inner region of comet C/2015 ER61 using the ALMA millimeter-band spectral scan. This particular observation offers a unique insight into the molecular composition in the inner coma due to ER61's slow approach to the Sun. ER61 features high H2O/CO ratios, low CH4/CO ratios, low CH3OH/CO ratios, and undetected emissions from HCO, HCS+, and NH2. By analyzing the line profiles, we found that the volatile sources diffuse into space rather than being confined to jets. In contrast, the CO emissions appear enhanced in the jet region. Furthermore, we found that the CH4 emissions are strengthened in the blue-shifted side. These analyses suggest that the molecules are released from the northern subsleeve through a non-thermal process. In the case of CO, we found evidence of a thermal mechanism linked to the jet origin. CH4 emissions are notably strengthened on the blue-shifted side. Additionally, the NH3 emissions are strengthened in the direction of the northern jet. We propose an unsupervised speech synthesis approach that relies on automatic phone segmentation, text-to-melody conversion, and pitch and energy extraction from pre-written synthesis scripts to produce raw audio without human intervention.

This research employs the Tsallis holographic dark energy model in two scenarios, 
non-interacting and interacting, to derive general expressions for pressure, energy 
density, equation of state and the slow-roll parameter for both cases. It then calculates 
key cosmological parameters such as deceleration parameter, EoS parameter, derivative 
of deceleration parameter, fractional energy density, equation of state for HDU, 
critical density threshold, derivative of critical density threshold, first turning point of 
CDT and the maximum value of f$_{TD}$ for both scenarios. In the context of a real universe, the 
fractional energy density must be less than one; if it exceeds one, the scenario does not 
accurately describe a real universe.

Multi-objective mixed-integer non-linear programming problems frequently arise in real-world contexts and demand being efficiently solved. This becomes a challenge due to varying priorities and conflicting goals which users have different levels of willingness to accommodate. A novel approach, hybridizing efficient construction heuristics and multi-objective genetic algorithms via NSGA-II, presents itself as a viable solution. This newly proposed method, referred to as BnB-NSGAII, offers a competitive alternative. Our case study compares its performance with a current state-of-the-art multi-objective multi-objective evolutionary algorithm, multi-objective ant colony, in relation to solving mixed-integer non-linear programming problems. Our case study compares its performance with a current state-of-the-art multi-objective evolutionary algorithm, multi-objective ant colony, in relation to solving mixed-integer non-linear programming problems. Results indicate that BnB-NSGAII yields better solution quality in a shorter amount of time when compared to NSGA-II. Furthermore, we analyzed the effects of varying CPU time on solution quality and found that BnB-NSGAII consistently yields more efficient results as the CPU time increases.

We refine and reinterpret the core principles of Lie theory, specifically Lie groupoids, through the lens of internal groupoids in synthetic differential geometry. Key concepts are re-expressed, incorporating new principles, and the connections between classical and refined frameworks are elucidated. It's proven that the internal Lie groupoids adhere to a Hausdorff condition if and only if their classical counterparts do, and a direct analogy has been established. Furthermore, this re-examination led to the discovery that Lie 2-groupoids can be seen as equivalent to internal 2-step Lie groupoids, providing a unified perspective that bridges various connectedness conditions.

The Dynaswap project is focused on developing a robust, trustworthy architecture for safeguarding holistic workflows in cyberinfrastructures, allowing for deployment on virtual machines via cloud services such as JetStream. This cloud platform facilitates user-friendly access to dynamic computing and data analysis tools on demand. Dynaswap's security architecture incorporates role management, hierarchical relationships, and adaptive access control to safeguard against data breaches and unauthorized changes. By integrating an automated tool for managing role-based access to sensitive data and introducing a social engineering component to its system, Dynaswap has addressed two key vulnerabilities previously exposed in the project. In this report, Dynaswap's role-based access control system is examined to evaluate its strengths and weaknesses, particularly its capacity to protect against social engineering attacks that exploit role relationships. An in-depth analysis of the underlying social engineering component reveals critical issues hindering its effectiveness and susceptibility to various types of attacks. Ultimately, this evaluation has led to the identification of multiple, critical vulnerabilities requiring immediate attention to enhance Dynaswap's overall security capabilities.

Aspect-based sentiment analysis focuses on determining the sentiment of a particular aspect within product reviews. Approximately one-third of reviews lack explicit opinion words, yet clearly convey human-aware sentiment, classified as implicit sentiment. Unfortunately, neural network-based methods have overlooked implicit sentiment in reviews. To address this, we utilize a supervised pre-training approach on extensive sentiment-annotated datasets drawn from relevant linguistic sources. By aligning implicit sentiment phrases with their matching sentiment labels, this pre-training method significantly improves the capture of both explicit and implicit sentiment orientations in reviews towards specific aspects. Our technique exhibits superior performance on the STC dataset and an established Q&A dataset, outperforming traditional baseline methods. Additionally, experiments demonstrate that our technique benefits the performance of a variety of ABA models.

We establish a method to calculate how stratified case-control design affects mediation analysis, particularly when using binary variables in the design and outcome. To address this, a novel estimator is proposed for the outcome under a given set of conditions, which is achieved through simultaneous selection of multiple factors. Furthermore, a new test is developed to assess multiple variables acting as confounding factors. The performance of the proposed estimator and test is compared to existing alternatives through simulation experiments and real-world data analysis.

This research addresses the challenge of maximizing minimal signal gain in a network of 3 users and 1 base station with an RIS-assisted communication system, subject to a constraint on maximum power at the base station and RIS elements. To achieve this goal, the problem is divided into two parts and solved using two different optimization techniques. First, the subproblem of maximizing minimal signal gain with respect to beamforming vectors is solved using a block coordinate descent technique. Second, the subproblem of optimizing phase shifts is solved using a deep learning method based on adversarial networks. A combination of these two methods allows for gradient-based optimization of deep learning and achieving better results than a standard adversarial network. A comparative study is also conducted to evaluate the performance of our proposed method against other existing techniques.

We begin by defining a task for few-shot continual learning and propose a theory to explain how executive function works through a self-updating decision-making system that reprocesses perception data through a review of past experiences in order to minimize prediction errors. This idea becomes practical due to the incorporation of a memory mechanism and a pre-trained neural network that is predisposed to follow rules of effective learning and adapts to optimize its chances of long-term success. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our model of executive function can facilitate the development of hypothesis testing as an internal reasoning process and might provide insight into observed abilities of human learning and the organization of the human brain.

We studied the solar wind energy flux near the inner edge of our solar system using data from four close-pass encounters with the sun as part of the Parker Solar Probe mission. These encounters took the spacecraft within 28.8, 27.2, 29.4, and 32.9 solar radii of the sun's center. The data we used was collected when the sun's brightness peaked during each encounter. By analyzing this data, we calculated the average energy flux at a distance of 20-30 solar radii from the sun's center, and it worked out to be around 22-23 W/m^2, with a 0.5 W/m^2 standard deviation. This estimate matches other data collected at a greater distance from the sun and it also matches our expectations based on theoretical research and past experiments, with the exception of one encounter where the energy flux was significantly higher than expected, at around 45 W/m^2.

In a noncommutative setting, where locally compact Hausdorff groups act on C*-algebras, we introduce the concept of a numerable principal bundle with quantum characteristics. This generalization involves defining a locally trivial G-C*-algebra as a noncommutative analog to the total space of a numerable principal bundle. By building upon the Pedersen ideal's multipliers, we transcend Gelfand-Naimark duality to create this framework. Additionally, when considering compact Hausdorff groups acting on unital C*-algebras, the finiteness of local truncation lengths in G-action implies that the corresponding G-C*-algebra is a unital simple C*-algebra.

We show that any family of maximal almost-disjoint sets can be eliminated via a specific method of adding new elements that preserves the cardinality of $P$-points. Using this finding, we establish that it is possible in a specific set of circumstances that the first uncountable ordinal is less than the least cardinality for uniformization, but the least cardinality for amalgamation is greater, resolving two problems that have been outstanding for nearly 20 years and a further issue proposed by Brendle. Furthermore, we will provide a simplified explanation for why it is consistent that $\mathfrak{u}<\mathfrak{s}$ as proven by Blass and Shelah.

The introduction of $q$-deformation into optomechanical systems reveals opportunities to amplify non-traditional optical phenomena. This insight drives an investigation of the optical behavior within a linearly coupled $q$-deformed optomechanical system. Composed of two deformed cavities interacting with mechanical mirrors and coupled by a transmission parameter, this study reveals that $q$-deformation can amplify or diminish (but not destroy) phase transitions that occur at $\tfrac{q^2-1}{\tfrac{q^2-1}{2}+1}$. Furthermore, the impact of $q$-deformation on tunneling and the visibility of non-local phenomena, such as optical quenching and unquenching, is observed in a wider range than in the standard optomechanical model.

In a previous study, I developed a model where the Two-Rotors Model's negative scissors states, consisting of two-sided classical bodies, exhibited 1 |K| = 1; 0 state formation due to rotation. Building on this work, a related investigation explored non-Abelian Duality Suggested by Smoluchowski's Rotation-Diffusion Equation and its Application to the Two-Rotors Model. The outcome indicated that the model's state formation could be understood from a novel, non-Abelian perspective based on quarks and gluons. The present research aims to dissect the underlying physical principles of the non-Abelian approach by analyzing the Two-Rotors Model's 1 |K| = 1; 0 state formation using a non-Abelian duality, specifically one derived from the two-dimensional hydrodynamic description of Smoluchowski's Rotation-Diffusion Equation. The focus is on identifying the range of two-body interactions necessary for the creation of 1 |K| = 1; 0 states according to this non-Abelian duality, revealing a scenario where short-range repulsion and long-range attraction can be present provided that the scattering is sufficiently weak, a condition that does not apply in the context of strong interactions.

A new method inspired by finite volume schemes leverages a cell-average based neural network. By employing a neural network to approximate the average value of a function across a spatial cell, this approach can overcome the restrictions typically limiting implicit time integration methods, such as the Beam-Wicke-Steger-Lin method. Specifically, this approach allows for a significantly larger time step, comparable to $O(\nu^{-1})$, compared to $O(\nu^{-2})$ for implicit time integration. Furthermore, this work outlines the principles of stability and provides theoretical justification for the new method. A neural network based on a specific architecture is used to demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach, focusing on the scenario where the function to be averaged is the Black-Scholes equation. By comparing the numerical results to analytical solutions as well as the performance of traditional methods, this approach showcases its potential.

The ALICE Collaboration has collected an extensive dataset during the LHC Run 2 from 2015 to 2018 for studying the production of heavy flavor hadrons and dielectron pairs with low masses. To further explore these areas of research, the ALICE Collaboration plans to utilize the ALICE 3 experiment, featuring improved detector resolution and enhanced acceptance capabilities. Specifically, several Upgrade Technical Design Reports outline advancements in the upgrade of the electron identifier, the time projection chamber, and the event builder, which include the integration of a new photon detection system for ring imaging Cherenkov setup. To better analyze the data, the ALICE Collaboration will employ a new trigger and data acquisition system. To demonstrate the ALICE 3 capabilities, the current status of various research studies on electron pairs with masses as low as 200 MeV is presented, along with future prospects for improving the precision of these measurements. These include the new data acquisition rates and reduced minimum bias cross sections resulting from the ALICE 3 upgrade. Furthermore, the potential to study the production of virtual photons at the LHC will be investigated with the ALICE 3 configuration.

The Unruh effect can emerge not only through the entanglement of left and right Rindler regions, but also between forward and backward light cones. Our analysis focuses on the geometric phase arising from this time-related entanglement between the future and past, showing that it can be effectively modelled by a $\Lambda$-system. This provides a new approach to detecting the Unruh effect, offering a different method from traditional Unruh-deWitt detectors. Due to the immense accelerations required by Unruh-deWitt detectors to trigger a response, their experimental verification remains unachieved. Conversely, we showcase that a $\Lambda$-system can exhibit a quantum jump triggered by even a single photon without necessitating extreme acceleration, thereby facilitating a potentially more feasible experimental simulation.

One of the primary objectives of Information Extraction involves recognizing event descriptions along with their related entities within a given text. This task has received significant research attention, yet efforts focused on non-English languages remain largely underrepresented due to a lack of quality datasets. To bridge this gap, we have introduced a new English dataset, IEWEB-Event-2019, containing over 37,000 annotated examples, and performed an in-depth analysis of event extraction across various languages using multiple models, while employing DistilBERT as the primary classifier. Our results indicate that the DistilBERT model achieves exceptional performance on the developed dataset, reaching a label-efficient evaluation accuracy of 90.3%. Furthermore, our study demonstrates the DistilBERT's ability to attain an average F1-score between 65% to 75% on non-English languages with limited training data as low as 500 examples, showcasing its potential for efficient task adaptation across languages.

We examine a complex manifold with a Hermitian holomorphic vector bundle and its flag bundles, coupled with their respective universal bundles, now endowed with the induced metrics. A crucial aspect of our research involves establishing the validity, pointwise in Chern forms, of the universal push-forward formula for all universal bundles. A fundamental step towards establishing this formula relies on an alternative expression for the Jacobi-Trudi identity in terms of Chern forms, a breakthrough achieved in our findings. This discovery not only provides a straightforward, elementary proof but also offers a more general, universal expression that extends the traditional notion of determinants for holomorphic line bundles. Furthermore, we utilize the established formula to derive a comprehensive expression for the push-forward of Chern forms across the Grassmannian bundle G(k, n), achieved through a deliberate choice of bundle maps, resulting in an expression independent of the chosen connection and metric. A key step in this demonstration involves constructing a bundle with Chern forms mimicking those of the tautological bundle on G(k, n), denoted as L_G. Consequently, this discovery allows us to offer an alternative, elementary proof for Weyl's bitorsion formula.

Observations from the XMM-Newton telescope revealed how a clumpy stellar wind from a companion star in high mass X-ray binaries impacts the variable absorption and timing properties of the source's X-ray emissions. We analyzed a 7.53 hour dataset from the source Cyg X-1 #3, collecting key parameters such as the source's luminosity, wind's absorption factor, and clump's cross-sectional area through fitting best models to observations. We discovered a significant correlation between the cross-sectional area and variability amplitude, growing from low to high frequencies, but broke this link when the wind's clumpy density increased, indicating that the source's short-term variability is influenced by the clumps' absorption and scattering effects, while long-term variability might be caused by the clumps' direct pressure. We verified our findings through simulations, confirming that the observed effects are unique to sources surrounded by a clumpy stellar wind.

The Yang-Mills-aether theory is analyzed to understand the implications of introducing non-abelian aether-like terms that violate Lorentz symmetry, specifically within thermal quantum field theory. By incorporating temperature effects and spatial compactification via Thermofield Dynamics, corrections to the non-abelian Stefan-Boltzmann law and non-abelian Casimir energy and pressure are calculated for both zero and finite temperatures.

Researchers have long sought to bridge the gap between syntax and semantics parsing but so far have had to make a choice between excelling in one area at the cost of the other, contradicting research highlighting the complex interactions between the two. To address this issue, we examine multiple model designs capable of tapping into rich data in the Universal Decompositional Semantics (UDS) dataset, parsing it alongside Universal Dependencies for high-performance results in both formats. Analyzing the effects of combining syntax and semantics parsing reveals patterns that are supported by linguistic theory at their interface. Moreover, we examine the effectiveness of joint modeling in multiple languages, discovering analogous trends in 8 languages tested.

The formation of magnetically-driven jets following the fusion of two black holes and a neutron star is a phenomenon that scientists have extensively researched. Yet, a fresh study presents a novel model for the evolution of a magnetically-driven outflow produced as a result of this black hole and neutron star coalescence. In this new theoretical framework, the analyst treats the spinning black hole as a uniformly magnetized, thick, disk-like structure, referred to as a "magnetized spin disk". When an extremely powerful magnetic field emanating from the magnetized spin disk comes into contact with the surrounding space, it triggers the formation of a jet that tends to align along the plane that contains the spin of the black hole and a line that joins the points where the magnetic field vanishes. In this model, the jet's motion is determined by the movement of the magnetic field lines and by the pressure produced by shock waves that form due to the breakdown of the magnetized spin disk's hydrostatic balance following the sudden decrease in the pressure produced by the magnetic field. In an attempt to validate this new theoretical framework, the analyst discovered that for a specific range of parameters, the model produces a relationship between the mass lost during the fusion of a black hole and a neutron star and the spin produced by the black hole. We utilized the Hyper-Suprime Cam to carry out a study on tidal features in a large sample of 1066 massive early-type galaxies from the Kilo-Degree Wondersim survey. The findings reveal that only 8.5% of the galaxies displayed prominent tidal features, accounting for more than 1% of their flux. For those with a stellar mass over $10^{11}$ solar masses, nearly a quarter possessed a tidal feature with a high flux ratio. Through spatially separated spectra, we detected tidal features in 17% of the galaxies, indicating they contained more than 8% of the galaxy's light. Additionally, we discovered that tidal features existed in more than half of the galaxies with multiple tidal features, where the features were mostly separated by over 30 thousand parsecs. For galaxies experiencing their first tidal feature interaction, nearly 60% exhibited a red countertourqamatic pattern, while the remainder showed green stripes. Comparing our data with mock observations, we found tidal features increased both the S\'ersic index and color gradient. Furthermore, we noticed a relationship between tidal features and galaxy environment; those in denser environments had more features, with a higher fraction of features being dominant. Using statistical tests, we concluded that at least 17% of primary tidal features and 33% of secondary tidal features originated from smaller satellites.

This paper is a part of a series exploring the Azimuthally Symmetric Theory of Gravitation (ASTG), a framework that deviates from established gravity theories such as General Relativity. Previous studies within this series have demonstrated the validity and practical applications of ASTG. This work aims to investigate whether ASTG can be utilized in conjunction with quantum mechanics to form a viable foundation for gravitation and quantum gravity. We begin with a review of ASTG's core principles and then examine Quantum Mechanics, selecting the de Broglie-Bohr model for in-depth analysis. Combining ASTG and Quantum Mechanics, we derive a mass-loss equation based on the de Broglie-Bohr model, which yields a loss rate consistent with astronomical data for low-mass stars. Furthermore, this study suggests that ASTG has the potential to eliminate the need for dark matter in specific contexts, such as galactic rotation, which is a long-standing challenge in astrophysics. This work also explores the concept of repulsive gravity in the context of ASTG, a novel aspect that has significant implications for understanding certain astrophysical phenomena. Finally, we discuss the key findings of this study in relation to General Relativity, Quantum Mechanics, gravitation, and quantum gravity within the framework of ASTG.

The connection between a historical X-ray flare and one of the brightest FRB observed so far, FRB 20121125C, has been established through simultaneous observations by the Gravitational Wave Optical Transient Observer and the CHIME/mkII telescope. Data from the Gravitational Wave Optical Transient Observer shows that pulsations continued for at least 434 seconds after the initial burst, with enhanced light emission ($\sim\Delta m_{V}\sim5.8\pm 0.4$ mag) occurring in increments of 2.8 s, matching the repeating nature of the FRB 20121125C observed by CHIME/mkII. A total of 40 optical pulses were detected during this period, with each exhibiting a similar shape to those preceding the initial burst, suggesting precursors to the FRB 20121125C event. A maximum optical flux of $\sim6.6\pm1.2$ mag was reached during these pulses, peaking at an optical flux of $19.6\pm1.2$ mag and signifying the strongest connection observed thus far between an FRB and an optical flare. Advanced laser systems produced through the application of specific technologies such as chirped pulse amplification and nonlinear optical conversion, have made a significant impact across multiple industries such as semiconductors, medicine, defense, and homeland security.  These impactful technologies include a range of laser designs each producing unique characteristics such as ultrashort pulses, high energy outputs, specific wavelength spectra, and polarized light.  In order to understand and optimize these complex laser systems, scientists utilize simulations informed by mathematical modeling and data from experimental studies.  In this study, various CPA and NLO system models are discussed along with their applicability to modeling ultrashort pulses.  A free, open-source software tool called ASP is also presented enabling users to investigate and optimize laser systems featuring ultrashort pulses.  ASP allows users to define custom CPA and NLO beam profiles, perform energy calculations, and generate desired output pulse characteristics through the manipulation of input pulse properties.  In addition, the tool supports the analysis of complex nonlinear beam interactions within NLO systems, produces visualizations aiding user interpretation, and integrates with other software and code to facilitate comprehensive modeling capabilities.

Multimodal language generation capabilities of models like GPT-2 and GPT-3 can be leveraged for producing high-quality text, but it is still uncertain how they can be directed by non-text modalities like images. We introduce MAGIC, an image-guided text generation framework, which allows a model to generate text based on an input image, by incorporating visual embeddings into its state to guide the text generation process. By experimenting with a GPT-3 model, we evaluated the effectiveness of MAGIC using two datasets and found it to outperform existing approaches in image captioning and visual question answering tasks, with the added benefit of flexibility in producing text of varying lengths and contexts. Additionally, we discovered that MAGIC can be trained on private datasets, without the need for generating visual representations or sharing data, which addresses concerns of data privacy.

We introduce an upgraded RingCT protocol that supports stealth addresses in conjunction with Delegated Proof of Stake.
The new consensus algorithm combines the benefits of energy efficiency and high throughput, which in conjunction with RingCT, promotes the privacy and scalability of decentralized cryptocurrencies.
The proposed protocol employs a transparent mixing process using a "sort-and-mix" technique within a specific time frame.
Additionally, it leverages a probabilistic mix mechanism to protect user transactions.
We also outline a reference implementation for the DRCPT protocol and present numerical analyses of its computational complexity.
Finally, we highlight key differences between our approach and the standard RingCT protocol, and discuss several potential security threats to the Delegated RingCT solution.

In 2015, CERN introduced "Emittance Scans," a new fast luminosity separation scanning method at the Large Hadron Collider. These scans were consistently carried out during physics production runs, utilizing full-intensity beams at the CMS experiment's interaction point. The emittance scans allowed for the simultaneous measurement of beam properties and closed orbits at the level of individual bunches, yielding precise insights into long-range beam-beam effects, as predicted by the improved TRAIN code.

Recent breakthroughs in artificial neural networks have accelerated the growth of data-driven modeling in molecular physics, where complex interactions and extensive data sets often necessitate the use of sophisticated neural network models.  However, a major limitation of such models has been identified in the problem of catastrophic forgetting - a phenomenon where continual learning is impeded by the neural network's inability to retain previously acquired knowledge.  In order to address this issue, research on various continuation learning techniques has been undertaken.  This study specifically evaluates the problem and explores solutions to the problem of catastrophic forgetting in the context of neural network models, focusing on applications in theoretical and physical sciences.  Continual learning techniques are categorized into non-gradient based and gradient based methods, with the latter further divided into gradient based replay, gradient based incremental learning, and gradient based neural structure learning techniques.  Both gradient based incremental learning and gradient based neural structure learning techniques, in particular, have been found to offer superior performance through gradient based approaches and data minimization strategy, respectively.  Furthermore, various reduction techniques to minimize data requirements while retaining accurate results have been discussed.  Ultimately, this study suggests potential future directions and proposes the term 'Continual Learning in the Sciences' for a broader range of applications in the physical sciences.

This research examines the decay of the $\Upsilon(10753)$ into a $\Upsilon(nS)$
state accompanied by $\pi^+\pi^-$ particles, where $n=1,2,3$. It's assumed
$\Upsilon(10753)$ belongs to a typical $n\Upsilon(10885)$ sequence. We find that
the observed branching ratios for these decays are compatible with the expected
values, but also take into account potential $b\overline{b}$-to-$D^{(*)}\pi^+\pi^-$
direct-ejector effects, which might influence end result. The direct-ejector
probability is estimated and the characteristic features of the direct-ejector
process are discussed.

This paper presents an efficient method for detecting chaos in a $N$-body system based on a Deep Neural Network that utilizes a binary quantized, per-layer fixed point arithmetic approach. To accommodate this approach, the DNN architecture employs an exponential activation function, previously used in Binary Neural Networks, and trains with respect to the time series' instantaneous phase and amplitude. Our implementation, consisting of a C code backend, has been successfully applied to a 3D billiard system and a hyperbolic system, yielding accurate results that outperform other competing methods in terms of computational efficiency. Notably, our DNN system can identify chaotic behavior up to 10 times faster than a Monte Carlo integration for the 3D billiard, and five times faster than a Gauss method in the hyperbolic system for an error of $O(10^{-6})$.

The Continuum Soft Robot project utilizes fully flexible mechanical systems to achieve robots that more closely resemble the anatomy of invertebrate creatures and flexible body parts of vertebrates. To introduce the concepts and challenges of this innovative area in robotics, we will be adopting a control theorist's approach, simplifying the entry into this field by systematically presenting current research and future obstacles through a uniform language and organized structure. The primary hurdles to participating in this area are likely the overlap of terminology from hard robotics and soft robotics, as well as the wide array of approaches used to design these robots, which hinders the sharing of knowledge among researchers. To address these challenges, we will explore various Continuum Soft Robot implementations and their corresponding control strategies, starting from a common point and building up to more complex ideas. The key intrinsic difficulties of Continuum Soft robots are their high non-linearities and significant non-stiffness, which are complicated by external factors such as unpredictable external forces and significant deformations of the robot itself, leading to a rich and dynamic control environment.

The real Jacobi group, denoted as $G^J_1(\mathbb{R})$, is a group consisting of affine transformations preserving a binary quadratic form, combining properties of $\mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbb{R})$ and the Heisenberg group. This article focuses on the geometric description of diophantine sets or diophantine filters within three-dimensional Euclidean space, determined by restrictions within the Jacobi group context. Moreover, the article examines Diophantine filters within the context of the Heisenberg group, Diophantine sets defined by $\mathbb{R}$-rational (rational in the reals) affine transformations, and Diophantine sets classified by $\mathbb{Q}$-rational (rational in the rationals) within the diophantine filters framework.

Verifying facts using structured data can be difficult, necessitating a model that accurately leverages both the data set and its underlying schema. We approach this problem by developing a graph-based unification model to easily access and process various data sets. Our model encodes the verification process as a graph unification task and employs the Graph-Based Neural Question Answering (GraphBN) framework to tackle this unification. We propose the SetGCN model, an extension of the GAT, to process both node and edge attributes using a Self-Attention mechanism. We evaluate the effectiveness of our model using the SchemaNet Fact #2B dataset and achieve state-of-the-art performance.

The state of the art in learned synthetic image generation involves generative adversarial networks. Initially, GANs were trained in an unsupervised manner, but recent research has revealed that supervised methods yield superior results. This knowledge gap highlights the benefits of supervised learning in the context of synthetic image creation. This work addresses two primary queries: Can the advantages of supervised methods be achieved through unsupervised approaches? and Are there inherent limitations in unsupervised learning that hinder synthetic image generation? To answer these questions, this paper investigates two newly-introduced unsupervised preprocessing techniques for GANs: optimization transfer and class-splitting loss. Experimental results demonstrate that while these methods may provide insights into latent space structure, they are ineffectual in producing high-quality synthetic images. Furthermore, this paper presents a theoretical explanation for why these unsupervised approaches fall short. Interestingly, experiments indicate that incorporating the class-splitting loss can exacerbate mode dropping in the resulting synthetic images. This finding contradicts the common assumption that integrating additional information would enhance visual quality.

To perform Bayesian inference using nested sampling, a specific prior sampling approach must be used, which involves selecting prior samples that meet a minimum likelihood requirement. Researchers have developed methods like Markov Chain Monte Carlo derivatives for this purpose, utilizing random walks to find high-likelihood prior samples. Although these algorithms excel in low-dimensional problems, they struggle with high-dimensional ones due to their inefficient sampling radius. To counter this, researchers have employed Bayesian optimisation-based algorithms, such as Spatio Spectral, to improve nested sampling's prior sampling method. These novel algorithms combine Bayesian optimisation techniques with spatial methods to scan the parameter space, taking into account the correlation between parameters. They also leverage secondary samples to improve the efficiency of their primary algorithms and utilize differential evolution principles to increase robustness and scalability. Moreover, introducing a warm-up phase incorporating triage and correlated sampling aims to improve the algorithms' performance across a wide range of problems. Testing showed that the new algorithms outperformed traditional Markov Chain Monte Carlo derivatives in almost all cases, specifically in finding more high-likelihood prior samples and completing runs much faster. As such, the new algorithms are recommended over their traditional counterparts for Bayesian inference tasks.

In fault-tolerant distance labelling, we're tasked with assigning brief descriptions to the points in a network so that knowing any two points' labels allows us to deduce their distance from each other. Our work focuses on this problem in graph topologies, offering an efficient labelling system for trees that can recover up to one point or edge failure. Additionally, we present a proof illustrating that some level of failure resilience is necessary.

In this research, we have explored two-particle correlations in the $1+1$ dimensional massive Thirring model, which exhibits complex phase transitions. Utilizing exact diagonalization of the finite but extensive Hamiltonian with two-valve boundary conditions, and by merging oscillating exponential terms with M\"obius function behavior, we have derived a two-particle correlation function. The frequency of these oscillations has been found to be in agreement with simulations at all stages of the phase transitions. Furthermore, the correlation function's amplitude, which displays oscillatory behavior, has been simulated at various stages of the phase transitions and during particle-antiparticle coupling up to the critical point of the model. The results also show that during particle-antiparticle coupling, the model exhibits a rapid change in the behavior of the correlation function from a fast to a slow decay rate.

For a given second-order linear elliptic equation with coefficients $A$, $\mathbf{b}$ and a parameter $\lambda$, defined within a bounded $\mathbb{R}^2$ domain $\Omega$ and satisfying specific smoothness and boundedness conditions, we establish existence and uniqueness of the weak solution in $W^{1,p}_0(\Omega)$ for the Dirichlet problem, where $2<p<\infty$, assuming that the equation also includes source and flux terms. Similar results are obtained for the corresponding dual problem under analogous conditions.

To ensure that medical imaging models produce accurate predictions, it is crucial to implement out-of-distribution detection capabilities. A significant, unsolved challenge exists in developing universal methods for detecting unnatural data, as algorithms typically fail or underperform in such situations. In this paper, three distinct optical coherence tomography data sets were utilized to train a multi-task out-of-distribution detection model specifically designed for detecting data manipulation. The model, which incorporates multiple signal processing techniques, has demonstrated remarkable performance in identifying artificially manipulated data from a trained data set while also successfully handling real-world out-of-distribution scenarios. The model's success highlights the potential benefits of multi-task learning and data-driven approaches in creating robust detection systems. Additionally, this study demonstrates the effectiveness of a data manipulation detection model trained on retinal images to predict retinal fluid, layer boundaries, and surface characteristics. Notably, this model has shown promise in identifying clinically significant data manipulations, such as ring sign detection, that are not addressed by existing methods.

Quantum systems that are influenced and connected to heat, such as a motor operating in contact with a thermal bath, require a specific balance to maintain stability and balance. In a typical scenario, when an open quantum system is driven and connected to a thermal bath, it eventually loses balance and becomes unstable. However, if the system is instead connected to a heat bath with carefully regulated temperature variations, it can maintain a stable and balanced state. Researchers discovered that this heat bath can be modeled as a thermal reservoir with a unique, intricate structure, generating long-lasting, intricate patterns of movement that help the system achieve and maintain a stable balance. This discovery led to a more detailed understanding of the unique properties of quantum systems in contact with such a structured heat bath, as well as possible ways to observe these properties using precise measurements of the system's behavior over time.

The article establishes that for convex functions with bounded H"older continuity, the Alexandrov maximum principle and convexity are interchanged only when the H"older continuity coefficient exceeds a certain threshold. This generalizes a previous observation concerning differentiability. By combining this outcome with the concepts of variational and differential mean curvatures, the article proves the Riemann mapping theorem's differential version. Moreover, the article defines and explores the properties of $\beta$-convexity, depending on the H"older continuity coefficient $\beta$. It also introduces a concept of convexity based on the variational curvature and applies it to explore the convex hull properties of sets with H"older continuity boundaries. Finally, the article defines and uses a notion of fractional convexity to develop convexity theorems for sets with fractional mean curvatures.

Counting the periodic occurrences of events allows us to measure time. Historically, developing stable and accurate timekeeping devices was a significant undertaking. This text introduces a method for creating a time-keeping device based on a counting principle. The device utilizes a combination of stable and unstable equilibria in a locally integrable system, subject to random disturbances. Random clicking times caused by chaotic dynamics near an unstable equilibrium serve as time events. The anti-pinning technique ensures a wide-ranging random walk around this equilibrium, resulting in time measurements following a discrete Markovian process and a finite memory time associated with the local exponential decay rate. The anti-pinning mechanism allows for a control parameter (the distance between the two equilibria) to be adjusted, thereby increasing the local conjugacy condition and enhancing the Lyapunov exponent near the unstable equilibrium. This approach provides accurate time measurements, with accuracy dependent on the average time between random clicks. The method can be applied to a horizontal droplet of oil on a substrate under gravity as a physical realisation of the clock design.

This research addresses the challenges associated with Software Defined Networks (SDN) by enhancing network performance through the introduction of Fog computing. The main objectives of this integrated model are to provide energy efficiency, cost-effectiveness, and real-time quality of service (QoS). To achieve these goals, we propose a Fog-SDN composite model, which combines the benefits of both systems. The main components of this model include application, storage, Fog-Gateway, and Edge-Controller layers. The network layer utilizes an advanced controller for enhanced flexibility and reduced processing delays. The virtualization of network equipment allows for the distribution of network functions, thereby streamlining network operations and enhancing efficiency. To manage and control these functions efficiently, we design an adaptive controller for the Fog-SDN integrated model, which automates the movement of virtual network functions in response to changing network conditions. The proposed controller interacts with the network and Fog infrastructure through RESTful APIs, enabling efficient function management and network topology adjustments. This model includes two key components: a function allocator and a function mover, which work in tandem to achieve optimal network performance. The former handles virtual network function requests from users and provides them to the fog-node for processing, while the latter is responsible for adapting and moving functions across the network. The controller utilizes an adaptive function mover to enable rapid service provisioninng in response to changing network conditions, thereby achieving improved quality of service and network performance. Metric learning's pair-wise loss technique is centered around optimizing an embedding that maximizes similarity between images within the same class, minimizing distance between images in distinct classes. Various formulations of pair-wise loss strategies have been proposed. To consolidate the array of loss function variations, this paper presents a unified framework for interpreting pair-wise losses within the context of embedding constraints. Specifically, the paper examines how to enforce an invertible embedding transform where its Jacobian determinant is constant. Additionally, the paper derives all existing pair-wise loss regularization terms based on this invertible transform constraint and shows that each unique loss function arises from combining the invertible constraint with distinct regularization strategies. Consequently, the paper provides guidance for selecting loss function variations depending on specific dataset characteristics and highlights their implications for their invertibility. Experimental validation using the Stanford Cars dataset shows that maintaining an invertible embedding transforms even across training and inference stages, while our findings also suggest that choosing losses that preserve invertibility may yield improved image retrieval performance on smaller datasets, while maintaining the transform's invertibility is irrelevant in the context of performance on larger datasets such as ImageNet.

In this context, we explore certain classes of holographic tensor networks, which can efficiently simulate various systems in condensed matter and holography, and possess characteristics suitable for quantum error correction. By developing an error-correcting code utilizing dense code segments within these networks, we demonstrate that it adheres to standard protocols for quantum error-correcting codes, and specifically demonstrates correction of HAPE-like errors. Additionally, we examine the potential degradations resulting from non-correcting code applications on these networks and discuss the potential connections to well-known degradations in tensor network theory.

Our study of magnetized radio filaments at the center of the galaxy utilizes MeerKAT data by examining the distances between groups of these filaments. A total of 63 groups, each containing multiple filaments, were analyzed and found to possess distinct properties. A small angle relative to the galactic plane was observed for many of these groups, with some grouped together based on their proximity to Sgr A* and specific layers of the galactic bulge. Notably, some filaments exhibit layered distributions when compared to the galactic plane, with some grouped into two distinct bands. Further analysis of the filament groups revealed that a quarter possess a curved shape and/or magneto-hydrodynamic shock-like features. The distribution of distances between groups suggests a band structure, with a specific layer approximately 20 parsecs thick at the center of the galaxy. By using a 3D fast-fourier transform technique, we have analyzed the cross-spectral density of the radio emission from these filaments to determine if it exhibits coherent 2-8 GHz radiation within a 10 parsec scale. Our findings indicate that a quarter of the filament groups display this property, revealing magneto-hydrodynamic streaming motions and/or a reflection of past gas flows. By mapping the orientation of the magnetic field for these filament groups, we have observed a consistent orientation across approximately 150 parsec. A proposed paper suggests a new method of distributed leader-follower control for achieving conservation voltage reduction in unbalanced three-phase distribution systems by optimizing DERs through the scheduling of smart inverters. The method considers primary-secondary networks and loads influenced by voltage. The system complexity is minimized through the creation of zones in the network based on connectivity. To address non-linearities from load models and power flow, the paper suggests a linear approximation technique using power and voltage measurements, enabling the online implementation of the proposed control for tracking fast system variations led by DERs. The method also allows for non-uniform update rates and robust communication in the presence of delays and failures. The method's efficacy is demonstrated through numerical testing on a real U.S. Midwest distribution feeder.

We investigate non-stochastic bandits and experts in a delayed context, where delays are contingent on both the time and the decision. While delayed settings with time-dependent delays have been thoroughly analyzed, the situation with situation-dependent delays is relatively under-explored. With a baseline regret bound of $\hat{O}\left((T+D_0)\sqrt{K\log(T)}\right)$, where $K$ represents the number of actions or experts, $T$ denotes the actual time elapsed, and $D_0$ signifies the minimum delay, we introduce an algorithm that reveals a crucial trade-off between regret and delay: increasing the delay can actually decrease the regret. When compared to a recent method with a regret bound of $\hat{O}\left((T+D_0)\sqrt{K\log(T)} + D_1\sqrt{K\frac{D_0}{D_1} \log(T)}\right)$, our approach boasts lower regret whenever $D_1 \leq K\frac{D_0}{\sqrt{T}}$, leading to a more favorable outcome in scenarios with extended delays or a narrow range of possible delays. Through experiments, we show that this algorithm can lead to substantial gains in real-time applications.

Recent studies in task-oriented dialogue have utilized reinforcement learning to model policy interactions. However, training only through dialogue transitions often leads to dull, uncreative responses by neglecting diversity in message content. We observed that reinforcement learning in task-oriented settings can actually decrease lexical diversity. To address this, we developed a simple yet robust approach that encourages diversity in training by rewarding the exchange of uncommon information during dialogue. Evaluations of the model on a sales dialogue dataset showed an increase in lexical diversity of over 30% while maintaining task-oriented performance.

Following Quantum Chromodynamics' 1972 formulation, a breakthrough in its regularization came when Kenneth Wilson applied it to Euclidean lattices. This opened doors for in-depth numerical analyses of QCD's non-perturbative features, exemplified in the initial studies by Michael Creutz, Wilson himself, and others. In the process, Euclidean lattice regularization became the standard tool for QCD computations, which it remains today. To provide a thorough introduction to this complex subject, we will begin by discussing the fundamental principles of regularizing QCD through Euclidean lattices, before delving into the various applications of this regularization in numerical QCD studies.

A probabilistic damage assessment model is developed for offshore wind turbines post an earthquake, relying solely on pre-seismic condition data. The model relies on a machine learning technique called Gaussian Process Regression, which accounts for the significant intra and inter wind-farm variability in damage progression due to heteroscedastic heteroscedasticity. The researcher then introduces a combined statistical and artificial intelligence method to accurately forecast load responses, which serves as the foundation of structural damage assessment. The proposed method exhibits superior performance when compared to conventional time-series empirical Bayesian approach, particularly for low to moderate damage levels. The findings are further illustrated through numerical simulations of 2D finite element models.

Turkey is prone to seismic activities with varying intensity earthquakes occurring frequently, emphasizing the necessity for swift and effective crisis information dissemination. Social media can provide valuable insights into public perception, beneficial for crisis communication and management. This research focuses on analyzing Twitter posts related to the 2020 Izmir earthquake to 1) identify popular hashtags and words that emerged during this period, 2) examine and categorize the content of these tweets, 3) determine the most shared hashtags and words, and 4) assess users' sentiment towards the government, Turkish President, and Prime Minister following the earthquake.

A group G exhibits property $R_\infty$ if an infinite set of real numbers generates a torsion-free subgroup of $\mathbb Z$. Equivalently, $R_\infty$ holds true for G when it possesses an infinite set of non-conjugate twisted conjugates. Research has proven that property $R_\infty$ is preserved under the core of subgroups. This study shows that property $R_\infty$ also applies to direct products of groups. As a consequence, it's discovered that the group $\widetilde{F_2}$ exhibits property $R_\infty$.

A new technique is developed to process time-sensitive data from ultra-fast experiments using an approach based on optimization in a pathway framework. This technique is successfully tested on data from experiments involving X-ray scattering and electron diffraction to analyze the breakdown of molecules. Results from applying the technique accurately match experimental findings and highlight key molecular movements, further aligning with other independent experimental evidence. What's more, this approach effectively considers the continuity of molecular structures and is resilient against noisy data.

This paper presents SceNDD: a novel naturalistic driving dataset derived from
instrumented driving experiences. Recorded over 120 hours in various urban and
suburban environments of three distinct weather conditions, this dataset boasts a
range of driving scenarios including critical events, multiple camera captures,
and diverse driving styles. SceNDD is made publicly available, complete with 24
extended range RGB-D cameras mounted on a vehicle for seamless navigation.
Key attributes of this dataset are its high-fidelity, multi-sensory, and vast
coverage of driving situations, making it an invaluable resource for researchers
and developers. As one of the few datasets recorded with RGB-D cameras, this
dataset has significant potential to drive advancements in stereo vision research,
particularly in the context of autonomous driving. Furthermore, the presence of
multiple cameras and rich dataset characteristics provide an ideal setting for
investigating various topics, such as camera calibration, 3D object
reconstruction, and SLAM engines. Website: https://scendd.github.io/

In connection with the information paradox problem, theories such as BCFT and ICFT are gaining attention. As a contribution to this area of study, we have developed an approach to reflected entropy in the context of BCFT/ICFT. Starting with BCFT, we defined reflected entropy and verified its semi-classical formula for a string theory example. A key outcome is a general formula for the semi-classical reflected entropy in BCFT, showing a connection to the entanglement wedge area. We then generalized this to ICFT, establishing a universal formula for semi-classical reflected entropy. Additionally, we explored the concept of vacuum entanglement wedge cross section in ICFT, demonstrating a non-trivial outcome based on two relevant string theory examples.

Research on Reconfigurable Intelligent Surface (RIS)-assisted Orthogonal Frequency Division Multiplexing (OFDM) systems has grown rapidly, driven by their potential for controlling channel propagation and enhancing system performance. Nevertheless, the precision of channel estimation in such systems can be compromised due to time-venergy loss and frequency-smoothing effects caused by an RIS-induced delay difference between consecutive subcarriers. Therefore, this study introduces an advanced channel estimation technique called the Delay difference-aware Adaptive Shifted-Orthogonal Approximation (DAS-OA) method to enhance the accuracy of channel estimates in RIS-assisted OFDM systems. Specifically, this proposed DAS-OA method adapts the Orthogonal Approximation (OA) technique to minimize errors resulting from time-smoothing and frequency-smoothing effects, then blends the estimated amplitudes of adjacent subcarriers to enhance channel estimation accuracy. Simulation outcomes demonstrate that the proposed DAS-OA method yields better performance than existing techniques, particularly under conditions of low delay difference.

In the context of the Schrödinger-Klein paradox, a simplified experiment is described where a quantum system consisting of a chiral wave packet is set up near a perfectly conducting plane. An energy measurement is made using a meter, which is modeled as a series of non-interacting, box-like cavities, to determine the apparent energy and uncertainty changes as a function of the meter's resolution and the spatial overlap with the plane. For overlap regions where the wave function isn't entirely dominated by the plane's reflection pole, using any type of meter will result in a relatively high energy and broadened uncertainty, which will also cause the self-energy to increase. However, when the wave packet resides entirely within the plane's exclusion zone, an ideal meter (infinitely high resolution) will report zero energy and zero uncertainty, which will also result in no self-energy. For a real-world situation where the meter can only be modeled using complex numbers, an extremely high momentum resolution will result in a nearly conserved total momentum.

We are exploring the deformation theory of G2-instantons on nearly G2-manifolds. A one-to-one connection exists between nearly parallel G2 structures and real Killing spinors, enabling the deformation theory to be formulated through the use of spinors and Dirac operators. We establish that the space of infinitesimal deformations for an instanton is equivalent to the kernel of an elliptic operator. With this approach, we prove that abelian instantons exhibit rigidity, and subsequently apply these results to demonstrate the rigidity of the fundamental class of 7-dimensional Princeponic manifolds.

The global spread of the 2019 COVID-19 pandemic caused by SARS-CoV-2 has resulted in widespread losses and economic devastation worldwide. To combat the outbreak, various national and regional authorities introduced contact tracing applications to track infections, which raised significant privacy concerns due to the potential for data misuse. To address these concerns, the present study adopts a quantitative approach to evaluate the interrelations between user anonymity and detection accuracy in contact tracing applications and introduces a scalable solution to accommodate diverse privacy levels. A widely recognized method for analyzing contact tracing data, the Time-Based Location Estimation technique, is chosen for the study. Based on this approach, the proposed study demonstrates how to achieve user-centric anonymity in contact tracing by adjusting the time-based radius, which compromises location precision but ensures anonymous entries in the distance distribution. Consequently, the proposed study provides a framework for the quantitative evaluation of trade-offs between user anonymity and detection accuracy in contact tracing applications.

The central underlying principle of quantum entanglement is that quantum particles in relationships exhibit predictable and interconnected patterns of correlation when measured. Currently used measures of entanglement cannot be applied to certain types of multi-partite entanglement in quadrupole modes found in optomechanical systems, which do not exhibit as clearly defined wave-particle duality. The entanglement of light in these systems cannot be measured using standard methods. Researchers have proposed a new approach to detecting entanglement between optomechanical quadrupole modes. The proposed method involves simulating a sample's entanglement using a data-driven model, which uses random data points to develop an equation. The method was tested using fictional data sets. Despite the central principle of quantum mechanics, the proposed method works for both quantum and classical systems. Researchers discovered that classical versions of certain entanglement measures provide a clear understanding of what entanglement means. The proposed method was also found to have some advantages over other measures of entanglement. Researchers discovered that classical versions of certain entanglement measures have some flaws. The proposed method has some benefits over other measures of entanglement. Researchers hope the proposed method will help the study of entanglement in optomechanics.

This research paper introduces a tool for automatically generating code skippers based on advanced type system mechanisms. The system is applicable to programming languages that utilize a type system called Lambda 2, including a specific language called Lindbo. It utilizes a description written in a metaprogramming language, which is processed by the generator to create a code optimization tool. The generated code optimization tool, implemented as a plugin for the Lindbo compiler, is inserted into the compiler's type system to facilitate code generation and analysis. The evaluation of this project involves examining its performance in code generation, analysis, and interaction with the type system, as well as exploring potential implications for the development of metaprogramming languages and type systems.

A cluster of young compact asteroids connected to 39991 Iochroma undergoes a dynamics analysis in this study. Our findings show the Iochroma family's location within two adjacent three-body resonance zones - specifically 3J-1M-3 and 5J 3S-2. This paper establishes the precise positioning of these resonances as well as their demarcation boundary, providing accurate calculations of the Iochroma family's mean eccentricity as a function of the resonance argument, thereby contributing to a greater understanding of the family's orbital evolution.

Building upon Ramanujan's well-known formula for odd zeta values, we establish a related expression for the Hurwitz zeta function, $\zeta(s,3)$, using a similar Bernoulli polynomial approach and identify additional, novel identities related to the 42A22 and 11B34 MathSciNet classifications, specifically Article 10204.13, as referenced.

We calculate rational T-equivariant elliptic cohomology of complex projective spaces derived from finite dimensional T-representations V. This is accomplished by establishing that the T-equivariant elliptic cohomology theory constructed in Gre05, and the T^2-equivariant theory constructed in Bar22, share a key decomposition. This key decomposition facilitates reducing the T-equivariant cohomology computation to T^2-equivariant cohomology of complex spheres, whose computation is already available from Bar22.

Recent uses of machine learning in algebraic geometry and physics are explored,  
connecting areas like geometry, physics, and machine learning. Two case studies  
illustrate how machine learning techniques can solve problems in algebraic geometry,  
namely, using deep neural networks and systematic hyperparameter optimization to  
reinforce and enhance results in geometry.

This paper provides a comprehensive, next-to-leading-order examination of the angular distributions in $J/\psi$ production, including $J/\psi$ from $b$-quarks, $J/\psi$ with high transverse momentum, and $J/\psi$ together with a second charmonium meson, within the color-singlet model. This model treats charmonium as being composed of two $c\bar{c}$ charm quark pairs interacting via Coulomb-like forces, excluding radiation-recombination contributions. In contrast, contemporary QCD models, such as the color octet model, also consider interactions that include a radiation-recombination process, but these are not analyzed in this paper. The production properties of $J/\psi$ from $b$-quarks, $J/\psi$ with high transverse momentum, and $J/\psi$ together with a second charmonium meson, including associated angular distributions, are detailed and compared with existing experimental results. In order to obtain accurate predictions for the angular distributions in an experiment, it is necessary to consider detailed production properties, including those related to $b$-quark production and $J/\psi$ transverse momentum, as well as $J/\psi$ fragmentation. In addition, $J/\psi$ production from $b$-quarks, together with its associated angular distributions, is predicted to contribute notably to experiments, including those conducted at the LHC.

Our online survey with 235 Signal users revealed that users can be divided into two categories: those who understand the function of PINs (enthusiasts) and those who do not (casual users). Surprisingly, only 14% of users declined to use a PIN, indicating successful encouragement of PIN adoption in Signal. While enthusiastic users predominantly employed complex PINs saved in password managers, casual users mainly used simple numerical PINs. To strengthen the security of casual users, enhancing awareness about the true purpose of PINs and the features they offer would be beneficial. Furthermore, enhancing the user education and communication about the security advantages of PINs would be helpful.

This technical note details the development of Gaussian quadrature rules suitable for computing the integrals of solar irradiance functions, which typically involve extremely high accuracy due to inherent non-periodicity and large non-periodic components.
