By employing an algorithm based on the Lomnitz approach, we created quadrature rules that effectively reduce computation complexity while yielding precise results, even at smaller table sizes than earlier methods. Notably, we demonstrate that these quadrature rules, when paired with the Lomnitz algorithm, require fewer computational operations than their exact counterpart, the trapezoidal rule. Various example applications, encompassing solar irradiance, atmospheric scattering, and radiative transfer, illustrate the efficacy and efficiency of the new quadrature rules.

The curvature formed by the Hessian matrix or its generalized Gauss-Newton approximation holds significant value in developing training algorithms for deep networks. However, current methods based on automatic differentiation and combinatorial optimization are plagued by storage and computational limitations associated with the training data dimensionality, specifically in relation to the number of training images. Our Circulant Matrix Theory based Training (CMTT) method offers a different approach in designing a spectral optimization algorithm that relies solely on the data's shift-invariance structure. Our experiments demonstrate that CMTT is capable of learning first-order gradients, whereas previous methods required either higher-order gradients or nonconvex optimization. As a result, CMTT has the advantage of being immune to the vanishing gradient issue in deep networks. Furthermore, our method also enables an analytical understanding of the regularization effects achieved through dropout and learning regularization. Interestingly, our findings also reveal that the spectral penalty associated with the generalized Gauss-Newton approximation offers superior performance compared to the Hessian itself. Our method of training deep networks using circulant matrices is versatile and can be applied to various deep network architectures, including those using residual connections. Our experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in addressing the problem of overfitting and achieving consistent results across different test cases.

Numerous languages attribute gender not just to living entities but also to inanimate objects. When such a gender-based distinction is present in a language, related words must conform to the noun's assigned gender, which can impose a grammatical constraint on these inanimate nouns. We've discovered that this distinction between inanimate objects according to gender is preserved in the word representations generated by neural networks. To illustrate this, we've conducted an experiment to demonstrate how the gender-based distinction of inanimate objects can be extracted from the word representations and used as a feature to predict the grammatical gender of a noun, much like a target variable, from various languages. Our study indicates that in these cases, state-of-the-art neural networks may inadvertently learn and solidify biases present in the input data, a phenomenon that could potentially be utilized to devise a zero-knowledge test to identify languages that employ such a gender-based distinction and where inanimate objects are assigned with the gender attribute. Furthermore, we've developed an innovative method to visualize the representation of grammatically consistent gender-based distinctions as points on a two-dimensional plane. Our experiments have revealed that the representation of inanimate objects is largely determined by the characteristics of the language rather by the characteristics of the noun itself. Lastly, we've devised a straightforward technique to "erase" the distinction of inanimate objects from the word representations by applying a neural network that has been trained on data from another language. Our experiments have indicated that the distinction can still be recovered even after data from

We categorize and understand a certain aspect of attractiveness in groups that use arithmetic, and derive statements indicating a dual nature related to their stable components, characteristics, patterns, and associated algebraic structures. To accomplish this, we study the movement patterns over the characteristics of the groups in question and derive statements indicating a dual relationship with the stable components, patterns, and associated algebraic structures. Notably, this study provides the first comprehensive analysis of the stable components, patterns, and associated algebraic structures of the groups in question. To achieve this goal, we introduce a novel approach based on the concept of 'discrete flexibility', utilize advanced techniques in the study of the expansion characteristics of the groups in question, and derive novel geometric understanding of the stable components, patterns, and associated algebraic structures.

Estimating an object's pose is a crucial aspect of most visual pipelines in robots, which our work addresses by enhancing neural network-based pose estimation through the association of known objects with their 3D models. This method, which we call'multi-modal,' utilizes the insights from a single instance of each object to prepare the network for recognizing the same object when it is presented for the first time. Although the method requires a large collection of objects, which is impractical in most settings, our research shows that the same model can be trained to recognize new objects without needing to be re-trained, a technique we call'multi-modal' or'multi-category' pose estimation. This method's effectiveness is demonstrated using the known 'YCB objects' system, which allows us to accurately estimate the pose of novel objects without needing to be re-trained, a technique whose feasibility is further tested using the 'Occlusion Bounding Box' object, which allows us to accurately estimate the pose of a pair of objects when one of them is hidden from view. This method's effectiveness is demonstrated through a simulation, which shows that the same model can be used to estimate the pose of a pair of objects when one of them is hidden from view.

Predicting short-term traffic is a widely researched area within intelligent transportation systems. However, existing forecasting systems face significant limitations due to their reliance on real-time data. The 2022 Traffic4cast challenge at NeurIPS addressed this issue by utilizing publicly available sparse data. Our team submitted a solution to the expanded challenge of predicting estimated time of arrival. Our method involves pre-processing and feature engineering to create a unified framework, and we employed model-agnostic meta-learning to combine the strengths of various algorithms. Our estimates ranked third in the estimation challenge and second in the ETA challenge.

This study presents VACA, a new family of variational graph autoencoders developed specifically for causal inference tasks where there are no hidden confounding factors, using solely observational data and causal graphs. VACA models key aspects of a Structural Causal Model (SCM) without requiring any assumptions about its underlying parameters. By leveraging these properties, it provides a versatile framework for simulating hypothetical scenarios and making predictions based on past actions. Our experiments confirm that VACA effectively approximates various interventional and counterfactual scenarios in different SCM setups. Moreover, when applied to the datasets of PHILRES and TTP, two prominent causal inference challenges, VACA consistently outperforms existing baselines while producing a scalable implementation suitable for real-world datasets.

State-of-the-art radio interferometers such as the LOw Frequency ARray (LOFAR) are now capable of producing massive data at speeds of hundreds of gigabits to terabits per second. This significant data rate complicates radio data analysis and necessitates costly computation. Although top-tier computing facilities are accessible for national and international institutions, local facilities operated by a single organization may not be equipped to handle these high demands. Consequently, it is crucial for organizations to possess their own computing capabilities to process scientific data effectively. We suggest developing an on-site data analysis system, incorporating a graph database to store raw data and facilitate real-time processing. Moreover, we propose a distributed hierarchical computing architecture to efficiently process scientific data at institutions lacking advanced computing infrastructure, such as the South African Radio Astronomy Observatory (SARAO). We showcase this system's efficacy by simulating the processing of various radio observations, including solar flares, geomagnetic storms, and the transients from the LOFAR BHIs.

In recent years, advancements in machine learning and artificial intelligence have driven significant growth in photonics research, leading to cutting-edge photonic systems including traditional waveguides, nanoantennas, and metasurfaces. The innovative application of AI-driven methodologies empowers the development of smart photonic devices rooted in fundamental light-matter interaction principles. Artificial intelligence and machine learning concepts are rapidly transforming the underlying physics of light, offering effective tools to investigate metaphotonics, which relies on optically-induced resonances. We now present an overview of metaphotonics, along with a concise summary of the core principles of machine learning, exemplified through its applications to metasystems and metasurface optimization.

The high-risk investment of producing a film can yield enormous returns with the right blockbuster hit. However, determining a movie's market potential is a significant challenge before investment. In this study, we address this problem by proposing a machine learning-based approach to estimate a film's revenue by analyzing its traits. We compiled a dataset of movies from IMDB and eBay purchase records to identify the key characteristics that influence revenue. The results show that revenue is linked to the movie's popularity, directed by an acclaimed filmmaker, and has strong marketing, while other characteristics have no significant impact. Additionally, our study compares the effectiveness of machine learning algorithms using revenue data at different time intervals and finds that a long-term analysis is best for making investment decisions. We also demonstrate that our revenue estimation model can generate more accurate predictions than the state-of-the-art methods in the field of natural language processing. By achieving low loss rates and top 10% prediction accuracy on certain data, the model can estimate a movie's revenue within 10% of its actual grossing.

The energy shift towards renewable sources necessitates a deeper understanding of how human behavior influences energy demand and supply interactions, leading to complex dynamic phenomena. Stable power grid operation relies on balancing demand and supply while maintaining appropriate voltage and phase levels across networks. Focusing on phase balance, this study combines power grid data with social complexity theory techniques to reveal patterns and relationships within electricity consumption data. Using both local and global clustering detection methods, researchers identified phase-balance phases in consumption datasets and discovered positive correlations between consecutive consumers during phase transitions. This social complexity theory insight could inspire innovative solutions for stable power grid operation, leveraging feedback control methods to optimize phase synchronization among network nodes.

Cyber physical systems create a foundation for a systems of systems approach in the automotive industry. This concept aims to achieve various objectives, such as smart mobility, safety, and efficiency. To address these goals, a hierarchical modeling framework consisting of two layers is developed: one focused on within-vehicle functionality and another addressing intervehicle and infrastructure interactions. The modeling framework incorporates basic modeling concepts for CPSSs, including composition, decomposition, hierarchy, and reuse, in both layers. Specifically, it applies object-oriented modeling, graph theory, and agent-based modeling to create a unified modeling language, which is illustrated through practical examples. The outcomes of this approach include developed models that simulate the behavior of systems of systems, offering valuable insights for creating sustainable, intelligent, and efficient mobility solutions.

Blazars with certain spectral patterns exhibit an excess of high-energy photons. Theoretical models suggest that inverse Compton scattering of highly beamed, anisotropic radiation from the central black hole's corona could generate such excesses. We simulated this process using a Monte Carlo code and considered various parameters to predict observable outcomes. Our study focused on "U-shaped" source spectra, in an effort to help constrain the Monte Carlo model and determine if it can reproduce the spectral patterns of multiple blazars.

In our study of intricate multi-dimensional environments, also known as complex landscapes, we explored their properties and dynamics, especially focusing on the stationary points. To analyze this, we developed a set of mathematical equations that describe the changes in a system as it moves through the landscape in a multi-dimensional space. Our investigation revealed that points of stability, where the system exhibits stable behavior over varying parameters, act as bridges between different types of stationary points. Through the application of the Jacobian matrix, we categorized the stationary points and mapped their relationships. Utilizing these insights, we created a framework to understand the system's behavior by identifying patterns of transition between different states, revealing the system's universal behavior across multiple dimensions. Our analysis also exposed a distinct difference in the system's behavior, depending on whether it starts from a point with positive or negative curvature. Ultimately, this work enables the systematization of the system's behavior and identifies the patterns of transition with high precision, thus generalizing the system's behavior across various dimensions.

To develop optimal methods for identifying identical pure states with perfect accuracy using limited resources, we investigate effective strategies for analyzing and discriminating quantum states.  Traditionally, this process is carried out through a series of repeated measurements on possibly distinct copies of the states, with researchers having control over how these states are prepared and processed.  We explore two main approaches:  an online method involving real-time discrimination and an offline method involving initial discrimination.  For each, we identify a specific protocol that minimizes errors and analyze its performance, with a focus on understanding its experimental implications.  Furthermore, we compare the effectiveness of these methods at distinguishing states with only minimal resources needed.

Baryon creation is investigated using a quantized fragmentation model based on QCD strings. Baryons are generated through a process that is straightforward to understand, which involves a QCD string breaking up into causally linked parts. A simplified model, representing a QCD flux tube with properties tied to the mass spectrum of light mesons, can replicate the masses of light baryons.

In the study of the sun's interior using seismic techniques, the rotation speed of the outer layers of the sun can be observed. However, the observation is often distorted by the movement patterns formed during the sunspot cycle. To understand these distortions, the University of Bordeaux team analyzed data from the SOHO/MDI and GONG networks to evaluate how flow patterns around areas with high solar activity affect the measurement distortions. It was found that the distortions in the sun's rotation speed observation could be attributed to at least two factors. First, the distortion fluctuates with the solar cycle, and the magnitude of the distortion peaks at the solar peak. Second, the distortion is the result of movement patterns around areas with high solar activity. To correct the distortion, the activity caused by movement patterns around areas with high solar activity needs to be taken into account during the analysis. Using the activity caused by movement patterns around areas with high solar activity in the analysis, the observed solar cycle variation amplitude with the solar cycle peaks at 0.16 rad/s^2, while the amplitude without the analysis peaks at 0.22 rad/s^2. As a result, removing the analysis based on activity caused by movement patterns around areas with high solar activity reduces the observed solar cycle variation amplitude by 28%.

Researchers have identified a possible explanation for a background of gravitational waves that dates back to the early days of the universe. These findings could validate a theoretical model of gravity known as TeV-gravity, which predicts that the universe began as a fractal structure governed by the Frauchiger-Rudolph protocol. This protocol led to critical points known as tricritical points, which in turn caused space-time to experience a phase transition around the age of 10^-13 seconds. This transition resulted in a background of gravitational waves due to critical fluctuations in the transition process. To validate the theory, researchers used a simplified model of the gravitational field to calculate expected characteristics of the gravitational wave background and found that the predicted properties align with observations from the Planck project and future projections for the LISA satellite.

Light field technology is currently gaining significant traction. It has the potential to replace conventional imaging methods with Light Field Displays (LFDs), which can project a dynamic perspective-consistent image. However, when a light source with a non-uniform intensity is used, LFDs can cause captured light fields to have varying intensity across different viewpoints. This results in a distorted appearance when trying to recreate a dynamic image using the captured light fields. To address this issue, we developed a novel method called LINFE. It utilizes a neural network to create a dynamic image with a uniform light intensity, even when the input light field has a non-uniform light source. This method can create high-quality images, preserve the input light field's perspective consistency, and enable the use of a light field captured with a non-uniform light source. Additionally, LINFE can handle both single and multi-exposure inputs, making it suitable for a range of applications. To our knowledge, LINFE is a unique solution for addressing the problem of non-uniform light intensity in LFDs.

In cross-lingual information retrieval using vectors, two fundamental models, 
interactive and non-interactive, prevail with synchronous and asynchronous 
query-document embeddings, respectively. To facilitate the development of 
efficient and accurate models for this task, our analysis provides an in-depth 
examination of the task's characteristics and a critical review of the existing 
research. Based on this analysis, we propose and evaluate an alternative 
approach to IRI for the task and demonstrate its effectiveness and efficiency 
using a newly created dataset, XLIReq, comparing it with the state-of-the-art models.

The urgent need for comprehensive health and demographic reports has driven an increased focus on geographic studies, often utilizing detailed, pixel-level maps that require accounting for the complex sampling methods employed in their creation. Failing to account for the sampling design can result in inaccurate estimates, jeopardizing the development of effective, targeted public health interventions if the demographic data lacks representative coverage of key population groups. To address this limitation, a new method utilizing Bayesian generalized linear models is introduced, which enables efficient use of data from different sources with varying designs, even when some sources contain missing information. This efficient method capitalizes on hierarchical modeling structures to make the most of incomplete data, making it well-suited for large-scale studies. Application of this approach to a nationwide health and demographic study in Nigeria highlights its utility, particularly in a setting where data was collected through a stratified random sampling process. To facilitate the efficient use of this method on larger datasets, the algorithm is designed to take advantage of parallel computing on a GPU and can also serve as an educational tool for understanding sampling designs and model efficiency.

The objective of this study is to propose a semi-classical model representing the owner's expected value of the capital under a betting scenario involving a spin-1/2 system, which utilizes the concept of ergotropy as a measure of the invested quantity. By extending a prior mathematical framework formulated by Scandolo et al., this work expands upon their methodology to a broader context characterized by a trinomial probability distribution for two-state systems. Furthermore, this study includes an exhaustive analysis of the model for the spin-1/2 system and extends it to higher experimental outcomes with arbitrary probabilities.

Building on the recently created two-dimensional semiconductor MoSi$_2$N$_4$, our comprehensive study of monolayer compounds MA$_2$Z$_4$ involves in-depth analysis of their band structure and excitons using ab initio GW and Bethe-Salpeter equation calculations. In contrast to the predictions of our previous study with static RPA, our results with the GW method show that the quasiparticles in MoSi$_2$N$_4$ are more dispersed and less charged, leading to a significantly increased direct fundamental gap of 3.25 eV in the high-energy limit, which significantly surpasses the on-site Coulomb energy. BSE/GW BSSE calculations of the optical properties of MoSi$_2$N$_4$ reveal an enhanced absorption spectrum with several prominent peaks that are missing in the static RPA results, where the spectrum shows a significant decrease in intensity at the fundamental gap energy. Our findings suggest that static RPA is insufficient for determining quasiparticle band alignment and exciton positions in these two-dimensional materials, requiring the use of the more accurate GW and BSE methods for precise results.

A comprehensive search has been conducted to identify the $\Sigma^+ \to p \mu^+ \mu^-$ decay at the LHCb experiment in proton-proton collisions at energies of 7 and 13 TeV. The investigation, specifically aimed at detecting rare $\Sigma^+$ decays in a data set totaling 7.4 fb$^{-1$, has resulted in findings that exceed the statistical uncertainty thresholds. The observed excess, amounting to 6.2 standard deviations, has been recorded and analysis was performed across a broad range of the square root $q^2$ domain, from 0.04 to 3 GeV$^{2}$/GeV$^{2}$, in order to determine the absolute branching ratio of the $\Sigma^+ \to p \mu^+ \mu^-$ decay. The resulting absolute branching ratio, calculated as $1.30 \pm 0.21 \pm 0.06 \times 10^{-8}$, is discussed in conjunction with findings from other experimental results and theoretical predictions, revealing a discrepancy that prompts further investigation to determine the underlying physics cause(s).

The traditional theoretical model of a star's formation through core collapse (spherical symmetry) is compared and contrasted with a new theoretical model of a star's accretion disk formation (disc symmetry) in the research. This new model proposes an innovative approach to understanding planetary development. The theoretical underpinnings of these concepts are explored through mathematical representations where a core collapses into a star in three-dimensional space in the initial model, and in contrast, in an accretion disk formation approach within the (2+1) dimensional spacetime. Analyzing these models, researchers identify several key similarities and differences, such as the core's mass influence on planetary development, the formation and utilization of a Eddington limit, the potential for star formation in pairs, the distribution of matter within a protoplanetary disk during its formation, the formation and potential of supermassive black holes, and the emission of radiation from thin disks. Studying these models reveals a disc symmetry that surpasses spherical symmetry in several key aspects, and the research also proposes an innovative approach to understanding a black hole's ringed appearance.

Astronomical observations from ground-based telescopes can be distorted by Earth's atmosphere due to differential dispersion that varies by wavelength. Observations made off-axis, other than directly at the zenith, necessitate the use of Atmospheric Dispersion Correctors. Current designs of these correctors are based on atmospheric models which have yet to be verified through on-site measurements. We've carried out a detailed analysis of these models over the 315-665nm wavelength range by cross-dispersion spectroscopy, employing a device that can accurately measure spectral shift and dispersion across this period. Our research reveals a strong correlation between observed spectral shifts and modeled predictions, albeit with some noticeable variations. On the other hand, the dispersion measurements don't closely match their predicted values. We've calculated average spectral dispersion factor values for the night, finding considerable fluctuations between different sites. We provide a direct formula to calculate this factor based on either spectral shift or dispersion, thereby enabling the development of improved atmospheric dispersion correctors that could significantly reduce the overall cost of their design and construction.

This paper develops a novel hierarchical latent variable model to study multi-period time series that exhibit dynamic patterns shifting over time. The basic framework is expanded upon by integrating temporal dynamics into a hidden factor model, thus creating HF-DIRCHI. The nonparametric nature of Dirichlet process mixtures with hierarchical themes enables HF-DIRCHI to accurately capture complex temporal patterns. Theoretical proofs are also conducted to derive consistency results for the model. Furthermore, empirical evaluations using real-world data demonstrate that HF-DIRCHI surpasses competing neural and Bayesian models in a range of applications.

In a setting that combines continuous logic, we establish a connection between Stone duality and Pontryagin duality by viewing Pontryagin duality as a specific instance of Stone duality. This is achieved in the context of a particular class of topological groups where the group's topology is fine enough, a condition that includes all locally compact groups. The local structure of the Bohr compactification is identified in relation to the logic's atomic structure, with the compactification serving as a representation of the logic's space of positive tests. This framework's properties are examined through the analysis of the test space's Boolean algebra of subsets, which is demonstrated to contain a particular kind of ideal related to the group's topology. Furthermore, the framework's and the logic's inherent symmetry properties are studied in detail; in particular, the logic's symmetry to the group's dual leads to an interpretation of the group's dual as a particular theory in the logic, with this duality displaying universality and injectivity properties.

The remarkable effectiveness of deep learning has sparked various concerns regarding ethics, encompassing skewed predictions and data security risks. To address these problems, experts employ fairness metrics, decentralized machine learning methods, or formal verifications. Despite ongoing efforts to solve each issue separately, no unified theory currently exists to address all these challenges simultaneously. Our study aims to establish a new theoretical framework, combining specific data processing constraints and graphical representations to achieve this goal. Our proposed approach is demonstrated through the analysis of previously inaccurate human age predictions in medical applications, specifically in the MOPED dataset. Our method not only examines constraints on model representations but also enables the identification of underlying representation principles governing age classification, revealing significant insights.

We explore an option for dark matter, where it stems from a stable, spin-1/2 particle, produced naturally through the seesaw mechanism in a supersymmetric model that preserves R-parity. By incorporating this particle into the model, we demonstrate that it can act as a dark matter candidate without requiring an extension to the model's Higgs sector. A similar, more substantial dark matter particle, created by the seesaw mechanism's large-scale suppression, can also be produced and stabilised. Consequently, this model enables the dark matter candidate to interact with neutrinos, as reflected in the dark matter's annual modulation signal amplitude. We examine whether this model aligns with the neutrino data from the LSND experiment, as reported in Phys.Rev.D79:092001,2009. In this context, we produce various constraints on the model, including those from the WMAP data on annual modulation and from direct dark matter detection experiments, such as the CDMS and Xenon experiments. We compare these constraints with the condition required by the LSND results in terms of the mass and mixing parameters involved. A similar investigation is conducted for a model where one right-handed neutrino plays the role of dark matter.

We investigate a smart reflecting surface-aided wireless-powered communication network where a multi-antenna energy transmitter broadcasts an exclusive energy signal to a powered transmitter with multiple antennas, located between the energy transmitter and the destination transmitter. The network's key elements include an energy-intensive transmitter at the destination, an energy-sensitive information-carrying message at the destination, and a wireless-powered transmitter able to harvest energy. To optimize performance, we formulate an intricate max-min optimization problem. By utilizing an alternating optimization strategy, we initially transform the original problem into a max-min min-norm optimization problem through an equivalent transformation, then utilize a split-and-coalesce algorithm to efficiently handle the resulting problem's properties. Another alternating optimization technique is used to decompose the min-norm function into smaller sub-problems via two different representations, finally applying a coalescence technique to achieve a solution.

For the first time, researchers used total absorption gamma spectroscopy to measure the Gamow-Teller strength distribution in $^{186}$Hg decaying into $^{186}$Au and compared it to QRPA calculations employing the Skyrme Hartree-Fock method with a self-interaction correction. The measured strength distribution, characterized by a broad and multi-peaked pattern, exceeded the theoretical predictions by about one order of magnitude. In addition, the measured decayed half-life for $^{186}$Hg deviated significantly from the theoretical predictions.

We explore the intersection of dark matter and leptogenesis within a unified theoretical framework, which includes three right-handed neutrinos, a scalar singlet that drives inflation, and a scalar doublet that induces the electroweak symmetry breaking. The scalar doublet's flavoured interactions, in particular, yield a viable dark matter candidate from a mixing perspective. Furthermore, our research indicates that while dark matter is not necessary for generating the baryon asymmetry in this scenario, the relationship between dark matter and baryon asymmetry exhibits a correlation. We examine and compare various dark matter candidates derived from the two-higgs doublet model, as well as a fermionic dark matter candidate inspired by the witten picture. We present a representative model sample that aligns with existing experimental limitations in terms of the relic density of dark matter and constraints on neutrino masses, while also accommodating requirements for lepton flavor constraints and leptogenesis, in addition to influences from reionization and the CMB.

We have designed a novel control method using learning techniques for complex systems whose behavior is unknown. This algorithm excels in environments where there is only limited, high-noise data from ongoing experiments. It achieves control effectively by utilizing knowledge from various sources of side information. When side information is scarce, we developed a method to estimate the system's dynamics, simplifying the control problem in the process. Our approach has been successfully tested on a range of challenging tasks, including the control of intricate simulations models. Moreover, we have applied our technique to the control of unknown dynamical systems in a physical environment, namely a quadcopter.

All Toda conformal field theories serve as comprehensive expansions of Liouville conformal field theory and the WZW models based on compact Lie groups. Toda conformal field theories' unique features include free fermion and free boson formulations, observability of TDT partition functions via a simple, well-defined path integral, and a well-defined and highly non-trivial target space for physical states. A key discovery in this class of theories is the existence of a second, Lie group-associated Virasoro algebra. Our paper delves into the integrable structure of the two-algebra model underlying the Toda series, where the co-algebra component exhibits Lie coalgebra properties. This understanding is highly beneficial, as it links the S-matrix of the theory to the elementary Lie coalgebra representations via a direct relation. Building on our previous research on the coalgebra side, we now introduce a novel, related Primitivity Theorem, which links the asymptotic S-matrix to the elementary Lie algebra representations. Moreover, we demonstrate that our integrable structure-based approach enables the determination of the general three-point correlation functions in each Toda conformal field theory.

Despite significant advancements in producing realistic images with GANs, a primary concern persists, particularly for high-resolution inputs and intricate datasets, due to training instability caused by a mismatch between the real and randomly generated distributions. To address this issue, novel loss functions have been explored in recent research, leading to more robust GAN training and divergence measurement. To rectify training instability, multiple approaches have been developed to manipulate the exploration-exploitation trade-off in generating samples. To produce more diverse and dynamic outputs, network flexibility has been increased by using deep networks and diverse sampling strategies. To assess the genuine creativity of the generated images, metrics evaluating novelty have been introduced. To confirm that the generated images indeed belong to the target dataset, rigorous testing has been implemented using multiple discriminative metrics and divergence measurements. To facilitate flexible network retraining and other GAN-based applications, network snapshots have been adopted instead of incurring the risk of data compression artifacts. To address concerns about data protection, open-source and anonymized datasets have been created along with techniques for protecting subject privacy. To gauge user perceptions without influencing decisions, subjective metrics have been utilized in studies, typically involving visual assessments by volunteers. To make GAN-based systems more approachable for non-experts, interactive demos have been developed, providing users with control over the generated output. To facilitate comparisons and discoveries, online platforms have been designed to store, showcase, and browse various GAN-based results, encompassing an array of applications. To facilitate comparisons and discoveries,

A novel approach for practical quantum communication over long-distance connections has been introduced. 
This approach utilizes free-space or fiber links for conducting measurements on signal phase without employing phase locking techniques.
Instead, a universal reference beam is used to stabilize the entire system.
Using this method, quantum key distribution experiments were performed over free-space and fiber links measuring up to 70km in length.
Key distribution experiments conducted over these links involved generating random signals, performing optical transformations, mixing signals with a reference beam, detecting correlations, and finally shuffling bits to secure an encrypted key.
By combining random signals with a universal reference beam, phase locking is eliminated, allowing for secure communication over long distances.
This approach shows promising results for practical applications in quantum communication.

In this study, we investigate the Toeplitz algebras of particular classes of Toeplitz operators on the p-Fock space and the p-Bergman space with 1 < p < ∞.  Let BUC(ℂⁿ) and BUC(ℬ_ᵐ) represent collections of uniformly bounded and continuous functions on ℂⁿ and ℬ_ᵐ (ℂⁿ's unit ball) respectively.  On the p-Fock space, it is proven that the Toeplitz algebra, having translation-invariant, closed BUC(ℂⁿ) subalgebra symbols, can be linearly generated through Toeplitz operators with those symbols.  On the p-Bergman space, the Toeplitz algebras having BUC(ℬ_ᵐ) subalgebra symbols are studied, and particularly, the Toeplitz algebra of operators symbolized by BUC(ℬ_ᵐ)'s elements is shown to be closed and unital, and also that it is linearly generated through Toeplitz operators with those symbols.  The latter result generalizes the known findings for 1 ≤ p < 2.

Recent breakthroughs in object detection using deep learning have greatly improved performance, particularly with open-set scenarios where models can identify detected objects without being told the class label. Our research introduces the first known open-world object detection framework, OpenOD, which builds upon this advancement. By utilizing a shared feature extraction network and distinct head modules for each task, OpenOD efficiently shares knowledge and adapts to various tasks through a shared transformer. To further enhance open-world object detection, OpenOD employs a innovative auxiliary training method using a secondary network that classifies background from a randomly sampled set of pixels during training, effectively eliminating biased responses due to background classification as '0'. This innovative approach has a negligible impact on computational resources, and our experiments demonstrate OpenOD's superior performance on multiple benchmarks, including PASCAL3D+, KITTI, and MS COCO, as well as its ability to work seamlessly with modern detectors.

A young B star in the Rho Ophiuchus cloud produces a dense photo dissociation region and a circular bubble. We analyze a high-resolution mid-infrared image and a spectral scan along a mid-infrared filament in this study. These observations reveal, in a PDR in the Rho Ophiuchi cloud, that the density mainly determines the density distribution. However, the observed features cannot be entirely explained by the simple collection of gas particles due to free expansion. Instead, the presence of internal processes such as accretion or turbulence is likely present. Additionally, the mid-infrared spectral analysis indicates that the temperature within the mid-infrared filament remains relatively consistent at around 200 K and that the observed emission is likely produced through both isolectric lines and the thermal continuum. Furthermore, the thermal nature of the observed emission suggests a lower minimum volume density of around 10^5 cm^-3.

The remarkable achievements of Transformer models in natural language tasks have piqued the interest of computer vision tasks. A crucial aspect that sets Transformers apart is their capacity to process a comprehensive understanding of language through self-attention. In contrast, conventional CNNs struggle to capture contexts at different positions, with their localized nature a significant hindrance. We propose the application of a novel, language-free technique, Deep Contextualized Augmentations (DCA), as a replacement for conventional data augmentation methods, to effectively inject context from farther-ahead positions within images. With deeper contextualization, DCA successfully conveys a richer sense of context in images, thus facilitating context-based modeling. Furthermore, it has been observed that DCA can be an efficient alternative to Token Mix, a method of data augmentation, in pre-training, with our results indicating that it accomplishes this task six times faster while achieving similar performance. We make our code and data available for public use.

Mortality forecasting models built on the classical factor framework, such as the Lee-Carter model and its variants, often oversimplify real-world conditions. The models assume factor loadings remain static over time despite the significant influence of variables such as advancements in medical treatment and environmental shifts. We expand the classical model to create a factor model that accounts for the evolution of factor loadings through time. We apply this model to mortality data in several countries and evaluate its performance using multiple metrics and model checks. The results indicate that the model accurately predicts mortality for older ages but underestimates deaths for younger ages due to limitations in existing databases. We utilize information on factor loadings to gain insights into the driving forces of mortality trends and make predictions for years 2010-2019. For years 2020 and beyond, we explore the potential impact of the COVID-19 pandemic and adjust the model's predictions accordingly.

Reducing the cost of neural architecture search (NAS) by sharing weights among different child models is a popular strategy. However, due to interference from other models, there is often a poor correlation between predicted performance and actual results. This study investigates the source of this interference and proposes a novel theory that relates the number of models sharing weights to the level of interference. It also reveals that minimizing interference scales sublinearly with the number of models. From a theoretical perspective, we identify the advantages and disadvantages of two key mechanisms - parameter sharing and gradient blending - used to share weights. To address the issue of interference in NAS, we develop a novel method that employs a gradient blend technique along with a mixture model to estimate expected performance. Experimental evaluations using SONAS on CIFAR10 and ImageNet show this approach achieves better results than current techniques.

Time series data, whether recorded scientifically or through monitoring, provide vital information about the world around us. Statistical features and summary statistics are frequently extracted from these data to capture their inherent properties, which are then applied in various contexts, including classification, detection, identification, and characterization. This knowledge is also crucial for understanding natural phenomena, predicting future behavior, and informing decision-making strategies. Ultimately, the extracted features serve as a precursor to machine learning techniques or human interpretation. In our research, a comprehensive and efficient open-source Python solution was developed to compute these features and summary statistics: time_series_features. This package encompasses a wide range of established techniques and algorithms found in various scientific literature and software applications, including some proprietary projects. A central repository makes it easy for users and the community to contribute their own feature computation methods. Additionally, the solution provides a unified workflow that streamlines the process of running features on datasets, writing the results to standard output, and saving intermediate data to disk. This package is designed to be compatible with popular data science tools and can be easily integrated with other feature computation methods. time_series_features is compatible with Linux, Windows, and Unix-based systems, supporting input data in various formats, including those commonly used by scientists.
We identify concrete, infinitely precise criteria under which a proper geodesically complete CAT(0) space has a semistable fundamental group at its boundary.

Human-assisted Translation Quality Assessment (TQA) is an extensively utilized method that helps gauge machine translation efficiency, negotiate translation contracts, and evaluates human translator proficiency.  Despite its importance, little research exists using quantitative methods to determine TQA's reliability.  In our investigation, we examine TQA as a multi-component process using complex data analysis, distinguishing it from simple quality assessment and incorporating an explicit expertise factor.  Employing Log-Linear Analysis (LLA) on a substantial dataset, we assess several null hypotheses to determine TQA's component-specific parameters and assess their statistical significance.  Our results indicate varying degrees of expertise among translators influence TQA reliability, and certain evaluation aspects show considerable consistency regardless of individual translator differences.  Ultimately, we derive explicit guidelines on how to apply TQA efficiently and effectively.

In random systems, the scattering matrix correlates incident wave patterns with internal distributions within a volume, and previously this correlation was leveraged to increase energy delivered to a target. This study determines a general set of constraints governing the eigenvalue problem associated with the scattering matrix, where we derive a lower bound for the largest eigenvalue value. Furthermore, we confirm that the number of eigenvalues exceeding a certain threshold scales linearly with the number of possible incident wave patterns, and we deduce from this that the dimension of the scattering matrix grows at least as $N_H$ where $N_H$ represents the number of possible harmonic fields at the system's input.

We've found that using pruning methods on artificial neural networks significantly
reduces their size while maintaining their performance, and can even reveal smaller
sub-networks with higher accuracy than their full counterparts. Our study focuses
on understanding the inherent biases of these "lucky network" solutions and their
connection to task-specific features. We looked at the effects of varying levels of
pruning on multiple classification tasks, as well as the impact of different
initialization methods, and found that the surviving neurons tend to group by task
in fully connected networks. This has led us to propose new insights into the
nature of biologically-inspired neural computation and the idea that task-specific
information is encoded in a hierarchical manner.

In lotteries with exceptionally large jackpots, as seen in Mega Millions and Powerball,
increasing bettor participation actually works to reduce the return on investment for each ticket.
The reason for this is a higher likelihood of multiple people winning with the same ticket.
In an effort to boost the return on a lottery ticket, we suggest an alternative approach.
By dividing the possible winning combinations among different vendors and pairing them
with distinct prizes, the potential for two people sharing the same ticket becomes much
less likely. Furthermore, this strategy allows the vendors to offer enhanced return on investment
to their customers, effectively increasing the return on a lottery ticket.
We develop a mathematical model to study this strategy, investigating the optimal configuration
of tickets and prizes that maximizes the return on a lottery ticket for sellers.
Interestingly, despite the complexities involved, finding the optimal configuration proves to be a computationally
solvable problem.

The large-charge expansion technique opens up a new possibility for calculating critical properties of high-charge operators $\phi^Q$, where the charge $Q$ is fixed. For operators of an arbitrary charge, one has to calculate their anomalous dimensions at the $1/z$ expansion level. When performing an expansion to the $1/z$ term for the $\phi^4$ model, one has to include five-leg operators, which becomes necessary for calculating the $1/z$ expansion of the critical properties of high-charge operators. Our work involves including five- and six-leg operators in the expansion to the $1/z$ term for the $J^2\phi^4$ and $\phi^4$ models to the six-loop level, which allows us to test the convergence of the large-charge expansion. Our results reveal that even at the sixth order, the large-charge expansion converges rapidly. We utilized the characteistic exponent $\gamma_0$ from the $1/z$ expansion of the $J^2\phi^4$ model to test the soft-branch large-charge expansion of the critical properties of high-charge operators at the $O(J^2)$. Our work involved developing a new large-charge expansion of the critical properties of high-charge operators at the $O(J^4)$, which was done by combining the $1/z$ expansion of the critical properties of high-charge operators at the $O(J^2)$

Our research systematically explores how different mechanisms affect the valley Hall effect in two-dimensional materials with multiple valleys. We begin by revealing that incorporating spin-valley characteristics into the valence band's structure's topological features yields an impressive valley Hall effect. Interestingly, the valley Hall effect is completely absent in scenarios where the conduction band's structure's topological features are prominent. Notably, the valley Hall effect is minimally impacted when static strain is applied, but dynamic strain can produce significant and predictable current responses due to its modulation of the band structure. Additionally, the valley Hall effect is diminished at low temperatures due to the presence of disorder-induced transport, but can be intensified through a corresponding increase in the carrier's scattering time. Lastly, we demonstrate that a substantial valley Hall effect can occur when the valley response is coupled with the spin Hall effect.

The VisDA 2022 Challenge seeks unsupervised domain adaptation solutions for solid object categorization, specifically semantic segmentation. Participants must train models on a source domain, typically an artificial dataset, and have it perform tasks on a target domain, which contains solid object images. To achieve successful adaptation, we leverage a cutting-edge method using self-training with pseudo-labels and a discriminative correlation alignment technique that aligns feature representations and maintains domain parity while minimizing domain differences. By combining these strategies, we developed an efficient framework comprising a ResNet-50 backbone and two stages: initial model training and self-training. Our implementation utilized PyTorch. Notably, we obtained the 2nd place solution in the VisDA 2022 challenge.

t-SNE is a widely employed method for reducing high-dimensional data to lower-dimensional representations, particularly in data visualization. Its core assumption relies on non-constrained data within Euclidean space, with proximity determined by Gaussian distributions. However, this premise doesn't always apply in real-world scenarios, especially when the data distribution significantly diverges from the analytical model underlying t-SNE. In this study, we investigate t-SNE's performance in nonlinear manifolds compared to other dimensionality reduction techniques. Additionally, we conduct an exploratory analysis of t-SNE's parameters and the dependence of its output on these parameters, and discuss its strengths and limitations. Finally, we offer some general tips for using t-SNE, along with avenues for further research.

We investigate the characteristics of the two-dimensional Fermi polaron model, where a single impurity is attracted to a sea of Fermi particles, under conditions where their interactions have negligible spatial range. By utilizing a sophisticated variational technique, our calculations for the polaron energy in different coupling regimes confirm a predicted critical transition from the previously observed droplet-to-gas state to a new droplet-to-droplet state, which occurs when the interaction strength meets a specific threshold. Our calculated energy trends are also compared and contrasted with an advanced theoretical model known as the medium polaron model. While the model provides an accurate approximation of the polaron energy at strong interactions but loses accuracy at weaker interactions, our research reveals that this loss in accuracy is caused by a failure to consider the quantum nature of the surrounding Fermi sea. To rectify this shortcoming, we developed a refined version of the medium polaron model that takes into account the quantum properties of the surrounding Fermi sea, resulting in a generalized form of the model known as the spinor medium polaron model, which significantly improves the accuracy in calculating the polaron energy at both strong and intermediate interaction strengths, thus greatly reducing errors by nearly two orders of magnitude in these contexts.

In this hybrid quantum computing approach, an analog phase is combined with discrete measurements to simulate complex quantum systems. A two-qubit spinless fermion system is explored as a test case to develop digital-analog protocols. The connection pattern of qubits is found to be the most efficient configuration for achieving high fidelity when using a digital-analog simulation for this specific fermion system. The ANO gate, a complex operation on two-qubits that has a 22% error threshold, is constructed from simpler 4-local gates to facilitate the simulation of entanglement. The time complexity for generating the ANO gate, a complex operation on two-qubits that has a 22% error threshold, is analyzed and compared to the optimal protocol, with results indicating that the time complexity is optimal protocol, with results indicating that the time complexity is proportional to the inverse cubic root of the qubit count.

Graph polynomials hold significant value due to their potential to develop algebraic formulas for various graph characteristics and their evaluations provide significant mathematical insights. Certain graphs, including complete and bipartite structures, can be identified through matching properties which enable the calculation of polynomial values at specific points, including -1, 2, and -2. The purpose of this study is to extend existing patterns by exploring evaluations at -1, 2, and -2 for all connected graphs, with a focus on graph order n being a prime number, with primes being a set of positive integers. The findings demonstrate that the order of graphs can be determined by evaluating the chromatic polynomial at -1, with a detailed explanation provided, and it is observed that only specific patterns of evaluations at -1, 2, and -2 exist. The study further highlights an interesting link between the alternating chromatic polynomial and the evaluation patterns associated with -1, with a descriptive analysis given.

We derive an expression for the pullback of the Hitchin connection, extending from the moduli space of genus two curves to a 10-fold cover of a Teichmueller curve, which was previously found by Veech. Subsequently, we calculate the monodromy representations of the fiber fibrations of the genus two level zero mixed Hodge structure.

The shift to remote working is transformational, influencing how businesses approach management and employees perceive their work environment. A critical challenge arising from this change is ensuring leaders can support their team's emotional and psychological needs from a distance. Research provides essential guidance on the key needs to focus on for maximizing employee well-being in a remote setting. A survey of 236 employees with varying levels of remote working experience helps to clarify their primary needs and potential areas of unmet needs. Leaders should prioritize supporting employees' basic psychological and safety needs to promote higher levels of job satisfaction and minimal turnover intentions. Notably, meeting these needs can help mitigate the negative effects of unmet needs, reducing employees' likelihood of quitting. Leaders can leverage leadership enablement programs to effectively address employees' needs and improve outcomes.

The concept of dichotomous matrices serves as an expanded interpretation of Hermitian matrices, with newly formulated guidelines identifying which arrowhead matrices fit this enhanced definition. Furthermore, specific calculations are carried out to determine the permanent of dichotomous matrices, as well as establish formulas for permanent and trace of Arrowhead matrices within the context of dichotomous matrices.

In a study using the ALICE detector at the LHC, scientists investigated the elliptical movement of electrons created when beauty particles decay at a specific point near the centre of a collision between lead nuclei at a high energy of 5.02 TeV. These scientists found that electrons produced from beauty decays exhibit positive elliptical movement, which indicates how beauty quarks interact within a collision medium. Furthermore, they calculated a specific value that represents the strength of elliptical movement in these electrons and compared it to what is expected from creating a medium made mainly of protons. These results are consistent with computer simulations that account for a complex interaction between various particles and a medium that is thought to exist briefly during the collision. Additionally, the scientists calculated the value of elliptical movement for electrons produced from light vector mesons and found it to be negative, which provides additional clues about how these particles interact with a collision medium.

In pursuit of breakthroughs in the medical field, we analyze chromatic configurations in three-dimensional space, employing topological concepts. Leveraging techniques borrowed from image processing, we develop mathematically sound indicators to capture both fine-scale and broad-scale interplay among color categories. Our proposed methods enable fast computation on large datasets, including those stemming from 3D medical scans, which produce volumetric data. A comprehensive repository containing the results of our proposed approach for various datasets can be found at https://github.com/cmlFPGA/Euclidean-Grid-Structures.

This work utilizes the concepts of extremal optimization and typology to study the gain achieved through optimal power control in interference-limited networks, featuring $N$ users transmitting to a single destination and being affected by an external interference power $\sigma^2$. By applying extremal principles to a tractable formulation of the power control problem in Nossek et al. [2020], a precise formula is derived to calculate the extremal gain as a function of $N$ and $\sigma^2$. Furthermore, this formulation is employed to investigate the properties of the extremal gain in different regimes of $N$ and $\sigma^2$, and to examine its connection to the total transmit power in these scenarios. By developing a typology based on the behavior of the extremal gain in various regimes, a unified understanding is gained about the gain achieved through optimal power control in networks with $N$ users and under a given $\sigma^2$. It is also shown that this gain is always greater than or equal to $1/\sqrt{2}$ when $N$ is less than or equal to $3$, and increases logarithmically with $N$ when $N$ is greater than or equal to $4$, for any given $\sigma^2$ exceeding $1/2$.

Auditing categorization processes using more transparent and understandable methods compared to traditional machine learning can bring several benefits.  This research applies the PART and LAR classification methods along with multiple explanation methods to categorize bank customers based on financial data.  The study compares the performance of various explanation techniques in terms of their precision and understanding of categorization results.  To measure the accuracy and understandability of explanations, three criteria are utilized: clasificación precision, understandability and a newly developed criterion for dealing with multicriteria decisions, through both numerical and statistical analysis.  The analysis shows that while explanations generated by linear models are precise and easily comprehensible, model-agnostic explanations demonstrate high accuracy and understanding but at a significantly higher computational cost.  To resolve this issue, the study proposes a new method for generating explanations that strikes a balance between model-agnostic solutions and the understanding of categorization results, thus offering a possible solution for applying model-agnostic solutions in practical scenarios.

The Strauss process is a point process, and its density is unnormalized relative to a Poisson point process, incorporating a weighting factor lambda, between zero and one, which is applied to each pair of points closer than a certain distance, denoted as 'r'. Traditional techniques such as basic acceptance-rejection algorithm and adaptive acceptance-rejection algorithm can be inefficient, especially when trying to sample multiple points. Therefore, this paper introduces a method to improve the efficiency of unnormalized probability-based point process sampling. Specifically, this new technique aims to optimize the acceptance-rejection process by utilizing a dynamic boundary function that shifts based on the location of previously accepted points, thus allowing for more efficient identification of relevant regions. When attempting to sample multiple points, this technique further refines acceptance-rejection by taking into account the distances between previously accepted points when calculating the boundary function. By doing so, it reduces unnecessary re-evaluation of unnormalized probabilities for each additional point. Furthermore, this technique is accompanied by a proof demonstrating its correlation with a specific type of process. The proposed technique is then applied to the sampling of an unnormalized probability-based Strauss process, which is a type of point process. The study provides empirical evidence demonstrating the efficiency gains of this new technique when sampling multiple points, and compares its performance to that of the basic acceptance-rejection algorithm and adaptive acceptance-rejection algorithm.

In the context of string theory and quantum gravity, the Generalized Uncertainty Principle revealed the presence of an inherent minimum length, confirmed through the deformation of Heisenberg's algebra. Utilizing this concept, the paper explores transformations linking coordinates and time between moving and rest reference frames within a GUP framework. In the non-relativistic scenario, it identifies a modified Galilean transformation similar to Lorentz transformations, where a large velocity takes the place of the speed of light, with an estimated value significantly higher than $c$. Moreover, it examines how GUP affects relativistic particles and the Lorentz transformation within a GUP setting, finding that GUP effects become apparent at $1/c^2$ relativistic scales, where a relativistic length, approximately $2\cdot10^{-52}$ m, emerges.

Multitasking scheduling in service industries has gained significant attention due to its practical relevance, especially in contexts where tasks are closely related and switching incurs significant costs. In the competitive pricing environment of such industries, job prices can be used as a tool to mitigate switching costs. This phenomenon is explored in a model where a service provider manages job arrivals and prices to minimize switching costs, effectively creating a multitasking scheduling problem. This model differs from traditional scheduling problems as job arrivals are not necessarily sequential; however, we propose a constant-factor approximation algorithm that minimizes makespan in multitasking scheduling problems. Additionally, we present theoretical evidence supporting the idea that job arrivals, prices, and switching costs are intertwined in multitasking scheduling, using a random job arrival model that outperforms constant-factor approximation algorithms based on worst-case analysis.

A significant issue in legged locomotion research is the uncertainty that arises when applying traditional models of legged locomotion to deformable terrain. This problem stems from the unpredictable interaction between the leg's contact point and the terrain's deformation, leading to inconsistent state predictions. Deformable terrain poses a particular challenge to state estimation because the movement of the leg causes discrepancies in state predictions among adjacent foot steps. Researchers have developed multiple state-space models for controlling legs on deformable terrain, but the complexity of this problem means that existing models cannot be fully utilized in advanced legged locomotion systems. This thesis presents a novel, multi-step planning framework called Differential State-Space Modelling (DSSM) that utilizes a differential filter to generate linear state-space models in real-time. By using precomputed nonlinear dynamics, DSSM creates a hierarchical framework for planning and controlling legs on deformable terrain. This framework allows the simulation of a leg's dynamics in real-time, providing an accurate model of the leg's dynamics. As a result, DSSM enables the planning and control of complex, dynamic movements on deformable terrain using advanced trajectory generation techniques.

In the rapidly evolving world of Internet of Things (IoT), ensuring that a large number of devices remain connected is becoming increasingly crucial. The deployment of new firmware in a distributed manner necessitates a reliable evidence-based approach for assessing its network impact before and after implementation. Although existing tools provide valuable insights into IoT network performance with their extensive measurement capabilities, they are often tailored to specific use cases and Quality-of-Service indicators. To facilitate informed firmware deployment, a comprehensive analysis is required, considering key performance indicators such as packet delivery, latency, throughputs, and network session connectivity. This paper presents an evidence-based approach for assessing firmware deployment effects on large-scale IoT networks. To facilitate reproducibility, the method incorporates advanced features, including automated execution, a structured measurement plan, and visualization of results, all applied to the Contiki IoT framework within the Contiki simulation environment.

Using a recursive Green function approach, we compute the Fock space self-energy in the one-dimensional quantum glass model with non-Hermitian quantum mechanics for any number of particles and imaginary potential strength. This self-energy's real part correlates with the decay rate of localized states, while its imaginary part predicts phase separation in the many-body localization phase. Our findings confirm that the phase separation occurs when localized modes interact, and that the number of particles influencing this separation is independent of system size. Moreover, the real part of the self-energy per site exhibits a finite limit at weak imaginary potential for any particle number, despite previously suggested logarithmic behavior. Conversely, the self-energy's imaginary part per site displays oscillations around a positive mean value that increases with an increasing number of particles, reaching a finite limit at weak imaginary potential. These results align with both numerical simulations and the non-Hermitian quantum spin glass model analysis. They also provide an understanding of the origin of the positive mean value. Lastly, the real part of the self-energy per site exhibits a finite limit at strong imaginary potential for any particle number, while its imaginary part per site exhibits oscillations around zero.

To make the most out of human insight, interactive graph search groups specific labels in a structured framework that benefits image recognition, product organization, and network system design. Researchers have proposed the kBM-IGS problem to quantify and demonstrate human insight in identifying meaningful groups within a graph representation of search queries. The kBM-IGS problem aims to identify clusters of at most k vertices, where each vertex belongs to a label i out of a given set of labels with at least b_i vertices, while the union of these labels constitutes a subset of m labels. The effectiveness of our algorithm in solving this problem on search queries graph with 12 possible labels, having at least 50 vertices each, has been evaluated and verified by experts across 144 categories. The outcome shows that an adapted greedy algorithm resolves kBM-IGS problems efficiently on real-world search queries with comparable results to our primary algorithm. We also observed minimal influence of micro-management on macro-outcomes and discovered that an elevated initial bias boosts our algorithm's performance. The analysis of our method further highlights the significance of reducing the search space by eliminating unimportant vertices and refinements by eliminating irrelevant edges before assigning labels.

In recent years, research has focused on mitigating noise's interference in near-term quantum machines, leading to the development of various techniques. This exploration has also been extended to the realm of machine learning, where quantum methods have shown promising advantages over classical approaches. This study delves into simulating quantum states using a principle-based approach to handle the noise prevalent in quantum devices. This work adapts the multilayer neural network framework and applies it to address the quantum state representation task. Experimental findings involving real-world data suggest that the proposed method is capable of achieving a high level of precision. Moreover, comparing the proposed approach to an existing quantum machine learning method has revealed that it boasts faster convergence rates.

We examine Steklov eigenvalues in nearly spherical domains of three dimensions.  Building on our previous research, which demonstrated the eigenvalues to be analytic functions of domain perturbation parameters, we derive estimates in terms of Sobolev norms of those parameters.  Additionally, we discuss how these findings apply to domain perturbations driven by a variational procedure.  We also analyze the isoperimetric structure of the first Steklov eigenvalue, showing that it does not necessarily increase with an expanding volume in spherical domains, unless a specific condition on Weyl's asymptotics for the first eigenvalue is met.  This investigation includes a discussion of partial results relevant to this issue.

Conformance checking focuses on comparing modeled process behavior to observed process behavior from actual event data. A recent technique, called alignments, identifies and measures deviations between process executions and predefined reference models, pinpointing the discrepancies. Notably, alignments require entire, unbroken process runs, which can sometimes be problematic if real processes are interrupted. As a result, an new approach, called partial alignments, has been developed to accommodate and handle interrupted processes. Building on this progress, this thesis delves deeper into the topic of alignments, offering a crucial improvement by integrating and leveraging contextual information from process logs into the analysis. A comprehensive framework is established to support this enhanced approach, providing flexibility through the selection of various, compatible contextual information representation systems. Furthermore, the usability of the enhanced alignments is demonstrated through the analysis of a real-world case study, showcasing its applicability.

Accurate prediction and simulation of radio wave transmission is essential for optimizing modern mobile networks. Existing propagation models can be broadly classified into two types - empirical and deterministic models. Empirical models, although computationally simple, are often inaccurate due to oversimplifications in their statistical basis. In contrast, deterministic models, like those based on ray tracing and physical wave propagation laws, provide precise predictions but require significant computational resources and can only utilize traditional geographical data. In this article, a novel data-driven approach for developing deterministic radio propagation models using machine learning techniques is presented. This method leverages extensive high-resolution data sets to learn the physical wave behavior behavior. Specifically, the article details the implementation of two ML models that estimate signal attenuation and phase shift. It further compares the ML model's performance in an urban environment with other widely-used propagation models within the frequency range of 1-6 GHz.

A straightforward semantics is proposed for temporal planning. We define and formally establish the logic within the interactive theorem prover Isabelle/HOL, and then obtain a validation algorithm based on that semantics. By using a formal Isabelle/HOL proof, it is shown that the validation algorithm faithfully represents the developed semantics. We also demonstrate through practical experiments that the verification of our algorithm is useful.

Power system expansion planning models, used to integrate renewable resources, rely on complex optimization problems involving various economic and technical factors. These models vary widely due to differences in spatial and temporal detail, leading to multiple spatial and temporal scales. Modelling the variability of renewable resources within a fine spatial and temporal framework is necessary, but it is typically compromised in expansion planning models due to computational constraints. These trade-offs are crucial to understand, and to integrate renewable resources into power systems, particularly in small-island power systems (SIPS). SIPS face distinctive challenges such as limited market analysis and a high level of variability in energy supply. This study reviews power system spatial and temporal modelling approaches, analysing the variability of renewable energy sources and exploring the trade-offs between spatial and temporal modelling of power systems. Furthermore, a comprehensive model was developed and applied to the power system of a small island, providing results that validate its applicability and efficiency.

This study establishes the global existence of classical solutions for the Vlasov-Poisson and the ionic Vlasov-Poisson models within confined areas, under specified boundary conditions that include a particular reflection scenario for the Vlasov equation.

When performing software maintenance, developers typically receive numerous, loosely written requests for changes that need to be understood and translated into a format compatible with the development tools. There has been limited research focused on utilizing artificial intelligence for expressing software modifications in a formal language. This study investigates methods for generating accurate and meaningful text that can be used as input for artificial intelligence-based tool assistance. An experimental analysis of the text produced by various advanced machine learning algorithms against a baseline standard reveals that two styles of pre-trained models, GPT-2 and GPT-3, consistently yield superior results. Furthermore, our investigation also involves applying the generated text to a practical application, where it is utilized as a starting point for guiding automated state-changing operations in a formal language framework. The effectiveness of the generated text is evaluated through a cost-benefit analysis, under multiple criteria, and our results demonstrate that the text produced by the pre-trained GPT-3 model offers a superior outcome, with benefits up to 6.1 times the cost. The practicality of the generated text is also validated through a comparative analysis against two established software methodologies, namely, two-round human-driven versus two-round tool-assisted transformation.

Researchers have found that exposing colloidal gels to ultrasonic vibrations causes them to become more fluid-like, even at rest. This effect is linked to the vibrations disrupting the gel's structure and increasing the rate of particle Brownian motion. An investigation has been conducted to better understand this phenomenon, specifically focusing on how ultrasonic vibrations affect the thermal properties of gels based on polystyrene particles and how this impact compares to the effects of shaking and static conditions. By varying the intensity of the vibrations, researchers observed a continuous increase in the thermal properties of the gels, ultimately leading to a phase transition from a gel to a fluid state. This research has led to the creation of ultrasonic-based techniques to regulate the thermal properties of gels and control the release of substances from gel-based materials.

This research paper explores the validity of the Collatz conjecture for a certain set of sequences with both positive and negative number properties. For the sets defined by even functions, f(n) = 2n^r, the conjecture is proven for r values between 2 and 35, and similar sets defined by odd functions, f(n) = 2n^r + 1, are found to always terminate in 1 when following the Collatz conjecture sequence. In addition, some general observations and the resulting sequences when using both even and odd number functions are presented.

To effectively organize digital collections and facilitate targeted searching within a particular field, precise categorization of document subjects is crucial. Currently, classification primarily relies on human expertise, but semi-supervised Machine Learning algorithms can aid this process by utilizing labeled data to predict subject classes for previously uncategorized documents. Despite their assistance, these machine-driven classifications often lack clarity as to why they were made. This study proposes a novel framework built on the 'etcs' ontology language to create context-sensitive search terms for classification purposes. By integrating this approach, researchers can gain deeper insights into the decision-making processes of machine-driven categorization. To demonstrate its effectiveness, the framework was applied to the classification of 1,562 STEM research papers using a multi-label categorization system developed through a self-supervised Learning algorithm.
