The framework's integration enabled researchers to access detailed, document-specific subject class sequences, a feature that allowed for the creation of a publicly accessible STEM research paper collection, complete with searchable subject class sequences. This collection can be accessed at https://doi.org/10.23636/2022-STES-CLASS/1.

The Gale-Shapley algorithm is widely utilized in many areas to perform matching in one-to-one settings. However, the algorithm's direct implementation falls short in terms of efficiency when dealing with large datasets, as it is slow by at least a factor of n. A faster approach proposed by Tan and Wu reduces the algorithm's runtime to O(n logn). This paper builds upon the Tan and Wu method, offering a novel technique that significantly reduces the algorithm's runtime to O(n) under certain conditions. The presented method also takes advantage of short preference lists to further enhance the algorithm's performance when dealing with datasets featuring such characteristics. The proposed technique is based on the concept of reporting, and it is applied to various scenarios, including both decentralized and centralized settings. The algorithm's correctness and runtime complexity are formally analyzed and discussed. The results show that the proposed technique outperforms existing methods in terms of both efficiency and usability. Finally, the paper showcases the algorithm's application in a real-world setting: online dating. The proposed technique is implemented in Python and evaluated using actual data from the Tinder app to further validate its performance. The results indicate that the proposed technique outperforms the state-of-the-art Gale-Shapley algorithm and its variants, and it is planned to be used in real-world scenarios within the company.

Current evaluation metrics for summarization models are limited, as they mainly focus on coherence and only consider summertime features, neglecting other essential dimensions like fluency, relevance, and quality. To address this issue, the proposed SummScore metric can effectively assess the quality of a summary. This novel approach leverages a set of 1.5 million annotated samples from professional summarizers, which serves as the foundation for development. SummScore is a four-dimensional metric that incorporates semantic, syntactic, and structural features, as well as overall quality, measured by a highly performing GPT-2(3b) model. Furthermore, SummScore exhibits superior performance in correlation with human judgments and outperforms existing evaluation metrics in predicting human ratings, correcting errors, and reconstructing summaries. Additionally, SummScore can efficiently supplement human evaluations by identifying underperforming summaries and highlighting areas for improvement. Finally, the metric can also be used for automated evaluation, as it successfully predicts human ratings, errors, and reconstructing summaries, thus serving as a superior alternative to existing evaluation metrics.

A new method for extracting a sparse signal from cross-related data is presented. This method reformulates signal recovery as an easy-to-solve problem of finding diagonal values in a 2D array, free from noise and model-related constraints. Cross-correlation is applied to the received data and a constant diagonal is assumed across all 2D arrays, allowing for fast solution extraction. The reliability of our method is demonstrated through comparative analysis with traditional signal recovery techniques in various scenarios. Additionally, a theoretical limit is established for extracting a sparse signal from cross-related data, based on an assumption of low signal sparsity and a specific data format.

In recent years, 3D object detection has received considerable focus, with camera-based approaches gaining momentum due to their efficiency and low cost. Unfortunately, traditional camera-based methods often struggle in harsh conditions, a problem that LiDAR-based alternatives aim to address, though they are often prone to malfunctions. To overcome these challenges, this study introduces an innovative fusion technique for 2D object detection, combining data from both camera and LiDAR, with a novel local-refined fusion approach. The newly developed algorithm uses early and local refinement steps to significantly improve performance, as validated by its performance on the KITTI object detection dataset. Moreover, this study's fusion strategy surpasses existing camera-LiDAR fusion methods by leveraging a dedicated decoder and employing heat-map-based local refinement, as well as an anchor-based local heat-map generation scheme.

The presence of thermal energy at the smallest scales of incompressible flow is well established, despite the ongoing debate surrounding its significance. A specific length scale, $\delta_{K}$, is commonly used to quantify these thermal effects. This length scale has been variously estimated as being on the order of $L_{0}/P^{1/2}$, $L_{0}/P^{1/4}$, or even independent of $L_{0}$ (where $L_{0}$ is the characteristic length and $P$ is the average power). To provide some insight into this dispute, we focus on the energy input mechanism that is most commonly used in turbulence models and for simulations without explicit forcing. At the scale of energy injection, this mechanism acts as the scale $L_{0}$, while the scale of local energy production is $\delta_{K} L_{0}/E$. By considering how these energy production scales vary with the rate of energy production $E$ and the size of the system $L_{0}$, we show that the energy input mechanism is most efficiently applied when the energy range is combined with a large-scale length. This hybrid approach to energy input is tested using simulations of two-dimensional flow and high-Re $d$2-component turbulence. It is found that by using this hybrid method, the energy input mechanism is most efficiently applied when the energy range is combined with a large-scale length. Previous studies on laser propagation in a laser-induced thermal wave-based system have focused on scenarios with no laser energy transfer. However, when a laser shares the same axis as a Gaussian heat source, its propagation is influenced by the heat field. Consequently, the fluid's temperature distribution is shaped by the interplay of both the laser and the heat source. Furthermore, in situations where laser energy transfer is not the primary concern, the propagation of a thermal wave in a heat-transfer-based fluid can be impeded or facilitated by varying the dimensionless heat transfer parameter. Building on this understanding, this study explores the coupled propagation of multiple lasers with a shared axis, each paired with its respective heat transfer parameter. As these lasers transmit energy to the surrounding fluid, their propagation is marked by spatial periodicities that coincide with the laser's input parameters. It has also been found that, when a laser experiences counter-propagating interaction with another laser, its propagation is characterized by a spatial frequency that is a result of the combination of the two lasers' input parameters. In theory, the propagation of a thermal wave can be facilitated or impeded by adjusting the heat transfer parameter in the absence of a laser, but when both heat transfer and laser co-exist, the propagation patterns exhibit a shift away from the previously observed symmetrical temperature distributions.

Discussions among developers encompass diverse topics like programming issues and design choices. Research in software engineering explores how to extract knowledge from these discussions, but exploring them through the lens of design is particularly underutilized. This paper outlines the field of design mining and utilizes case studies to illustrate its applications. It also highlights various challenges and opportunities within design mining before delving into future avenues of investigation. Ultimately, the paper serves as an entry point for researchers interested in design mining and its potential in the software industry.

This paper introduces a novel evaluation engine for big stream and data processing pipelines called H-STREAM. It combines the core components of Apache Flink and Apache Spark to create a hybrid framework called HYDRA that facilitates the management, coordination, and execution of complex stream and data processing pipelines on distributed resources. HYDTRA's main functionality is to provide high-level abstractions for task scheduling, resilient rescheduling, non-blocking execution, and fault-tolerant recovery to ensure seamless execution of processing pipelines. Through a hybrid approach, HYDRA achieves improved performance, resource efficiency, and enhanced support for pipeline rescheduling and fault-tolerant recovery. Our approach expands the boundaries of existing research by integrating the task management mechanisms of Apache Spark and Apache Flink to accommodate sophisticated stream and data processing pipelines.

The hunt for Top and Bottom companions is a key area of study for both the ATLAS and CMS experiments, as their single production offers a wide range of observable signals. In-depth analyses have been conducted to establish boundaries for their respective mass limits, considering various theoretical models. To broaden these limits, researchers are exploring double production of these particles, a process that has been a focus of earlier studies, though the resulting signals often lack distinct characteristics, making it challenging to gain insights into the underlying physics. Our current study, however, focuses on the full double production channel, including the case where these particles decay into a pair of jets or bottoms. By using data from LHC proton-proton collisions gathered at 13 TeV, researchers have established new limits on the mass of Top and Bottom companions, assuming their interactions conform to the Standard Model. These new limits effectively extend the existing ones, with the potential to further expand them in upcoming studies.

A recent study explored the application of Neural Machine Translation (NMT) models to automate the formulation of SPARQL queries, a query language used in RDF databases. Despite advances in NMT models, the research found them to be ineffective in generating complete and grammatically correct SPARQL queries. To address this limitation, the study proposed a new framework called RMT-2SP, a Reinforcement Learning based method using a Memory-to- Memory model with a Transformer structure. The framework includes a SPARQL memory module to encode the subject and object sequences based on the class labels distribution, a query memory module to encode the query given a reference translation, and a decoder to produce the complete query from the two memories. The research showed that RMT-2SP achieved better results compared to existing models in generating accurate SPARQL queries.

This work introduces a novel method for systematically categorizing and assessing the quality of diverse publishing outlets in Computer Science. Leveraging a substantial subset of the extensive DBLP dataset covering over five decades, our technique evaluates millions of contributors and six million articles across more than 29,000 distinct publishing venues. We propose a couple of alternative approaches to evaluate and rank authors and institutions based on their work published, incorporating a sophisticated method using a combination of expert-curated and automated quality metrics. Moreover, our system enables the assignment of qualitative scores to publishing venues, or "venue scores," which can serve as metrics for evaluating venues, as well as facilitators of collaboration and knowledge transfer between institutions. These venue scores could also function as metrics for evaluating individual researchers, potentially offering a more accurate measure than traditional citation-based indices, as they provide a clear, explicit connection to specific, curated content. We present various applications of our system, or "Velmer," extending beyond its primary goal, encompassing automated quality scoring of conferences, facilitating open-access content creation, and serving as a tool for explicit collaboration between institutions.

Advanced learning methods can address longstanding control challenges, but the complex neural networks used pose significant analysis difficulties regarding the safety of control systems. Fortunately, research has begun exploring the application of symbolic methods to complex neural networks and control systems. The safety verification of recurrent neural networks (RNNs) remains an unresolved issue, but we take initial steps in this direction. We introduce an approach to convert RNNs to equivalent piecewise linear systems and propose a new method for the symbolic reachability analysis of neural networks that utilizes convex polytopal approximations of ReLU activation functions and the hybrid CoCoSP solver. The proposed tool allows for the safety analysis of control systems and control policies derived from convoluted neural networks, including those composed of multiple RNNs, offering insights for the validation of deep learning methods.

This study generates a comprehensive framework for a learning theory centered on clustering based on dissimilarity. By integrating concepts from three distinct areas of research - namely, $k$-center graph cuts, nearest-neighbor techniques, and clustering derived from graph structures - a robust clustering framework is established, which is capable of withstanding adversarially manipulated data. This developed theory, in turn, informs the design of a robust clustering algorithm. Through various computational experiments, the practical efficacy of this approach is demonstrated and compared to state-of-the-art methods.

Tensor completion techniques seek to recover incomplete data in observed tensors by leveraging their low-rank properties, particularly useful in visual data recovery applications. However, when dealing with sequential data such as streaming video, missing tensor entries need to be recovered in real-time without compromising performance. Existing streaming algorithms may not be effective when the data structure significantly changes over time, as seen in videos with rapid scene shifts or intense motion. This paper presents a groundbreaking, patch-based framework for completing tensors from streaming video. For each incoming frame, small image segments are identified by tracking them from the previous frame, and a unique tensor is created by combining similar segments within a sliding window. This tensor is then recovered using a real-time tensor completion algorithm. Our novel algorithm can adapt to rapid changes within a streaming window and recover incomplete data in real-time at frame rates. Our experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach over traditional methods, particularly in challenging scenarios with intense motion or rapid scene changes.

It is demonstrated that except in three specific instances, the conjugacy classes of classical Weyl groups $W(B_{n})$ and $W(D_{n})$ take the form of type $D_{x}$ $(0\leq x\leq \frac{n}{2})$. Utilizing this insight, we establish that the irreducible Yetter-Drinfeld modules over $W_{n}$ form a bosonic Fock space and generate a type $A_{2n-1}$ tensor product algebra. Furthermore, the same conclusion applies to the irreducible $1$-cojets in the specific cases of $W_{8}$ and generalizes to the Weyl groups $W_{D_{2n}}$ for odd n>2.

Three-dimensional rotating turbulence, once believed to be dominated by stable geostrophic vortices, has recently been observed to support a persistent, non-stationary state characterized by a mixture of geostrophic vortices and turbulent wave-like behavior in the velocity field. This new finding challenges the long-standing concept that geostrophic vortices inevitably suppress turbulent activity. Instead, it appears that a combination of these vortices and protonekhalsteyn energy spectra is a natural outcome when a strong, stable current field is subjected to external energy inputs or existing sources of turbulence. Furthermore, the observed behavior is strikingly similar to what has been seen in the context of magneto-hydrodynamic turbulence in the presence of a strong, stable magnetic field.

We investigate a basic model called Iterative Graph Normalization, effectively reducing it to finding the highest ranking elements in an iterative process among all maximal independent sets within a graph's iteration space. Although it's relatively straightforward to compute a single maximal independent set, achieving this across all maximal independent sets in a graph is computationally challenging and highly resource-intensive for most real-world data sets when utilizing the best available algorithms and hardware. As an alternative approach, we develop and implement a local search model that enables us to generate the best element from the set of all maximal independent sets, providing empirical results that support our findings.

This research focuses on the electric modulation, control, and transport characteristics in a single-layer graphene subject to a gate bias, with comparison to a conventional two-dimensional electron gas. Through analysis of modulation techniques and electrical transport properties, the study reveals distinct thermal behaviors between graphene and a standard 2DEG, with implications for device applications. Further investigation encompasses graphical presentations of mobility and relaxation time in graphene systems. Notably, the study shows that relaxation times for graphene and a conventional two-dimensional electron gas exhibit opposite dependences on temperature, with specific graphical demonstrations provided.

Recent findings have identified low-frequency radio emissions from systems that host close-in and super-jovian planets. The emission patterns resemble magnetospheric storms caused by the precipitation of electrons, which could imply the presence of a highly inflated atmosphere that enables particle interaction with planetary magnetic fields. Since early-stage planets are ideal candidates for storm formation, the detection of radio emissions might serve as a criterion for planetary system maturity. Moreover, the detection of storm emissions could provide insights into the size and atmosphere characteristics of such planets, thus serving as a valuable observation target for future radio telescopes, such as the Square Kilometer Array.

By combining traditional rendering techniques with neural networks, researchers have developed novel approaches to creating realistic virtual human avatars. Despite these innovations, articles and conferences continue to feature outdated content on this topic. For instance, several recent papers rely on datasets created in 2017-2018 and employ the same outdated datasets from the community, failing to make any significant contributions. Furthermore, experts in the field have expressed frustration over the proliferation of low-quality research papers on this subject. To stimulate more effective and consistent research, we are presenting a comprehensive, easy-to-use platform that integrates real and virtual avatar datasets to facilitate comparison and assessment of novel rendering techniques. This platform, known as DAVAC, allows researchers to evaluate and demonstrate their techniques using diverse, extensive datasets. By adopting DAVAC, we aim to promote high-quality research in neural human rendering across articles and conferences.

Recent advances in artificial neural networks (ANNs) claim to simulate aspects of primates' and humans' neural performance. However, these ANNs primarily rely on basic visual characteristics when performing object recognition tasks, unlike humans. Additionally, ANNs are hindered by complex visual issues such as transformations involving multiple objects, similar objects, and degraded images. In an effort to fine-tune these ANNs and enhance their resilience to difficult visual phenomena, researchers are exploring novel training methods. A proposed training method employs a dataset featuring images along with the necessary visual transformations, which allows the network to generalize better to unseen scenarios. This method was found to improve the network's performance on a range of benchmark tests focused on complex visual recognition challenges.

The connection between the Askey-Wilson algebra and both the SU(2) Chern-Simons theory, along with its relationship to the Reshetikhin-Turaev link invariant, which uses quantum algebra $U_q(\mathfrak{su}_2)$, is examined in this exploration. Certain tangles, related to the AW algebra's generators, are introduced and their relation to link invariants is established, providing a more direct understanding of the AW algebra's impact on the Chern-Simons theory's link data. This analysis draws on the re-normalization of the Chern-Simons theory, and the AW algebra's generators are shown to be generated by the trace of certain matrix elements containing the Chern-Simons theory's flat connections. It is also established that the Chern-Simons theory's link invariants provide a linear basis for the AW algebra.

Our study presents computational findings based on a novel trimer-cluster quantum Monte Carlo algorithm for the spin-1/2 model of the anion-displaced kagome lattice (ADKL) in the paramagnetic phase. We analyzed the thermodynamic properties of the model, incorporating both the effect of displacing anions and the underlying geometric structure of the kagome lattice. We observed specific heat variations in distinct regions, exhibiting two-peaks in the high-temperature limit, which can be attributed to the anomalous high-temperature behavior caused by the wrapping of near hexagonal structures as we progress in the anion displacement towards the center of the unit cell. Furthermore, we determined the anion displacement value that yields the standard kagome structure, identified via an inspection of the nearest neighbor structure. Additionally, we calculated the standard kagome lattice limit heat capacity, finding it to be C_{\perp} \approx 0.107 in units of k_{B} per spin per unit cell, which is in agreement with previous Monte Carlo simulations. Lastly, we discussed the relevant connection between the ADKL model and the experimentally-studied material Zn_{1-x}Cu_{x}Ge_{2}(OH}_{4.

Pre-trained language models, exemplified by GPT-3, have exhibited an unexpected capacity for zero-shot learning. Specifically, to accomplish this, users train the model on a particular task by incorporating task-specific prompts into its training data. Research has been directed towards understanding this behavior and improving zero-shot learning capabilities. Our study centers on the meta-tuning approach developed by Gao et al., which refines pre-trained language models through self-supervised learning on a diverse set of tasks. We demonstrated that models incorporating the meta-tuning approach can eliminate the necessity for task-specific prompt engineering and significantly boost zero-shot learning performance. Additionally, we highlighted the utility of the meta-tuning approach in facilitating generalizable reasoning.

In order to create the matter-dominated universe we live in today, a process called electroweak baryogenesis must have occurred and been successful. For this process to work, a strong first-order electroweak phase transition is required. First, we examine whether this phase transition occurs in a specific theoretical framework known as the $Z_2$ symmetric non-supersymmetric universal extra dimension model. Next, we explore how this phase transition is influenced by additional particles that could potentially be present in this theoretical framework. Finally, our results are confirmed through a complementary approach using lattice simulations.

We introduce novel approaches for visually identifying reliable redshifts through emission lines in the millimeter and submillimeter spectrum. Our methodology involves evaluating the effectiveness of diverse millimeter and submillimeter observational methods in measuring spectroscopic redshifts and optimizes future observations to maximize the proportion of robust redshifts. To support these advancements, we compile redshift data from 77 galaxies with millimeter/submillimeter spectroscopy and a publicly accessible dataset of millimeter/submillimeter spectra. However, detecting emission lines in the submillimeter regime proves challenging due to the weak signal and poor spatial resolution, which hampers the visual identification of robust redshifts via line scattering. To overcome these obstacles, we employ two techniques: a machine learning algorithm trained on datasets of millimeter/submillimeter spectra and simulated galaxy spectra, and a second method involving iterative fitting of millimeter/submillimeter spectra using estimated redshifts. These algorithms produce visually identifiable robust redshifts in approximately 34% and 43% of cases, respectively. To facilitate the visual identification of robust redshifts in the future, we will make the trained model and simulated galaxy spectra available online.

This research uses large-scale matrix product state simulations to determine the dynamical spin structure factor of the $J_1-J_2$ Heisenberg model on a triangular lattice with antiferromagnetic properties. A highly complex phase diagram arises from the lattice due to the conflicting interactions between adjacent spins and their neighbors. By simulating both the ordered 120-degree phase and a potential spin liquid phase at a specific ratio of $J_2/J_1 = 0.125$, we identify the nature of the low-energy excitations in each. In the ordered phase, we find evidence of four-spin clusters that are separated from the ground state by an energy gap. Conversely, the spin liquid phase exhibits features indicative of long-range correlations with diffuse, high-intensity spots in the spin structure factor. A comparison of the results from simulations at different matrix sizes reveals the presence of a spin liquid phase at $J_2/J_1 = 0.125$ with low-energy excitations that are consistent with a potential spin liquid ground state.

The study explores lattice cutoff effects on the confinement-deconfinement transition in $SU(3)$ Higgs theory with two different types of lattice cuts: $Z_L$ and $Z_R$. By adjusting the temporal lattice sites from 4 to 32 for $Z_L$ and from 4 to 64 for $Z_R$, researchers find that the cutoff dependence of the Debye mass and the string tension reveals two phases in the phase diagram. The phase at large $Z_L$ shows re-entrance of the confinement phase, whereas the phase at large $Z_R$ indicates percolation of center-vortex-strings throughout the phase diagram. These findings suggest that the convergence to the continuum limit could potentially alter the phase structure of the $SU(3)$ gauge theory when coupled with three massless adjoint Higgs fields.

Cr$_2$Al exhibits a tetragonal structure similar to the Mn$_2$Au type, suggesting it shares properties with other 3d transition metal pyrazines.  Cr$_2$Al, composed of ferromagnetic Cr and paramagnetic Al, displays ferromagnetic properties.  Research focused on the magnetic, electronic, mechanical, dynamical, and other key properties of the Cr$_2$Al compound.  Calculations using the generalized gradient approximation and self-interaction correction methods revealed a N\'{e}el temperature of 107 K, 3 K higher than results from magnetometry and other measurements, but close to the experimental magnetic transition temperature.  Calculated mechanical properties match known values, while a suppression in spin-polarized $d$-wave sputtering yields temperatures where the spin-orbit interaction significantly affects electronic structure.  Calculated dynamic values were also in agreement with experimental data.  Comparing results for Cr$_2$Al and Mn$_2$Au compounds highlights similarities between their properties and highlights the importance of spin-orbit coupling in certain properties.

A new kinetic model, the $\nu$-model, based on the spherical Knudsen number, is suggested. This model is an extension of the $\tau$-model from rarefied gas dynamics, incorporating a unique relaxation time tied to the collision frequency. To determine this relaxation time, the $\tau$-model's Gaussian distribution is applied, enabling a straightforward expression for the model's matrix that can be computed numerically outside the gas's collisionless regime. To validate the new model, its accuracy is compared with Monte Carlo Direct Simulation (MDS), a reference method for simulating rarefied monatomic gas flows.

Voice assistant applications, such as Alexa and Google Assistant, significantly benefit from advancements in semantic parsing, a core challenge in NLP. The latest state-of-the-art semantic parsers employ sequence-to-sequence models, built upon advanced transfer learning techniques like pre-training. The concept has shown immense potential in various NLP tasks, including our 2020 challenge on semantic parsing, where our approach significantly improved the output of users by directly integrating semantic parsing into language understanding through continuous learning. This process draws on a vast, static knowledge base to validate predicted results and ensure they align with actual user intent and real-world facts. Our technique notably demonstrated resilience to errors resulting from incorrect parameter choices in predicted logical forms without compromising accuracy.

The Electron-Ion Collider's future will involve utilizing electron-proton and electron-nucleus collisions to thoroughly investigate the fundamental components of matter. To determine the precise distribution of particles within protons and nuclei, it is crucial to understand the energy release patterns of heavy particles such as charm and bottom. To achieve this, researchers will closely monitor these particles and their fragments at the detector by utilizing cutting-edge technology. In addition, by studying the interactions of these particles in high-energy events, researchers will gain insights into the distribution functions, thus contributing to a more comprehensive understanding. This paper outlines and justifies the key measurement requirements, including observation rates, precision levels, and confidence levels for each essential measurement.

A new classification of X-ray variability patterns called the Hydrodynamic Variable Unstable Flow Model has been suggested to better organize different types of observed patterns. To date, this categorization has covered patterns seen in the Black Hole X-ray Binary system H174 Mon, as well as patterns seen in Steady Soft X-ray Emitters. This study aims to discover whether the new classification can also apply to newly detected patterns found in the spectral data of H174 Mon. Our analysis of 35 days' worth of data from which the light curve was extracted using the MAXI/GSC, revealed the presence of Quasi-Periodic Eruptions with frequencies between 0.8 to 2.2 times that of Schwartzschild frequencies, in addition to Type-I and Type-II variability. Our findings demonstrate that the Hydrodynamic Variable Unstable Flow Model effectively explains the observed properties of Quasi-Periodic Eruptions, while also highlighting the distinct characteristics of Quasi-Periodic Eruptions, Quasi-Periodic Oscillations, and Steady Soft States.

The existence of magnetic fields in stars has long sparked debate about their influence on the atmospheres of stars. Our research provides new evidence from spectropolarimetric analysis on how the strength of a magnetic field in HD58260, a magnetic star, decreases as you move higher in its atmosphere. The results suggest that the outer atmosphere has a magnetic field roughly one-third as strong as its inner layers. The increased flow of high-energy particles in magnetic fields near these stars may explain their surrounding magnetospheres and the high-energy events they exhibit. Our findings also identify a set of useful spectral lines that can be used to measure the surface magnetic fields of stars.

A link exists between a Dunkl operator over a field with two elements and a first derivative, 
exemplified through its equivalence to a operator set representing one-dimensional oscillator motion.
This equivalence holds in that the operator translates the classical Hermite polynomials into the generalized Hermite polynomials.

We observed 13 local dwarf galaxies with the Multi-Universal Linearly Regularized Imaging Piano (MULRIP) telescope, which features a 30 cm primary mirror, capable of observing a $\sim$16$^\prime$ diameter field of view at high resolution.  Our study focused on spectroscopic observations of seven HII regions, obtained using the volume phase holographic (VPH) grating at a resolving power of 2000, covering the 6500--7500 \AA{} range.  Our data, supplemented by data from the Hubble Space Telescope Advanced Camera for Spectroscopy (ACS), allowed us to measure metal abundance, star formation rate, and kinetic temperature within the regions using the R23 ratio, Seagren et al.'s (\2004) recipe, Krugel (\2003) recipe, and the diamond square algorithm, respectively.  In particular, kinetic temperature measurements indicated that the kinetic temperatures of all observed regions exceeded 50 K, with three regions displaying temperatures above 100 K, specifically H30α, which may be associated with shock heating, and two regions in NGC 5253, as well as a region in Fornax.  Our data also revealed a correlation between star formation rate and metallicity in the sample, with an established relationship similar to that reported by Kirkman et al. (\2008), but with a greater level of scatter than predicted by Kirby (\2013), which may be attributed to uncertainties in

We demonstrate that two continuous minimal actions of the infinite dihedral group on an infinite compact Hausdorff space can be orbit equivalent if and only if they are conjugate, provided the group in question remains unchanged. However, this equivalency breaks down when considering other virtually cyclic groups like the direct product of the integer group and a non-abelian finite simple group, especially when these are used instead of the infinite dihedral group.

We analyze the statistical approximation of the $L^2$-operator defined as $[Pf](x) = \mathbb{E}[f(Y) | X = x]$ given the joint distribution of $X$ and $Y$ on a certain topological space under minimal assumptions. Since direct evaluation of this operator is challenging due to the conditional expectation of random functions, we resort to Monte Carlo integration for a finite sample, which results in an approximation error related to the complexity of Hilbert--Schmidt operators. To this end, we establish a new inequality that upper-bounds this error by a term proportional to the Hilbert--Schmidt norm of the difference between two such operators, which has significant implications of its own. Interestingly, this result reveals that the rates of convergence are essentially independent of parameters characterizing the distribution of $X$ and $Y$, which suggests that the sample size determines the rates of convergence. Furthermore, this result is crucial as it enables the proof of central, normal and Poisson convergence theorems without assuming smoothness or density, and it also enables the derivation of an inequality relating the weak convergence of probability measures and empirical processes. Additionally, this result has the potential to simplify and improve the current rates of convergence of algorithms used to solve various inverse problems and has been successfully applied in this direction.

Designing effective state observers for nonlinear epidemic models is an increasingly significant challenge, largely due to their highly complex and non-linear characteristics. This difficulty is further exacerbated by the inherent model errors often encountered in real-world epidemic scenarios. This research work focuses on developing a state observer capable of adapting to unknown model errors, leveraging the fundamental Kalman filter framework. Building upon this concept, we introduce a state observer designed to mitigate the effects of unknown model errors by incorporating an error correction term incorporated into a novel Kalman filter formulation. To evaluate the performance of this innovative observer, we establish a convergence criterion based on the spectral decay rate of a corresponding Lyapunov-Schmidt operator. Ultimately, we validate the stability and adaptability of this observer through theoretical analysis and numerical simulation with specific SIR models.

The consideration of temporal contexts within knowledge graph embeddings presents a chance for enhanced performance in resultant models, especially in applications utilizing these models. Presently, there is a lack of understanding regarding how temporal contexts impact knowledge graph embedding and the optimal method to account for this context. To explore this, we examine data quality issues resulting from missing temporal context information and validate that considering temporal contexts yields superior results in inductive rule learning applications of knowledge graph embeddings. To address the issue of which temporal context to consider, we introduce a method called Temporal Context Weighted Adversarial Learning (TCWeAL) that dynamically selects and incorporates multiple temporal contexts for enhanced knowledge graph embedding. Experimental results on NFBerlin and MultiGCN datasets show that TCWeAL surpasses existing methods, achieving a 5.0% elevation in accuracy.

Research driven by ultrashort pulses from optical cavities and quantum systems has generated interest in resonators with multiple loops and geometries.  The study of these resonators is typically limited to linear analyses, but our work shows that a dynamic treatment is necessary when dealing with strong pulses.  By applying a non-linear theory based on the variable phase change approach, we investigate the dynamics of ring-shaped resonators connected to Kerr cavities and show how certain design features can safely handle extremely high energy levels.  This advances understanding of these systems and enables the design of reliable devices for multicycle pulse durations and varied two-dipler frequencies.

A decentralized learning approach called federated learning overcomes concerns about user data privacy. However, several challenges persist in practical applications, with unequal data distribution being a significant issue. To address this problem, researchers developed an adaptive method called ADAPT-FL, incorporating a drift detection mechanism that allows for adaptive client participation in FL. Specifically, this approach adapts the data distribution within each client cluster and adjusts the model aggregation frequency. Experimental results using synthetic data for a binary classification task showed that ADAPT-FL enhances the FL model accuracy, efficiency, and privacy. Compared to conventional FL, this approach improves accuracy by at least 1.1% while reducing communication overhead by nearly 49%.

To improve the energy conversion efficiency of thin-film silicon solar cells with a limited active layer thickness, researchers have suggested replacing metal back reflectors with more effective optical designs. This study compares the absorption capabilities of nanostructured 1-D photonic band gap crystals with metal. Numerical results for various 1-D photonic structures made of germanium and silicon demonstrate their potential to significantly enhance absorption for active layers as little as 50 nm thick, potentially increasing efficiency by a factor of 8. Optimal 1-D photonic band gap crystal design is proposed to achieve maximum absorption within the active layer, fully utilize the solar spectrum, and minimize reflection loss.

We have derived a set of holomorphic functions, denoted by $\beta_{a,b}$, where the iteration of the function $f(z) = a + \log(1) + \log(1) + \ldots + \log(1)$, corresponds to the behavior of $a$ within the right half-plane. In a similar fashion to the $\eta$ function discussed in the preprint "On the iteration of the exponential function", we find that $f(z) = a + \log(1) + \log(1) + \ldots + \log(1)$ may be approximated by $ \beta_{a,b}(z) = a + \frac{1}{2}z$. Additionally, the function $\beta_{a,b}$ is meromorphism if $b$ is an integer, and we establish a relationship between $\beta_{a,b}$ and the iterated exponential function $e^{e^{...e^z}}$ if $b=0$, and compare it to Ramanujan's famous result.

We have developed a novel method of constructing high dimensional expanders by utilizing covering spaces of simplicial complexes. Building upon expander graphs, high dimensional expanders play a vital role in theoretical computer science but unfortunately, there are only a few constructions available that offer arbitrarily high dimensions. Our research has led to the creation of the first systematic approach for constructing high dimensional expanders based on a given building block, specifically a high dimensional expander, and a finite group that operates on it. Furthermore, we have demonstrated the existence of groups that operate on the Cayley complex of a particular group to construct the sought-after high dimensional expander. As an additional contribution, we have discovered a novel method of constructing the Nornroth group, a particular group that operates on an 8-dimensional cross product of projective spaces, to illustrate the application of our construction by operating on the Nornroth group.

Researchers investigated the crystal and magnetic properties of the single-crystal, hexagonal GdInO3 through an integrated approach that combined experimental and theoretical methods. A 15-parameter, P6/mmm symmetric model was used for the crystal structure, while the magnetic structure was examined using a 15-parameter, AAM model. Both the crystal and magnetic structure refinements were conducted using powder data from X-ray diffraction and neutron powder diffraction, respectively. Following this, the structural model was validated using single-crystal X-ray diffraction and further refinements were made to determine the occupancy of the two indium sites utilizing single-crystal X-ray diffraction. A variable-temperature study of the magnetic structure using neutron powder diffraction revealed two AFM phase transitions at T = 5.5 K and 3.4 K. A variable-temperature study of the magnetic structure demonstrated that the arrangement of the Gd spins remains nearly unchanged while showing a gradual decrease in ordered magnetization below the second transition. A near-equivalent energy boundary exists between these two AFM states. A variable-temperature study of the magnetic structure using muon spin resonance revealed a continuous transition in the magnetic structure at T = 3.4 K, a finding that is consistent with neutron powder diffraction results. The application of graph embedding for predicting links in complex networks has shown significant progress recently. However, traditional graph embedding methods focus solely on link prediction and do not take into account the underlying structural connections within a network. This deficiency limits their ability to generate realistic and meaningful visual representations of networks. To address this limitation, we introduce Sparse Structural Network Embedding (SSNE), a novel embedding technique that utilizes a sparse and differentiable structure encoder to map large networks into low-dimensional representations. SSNE utilizes edge saliency to determine the importance of structural connections, enabling the development of diverse and meaningful visualizations. Furthermore, SSNE extends the capabilities of existing metropolis transition methods by introducing a sparse sampling technique, which generates high-quality node representations in a significantly shorter amount of time. Our research showcases the effectiveness of SSNE using real-world network datasets from Airline Transportation and Wikipedia co-authorship networks.

A low-cost water jet process is employed to achieve a 6mm deep silicon etch, overcoming depth limitations and enabling the creation of a deep atomic vapor cell. This 6mm cell shows near-ballistic laser linewidth improvements of 5.9(0.3) nanometers at 1064nm, offering comparable performance to advanced silicon wafers at a significantly reduced cost.

We evaluate the precision of a recently proposed nonlinear interference model for a wide range of dual-polarization 4D formats, exhibiting an average disparity with split-step Fourier simulations of no more than 0.1 dB.

Preemptive wildfire detection is critical for minimizing ecological harm, property damage, and human loss. Recent research has shown that fire detection through image analysis can be an effective method, and this study employs a highly effective deep learning model to identify fires in images. A scalable deep learning structure, commonly used for object detection, was adapted and refined with fire-specific features to enhance its performance. A comprehensive dataset with varied fire sizes and contexts was employed to train the model and validate its efficacy. Performance metrics indicate that the model can accurately detect fires in diverse settings with minimal noise interference. Notably, the model also identifies the fire's center point and size, providing valuable context for context-rich fire detection and characterization applications.

Early detection and treatment of depression is essential to prevent severe repercussions, making the utilization of multiple detection methods necessary, including both human and technological methods. To aid in the identification of depression's various levels and enhance machine learning model performance through data enrichment, a comprehensive dataset categorizing depression levels has been developed. By employing both qualitative and quantitative research methods to analyze social media posts regarding individuals suffering from depression, three distinct depression levels were identified: mild, moderate, and severe. These categories were established through an in-depth analysis of 1,564 social media posts and 40 expert feedback responses. The identified categories are subsequently used to establish ground truth labels for data collection, which is then utilized to train machine learning models. By employing the k-nearest neighbors algorithm with various feature selection techniques, a comparative assessment of performance is achieved. Moreover, the use of dataset levels in training neural network models results in improved accuracy and performance. By utilizing the proposed dataset levels, improvements in performance of machine learning models while validating depression levels can be achieved.

We've developed two probabilistic models for the COVID-19 pandemic. We've derived the statistical properties of these models, including correlation functions and probability distributions. The models we've created address two key aspects of the outbreak: a basic model for basic control and a more in-depth analysis for situations involving lockdowns and other targeted measures. By comparing correlation functions, we've determined that removing lockdown measures won't significantly impact the pandemic, suggesting that lockdown measures primarily delay the spread of the virus. The models we've developed also provide the likelihood and correlation functions of a certain range without the need for complicated simulations. Additionally, we've determined the specific range in which the probability of a certain outcome is non-negligible. In this range, we've developed a simpler model that accurately replicates the more complex model's behavior, offering a convenient and efficient way to simulate basic aspects of the pandemic's progression.

The ISGMR and ISGQR strengths in $82<$N$>$ island-of-inversion nuclei undergo detailed analysis through the analysis of proton scattering cross sections. Notably, in $^{108}$Ce a $IS$ double-peaked structure is discovered at 60.4 and 90.5 MeV, attributed to ISGMR and ISGQR, respectively, in line with the GQR-ISGQR splitting observed in nearby even-even nuclei. In contrast, ISGMR and ISGQR in $^{104}$Xe exhibit a double-peaked structure at 58.1 and 82.9 MeV and a single-peaked structure at 61.3 MeV, respectively, indicating a disappearance or a highly distorted ISGMR. Studies using the Skyrme energy-density function and the peaking approximation demonstrate that the ISGMR strength and peak energy are highly influenced by the incompressibility modulus $K_\infty$. Comparisons with theoretical predictions, made using the same interaction as the transport code, show that the measured ISGMR strength and peak width exhibit a good agreement both with the predicted saturation value and the value influenced by $K_\infty$. Additionally, the ISGMR strength and peak width indicate a strong indication for a negative $K_\infty$ valley.

A study on stick-slip dynamics and the convergence of motion paths in systems governed by Coulomb friction is conducted. The existence of a universally accessible and attractive region, near an equilibrium state, is confirmed through analytical means. Theoretical findings reveal that the system can only converge asymptotically, and this applies regardless of the presence or absence of frictional losses due to impacts. Moreover, the system's ability to converge is compromised when losses due to impacts are absent and the friction coefficient exceeds a certain threshold. Numerical simulations are used to support the theoretical framework, particularly in systems where velocity-dependent dry friction applies.

A novel reinforcement learning method based on the actor-critic type has been developed to tackle portfolio hedging challenges for a variety of financial securities and derivatives using historical data only. Key aspects of this approach involve leveraging various derivative types such as forwards, futures, options, and taking into account factors such as trading costs, liquidity constraints and other frictions. This algorithm can effectively handle portfolios of any nature and features continuous action and state spaces with a risk-adjusted objective. Most notably, the model allows for optimal hedging without the need for additional training in diverse initial conditions, thereby saving significant processing resources. Furthermore, theoretical analysis of the Bellman equation confirms the existence of feasible solutions and highlights the connection to our previously established Deep Hedging framework.

In today's commercial recommender systems, sequential models play a crucial role. These models predict the items users are most likely to engage with by analyzing their previous platform interactions. Despite their importance, many of these models struggle to grasp the underlying motivations driving users' actions online, making intent modeling vital for user understanding and optimal long-term engagement. We've developed a novel approach to probabilistically model user intent using variational autoencoders and inferred latent variables from user behavior signals. Our approach then adjusts the recommendation policy accordingly, based on inferred user intent. We've validated the efficacy of our approach through offline and live testing on a massive industrial platform.

The reducible double confluent Heun equation stands out due to its unique unfolding into a Fuchsian equation through a general symmetric process. The Fuchsian equation resulting from this unfolding has five distinct singular points: three located at $0$, $1$, and $\infty$, as well as two specified by two given solutions at $0$ and $1$. Three of these singular points are present in the original DCHE equation, while $\infty$ becomes a singular point after unfolding, and the point $e^{-\gamma}$ is absent but replace by $\infty$. Unfolding equations related to the solutions at $0$ and $1$ can be calculated using two established methods, and the resulting Fuchsian equations at $\infty$ depend on the monodromy properties of the initial DCHE equation. The equation at $\infty$ is constant for equations with generic monodromy, while it varies for equations with non-generic monodromy. The Fuchsian equation at $\infty$ related to the third specified point can be calculated using the AdS/CFT correspondence. The paper concludes with the provided solutions and monodromy data at $\infty$ for the Fuchsian equation resulting from the unfolding of the DCHE equation.

Low-rank matrix recovery issues with complex high-dimensional data face several obstacles, including considerable computational demands and limited data availability. The problem becomes more complicated when data is divided into separate blocks, each with different levels of observation noise. The combined issue of high dimensionality and fragmented data, known as the block-rank matrix completion problem, poses a significant challenge. Our approach to this issue involves a two-step process: initially, we use optimized block divisions to reduce the dimensionality of the incomplete matrix; subsequently, we apply a weighted nuclear norm minimization to reconstruct the original matrix. The block division process is complex and requires the use of a grid-based search to determine the optimal splitting method. To overcome this issue, we propose the use of a dynamic optimization technique to facilitate the reconstruction process. The proposed method significantly outperforms existing versions, as confirmed by comprehensive numerical simulations.

In this research, we examine the vibrational spectrum of a constrained ring, taking note of its distinct properties that defy symmetry constraints often inherent in these systems. Due to a unique symmetry breakdown at an 'exceptional point', the constraint's equilibrium position exhibits peculiar dynamics displaying equal superposition of translational and rotational movements. Moreover, this breakdown also causes a symmetry transition in the frequency spectrum, resulting in distinct groups of modes that separately increase and decrease in frequency. A mathematical model is developed to determine the spectrum's asymptotic behavior, with the scale of frequency change being constantly applied to a limiting value as the system's size increases. Interestingly, this model uncovers a previously unseen pattern in which, at the scale of which the frequency change pattern is visible, the system's dynamics behavior at the scale is identical to its unconstrained version. With the aid of an 'atlas of vibrational motion', a qualitative description of this dynamics can be obtained from that of the unconstrained system.

We introduce the semi-inclusive Lepton Flavour Universality ratio $R_\Sigma$ to verify electron and muon universality in the $b\to s\ell^+\ell^-$ process at $e^+e^-$ B-meson facilities. This combined observable enhances our capacity to detect discrepancies $a_{\rm SL}$ between $R_\Sigma$ and the theoretical value predicted using $\Delta B=1$ four-fermion interactions. A generic $|A_{\rm Cub}|/M_B$ correction to $R_\Sigma$ is also calculated, demonstrating its small but non-negligible impact. Our work supplements previous analyses with enhanced corrections to $R_{\rm SL}$ and $a_{\rm SL}$, offering a detailed exploration of systematic uncertainties in $R_\Sigma$ and $a_\Sigma$ and shedding light on the physics behind possible discrepancies between $R^0_{\rm SL}$ and $R^0_\Sigma$.

This study presents a novel approach to designing a decentralized controller for a network of interconnected agent plants, where each agent's plant is described by a linear time-invariant system, influenced by its own and neighboring agent's control inputs. Focusing on output feedback decentralized control strategies, a decentralized output controllability decomposition is introduced and along with it, decentralized output stability assessments are developed via output circulation pattern analysis. Furthermore, two design methods are proposed for output-controlling decentralized controllers, one absolute and one contingent, aiming to maximize output reduction or maintain a desired output level. It is shown that these methods result in outputs converging to expected values with adjustable convergence rates. The approach is illustrated by examples and simulations.

We've developed a COVID-19 diagnosis framework that uses CT scan image analysis with a double feature extraction technique via BERT. The initial step utilizes a 3D-CNN to extract spatial information from the CT images and then employs BERT for temporal aggregation of these features. A classification model is trained on randomly sampled CT volumes, and subsequent steps utilize the network to extract embedding features from the full scan volume. Averaging these embedding features generates the input for our BERT-based model, which aggregates temporal dimensions and produces a unified feature set. A BERT-based model operates on these features, aggregating them across the full scan volume to generate a diagnostic output. A self-designed system generates training data by randomly sampling CT volumes, which are used to train the network. A BERT-based model is used to pre-train the network, followed by fine-tuning on the BERT-based model. Evaluation of our proposed framework showed a high AUC score of 0.86 on a public dataset.

Network science is the multidisciplinary study of intricate systems, which can be represented as interconnected networks consisting of nodes and edges with various attributes. These seemingly straightforward structures conceal an extraordinary depth of complexity due to their vast array of configurations and numerous underlying physical and information systems. The boundless applications of network science have given rise to a diverse community of researchers, who are actively working at the intersection of computer science, engineering, mathematics, physics, biology, medicine, and sociology. In this article, the fundamental concepts of graph theory will serve as the foundation to explore the key challenges and opportunities presented by network science, which will be illustrated by referring to the prominent fields of study in this area, including systems biology, statistical physics, and computational intelligence. Additionally, this article will provide a comprehensive overview of network science and highlight its most notable achievements, while also addressing some pivotal challenges that are particularly relevant to the network biology field. Finally, this article will serve as an entry point and a reference for readers who are interested in further exploring network science.

The study of eco-evolutionary dynamics is being limited by the complexity of non-linear interactions and the need for more comprehensive statistical models. To better understand how changes to these systems unfold over time, researchers are investigating a specific type of simple model that incorporates both environmental and evolutionary pressures. By focusing on the characteristics of these systems when they experience unstable, chaotic behavior, researchers have found patterns in the patterns of change, specifically a unique arrangement of lines in the complex plane. By analyzing these lines, researchers have been able to develop new predictions about the long-term behavior of these systems, regardless of specific conditions. To further illustrate this approach, researchers have visually demonstrated the progression of one specific type of system through this complex region and shown how it relates to real-world changes in the study of eco-evolutionary dynamics.

A new challenge, Speech Super-Switch, has been introduced which includes Fine-grained Speech Transformation, a combination of the FSTW and BAKING datasets, containing data transformed by both signal and signal-independent factors. The goal is to improve the state-of-the-art performance in speaker identification, speech recognition, and emotion recognition tasks using end-to-end speech models. A self-supervised learning paradigm, known as speech super-switch, has been proposed to improve model performance in speaker encoding and speech modelling. Four different speech representation tasks have been created to handle the multi-factor transformation process. The speech dataset, Speech Super-Switch, is a combination of two datasets, Fine-grained Speech Transformation and BAKING, containing data transformed by both signal and signal-independent factors. Seven variants of the speech dataset, Speech Super-Switch, have been created to handle different types of speech representation tasks. The performance of speech models, encoded using speaker information, has been evaluated on multiple tasks and compared with other models, resulting in improved performance in speaker identification, speech recognition, and emotion recognition tasks.
