Our research focuses on the underlying structure of Automated Market Makers (AMMs), 
a prevalent form of blockchain-based, decentralized exchanges. 
We reveal that the order processing mechanism results in token value diminishment for liquidity providers, 
causing them to lose money over time. To offset this, providers must compensate each other 
through payment of a premium, leading to a complex token transaction process. 
Our mathematical model, verified through empirical analysis of real-world BEP20 tokens, 
investigates the mechanisms driving token price volatility, 
a key factor determining the net worth of liquidity providers. 
We discover that the token exchange rate stability and pool funding rates have the 
greatest impact on liquidity provider net worth, 
followed by funding rates, while other factors, such as service fees and token supply, 
play a relatively minor role.

A new analytical framework, referred to as Sensitivity Analysis, evaluates how conclusions based on incomplete data can be affected by uncertainties in underlying assumptions. We build upon an existing metric known as the E-value, which measures the reliability of causal inferences, and apply it to scenarios with missing outcome data. Through case studies on Facebook's partially-observed conversion events, we develop an approach to make the E-value a practical tool for analytic research, incorporating Bayesian estimation to handle the uncertainty of missing data patterns and potential confounding variables. This research also sheds light on the constraints of using the E-value in analytical settings.

This study focuses on the definition, identification, and classification of $U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$-symmetries within a larger algebraic framework. It builds upon previous work by the same authors in [arXiv:2103.01223, arXiv:2108.04944], complementing the findings with new results and insights. Several examples illustrate the concepts developed in this work, including the case of a quantum deformation of the Martinet-Zirnbauer symmetry.

The integration of Artificial Intelligence techniques and improved information systems within Internet of Vehicles (IoVs) has yielded substantial benefits, albeit with heightened risks of security breaches and compromised privacy. As IoVs technology continues to evolve, there's growing interest in privacy preservation methodologies that adapt to its shifting needs. The emergence of edge computing and Federated Learning (FL) techniques have improved data privacy through differential privacy and privacy-by-design methodologies, respectively. This survey provides a thorough examination of symmetric and asymmetric encryption methodologies and their applications in IoVs privacy issues. Additionally, it reviews various computational methods and highlights their strengths and limitations, while also proposing potential solutions to enhance FL and maintain optimal data security in the presence of adversarial attacks.

The ALICE experiment at the LHC has measured the cross sections for the production of ps Ps and ps Ps mesons, which then decay into muon pairs, in pPb collisions at an energy of 5.02 TeV. The data, recorded at the ALICE detector, covered a wide range of transverse momentum from 1 to 20 GeV/$c$ for low-mass Ps mesons and 4 to 20 GeV/$c$ for the higher-mass Ps. The results were compared with predictions from two different theoretical models, including a calculation that included all possible particle interactions and another based on a specific theoretical framework, both of which agreed well with the observed cross sections for the production of Ps mesons. The results were also used to determine the cross sections for the production of light vector mesons, which were then used to calculate the cross sections for the production of the J/$\psi$ vector meson in the same collisions.

The escalating demand for larger cooling systems to support increasingly larger numbers of cryogenic qubits in quantum computing applications is prompting innovation.
Through the National Quantum Initiative and Department of Energy's support, our work at the Superconducting Quantum Materials and Systems Center at Fermilab involves designing a 2-meter diameter by 2-meter tall cryogenic storage facility.
This facility will employ a traditional top-down versus bottom-up approach using four layers of superconducting magnets for 4 K cooling, assisted by one stage of pre-cooling and two additional stages of cold compression using approximately 450 meters of thermal transport loops.
Furthermore, our work includes the design of a novel cryogenic storage platform utilizing a novel "platform within a platform" concept which allows for increased volume efficiency at lower operational temperatures with fewer heat exchangers.
This facility will provide approximately 100 liters of dedicated storage at 350 mK, 100 liters at 3 K, and 350 liters at 4.5 K with a goal to deliver a total of 2 liter per second at 4.5 K.
Our designs focus on providing natural ventilation and access to the platform via three 1.5 meter diameter openings allowing for efficient and reliable cryogenic control and monitoring systems including temperature, pressure, and vacuum control as well as helium and nitrogen gas handling.

To assess the extent of misuses in crypto API calls, we evaluated 1,525 Python projects, identifying specific instances of misuse in approximately 61% of the projects examined. Our study provides qualitative analyses of the detected misuses, highlighting common errors. We found that using the correct hashing and digital signature functions poses a challenge, with many projects opting for low-security or obsolete crypto APIs. Based on our findings, suggested best practices are proposed to prevent such misuses. The research suggests that projects utilizing crypto APIs should integrate thorough testing to prevent similar misuses in the future.

This paper presents an effective approach for locating objects within 3D models using a combination of data captured by RGB-D cameras and 3D LiDAR data. A significant challenge in detecting and tracking objects in real-world settings involves the absence of usable training data. To overcome this limitation, our method utilizes a simulated environment to develop an initial detection and tracking strategy, which is subsequently applied to a real urban scenario. A crucial aspect of our approach involves integrating data from RGB-D cameras and LiDAR sensors to generate pointclouds representing visible general aspects of target objects. To evaluate the efficacy of our method, our experiments employ a combination of simulated and actual data. Notably, our results demonstrate that our approach achieves more accurate results than existing state-of-the-art methods on both simulated and real-world datasets.

We address the challenge of deconvolving sparse signals within seismic reflection inversion to retrieve the subsurface reflection coefficients with high resolution. Our model uses a compactness constraint on the inverse, achieving the desired deconvolution. Additionally, we incorporate an analysis domain-based penalty term to maintain stability. Our method is aligned with the principles of convex optimization and maintains consistency with the deconvolution operation. Our results on synthetic and real seismic data demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach.

This article proves that every semigroup of composition operators on BMOA-type spaces that is closed, invariant to translation, and satisfies a certain uniform continuity condition is finite. We derive two key consequences from this result: the first shows the semigroup's bandwidth is not influenced by the nature of the generating function, while the second indicates it does remain influenced by the characteristics of the generating function when the semigroup is closed and contains translations, in the context of the BMOA space. These findings generalize previously established results for standard BMOA spaces. Additionally, this article proves that semigroups of composition operators on p-BMOA spaces that are closed, invariant to translation, and satisfy a uniform continuity condition are finite. We then establish two key consequences, demonstrating the independence of the semigroup's bandwidth from the generating function's properties when the semigroup is closed and contains translations, in the context of the p-BMOA space. These findings are a generalization of previously established results for BMOA spaces.

Understanding universal properties of a critical quantum spin chain model involves analyzing its conformal field theory (CFT) representation, where calculating universal properties reduces to determining operator product expansion (OPE) coefficients in the CFT. These coefficients can be computed using conformal perturbation theory, a method that applies to translation-invariant systems. We generalized this method for use in translation-invariant systems with constraints. Two key outcomes result from this application, the first being the derivation of universal properties based on numerical diagonalization, and the second being the prediction of previously unknown universal properties in systems with a U(1) symmetry, specifically twist field two-point functions in the isotropic spin chain model with spin 1/2.

Automated part-of-speech (POS) annotation is a crucial task for linguistics and natural language processing, typically addressed through machine learning. Although the challenge of POS annotation is more pronounced in historical corpora due to orthographic irregularities, the difficulties encountered in accessing these texts are mitigated by recent advancements in digitization. As the availability of such texts increases, the need arises for automated POS tagging to facilitate linguistic research, posing a significant challenge due to the peculiarities of historical language forms. In addressing this issue, the present study proposes a multi-stage process for POS tagging, characterized by the integration of domain expertise and the utilization of unsupervised language analysis. The proposed method, developed and tested on a dataset of 18th-century texts written in German, yields satisfactory results, achieving an average accuracy of 73% across different POS categories, with considerable emphasis placed on leveraging domain-specific knowledge.

This research focuses on developing a method to determine if a proposed candidate for a demand function meets the necessary criteria for a valid demand function. Our investigation extends beyond identifying distance constraints and instead explores a more comprehensive approach that can be applied across various dimensions. This methodology has the added benefit of being able to pinpoint the specific dimensions along which a candidate's requirements are breached. We utilize this methodology in two separate case studies to analyze the Shafer demand theory, with a particular emphasis on the first three dimensions. Our results from these case studies enable us to make some general observations about the inherent characteristics of valid demand functions in certain contexts.

Smart assistants like CitySpec, designed for smart cities, aid citizens in acquiring local and timely information without human involvement. Effective specification of these systems relies on a thorough consideration of ethical and moral aspects, which often conflict with each other.  Despite the significance of ethics and morals in these systems, there is currently a lack of a unified solution to address these issues.  This research proposes a framework called SpecGen that uses natural language inputs to automatically generate specifications for CitySpec systems, incorporating diverse user preferences and safety standards.  An empirical study is conducted to validate the importance of user preferences and safety standards in smart assistant-based decision-making processes.  SpecGen is then demonstrated through a practical case example where it yields superior performance over pre-existing methods.

Our new learning-based method for error mitigation combines conventional techniques. It involves adding an extra layer, hidden, and reversible transformation to the quantum circuit, which can be viewed as an inverse of the existing errors. However, unlike conventional error correction methods, this learning-based approach does not require the explicit characterization of the quantum system's errors. In contrast to previous mitigation methods that learn the inverse of the quantum channel, this new method can handle a broader range of error types, including those caused by faulty gates. Furthermore, by utilizing a hidden inverse, this learning-based approach can decrease the number of measurements needed, which is particularly beneficial for small-scale but noisy quantum processors. To support this new method, we also provide additional resources, including a simplified tutorial on learning-based error mitigation and a publicly accessible code repository.

In a category with regular structures, taking the direct image of a given category under a surjective morphism fulfills a specific condition related to the existence of upper bounds. This property is particularly significant in categories of ordered structures, where it has the equivalent form stating direct images of substructures are substructures. In categories with more complex suprema, the existence of direct limits that are suprema in a broader category consider the situation of partial orders, where the existence of infinite upper bounds becomes the presence of a countable suprema. This property is referred to as the "suprema can be taken in a sequence" form and it is demonstrated that taking the direct image of a substructure under a surjective morphism in a category with the "suprema can be taken in a sequence" form also yields a substructure. This theorem has implications that extend to the description of varieties of ordered structures, enabling the determination of a specific form of substructure under a surjective morphism in categories of ordered structures. Furthermore, the theorem has the complementary effect in categories with the "suprema can be taken in a sequence" form, enabling the determination of a specific form of suprema in a broader category consider the situation of partial orders.

Using a joint multivariate spatial model based on work by Heffernan and Tawn and further developed by Cabras, Matier, and Tawn, we examine the joint dependence structure of wind speed and significant wave height data collected in the North East Atlantic between 1980 and 2011. Our analysis focuses on the Kustenfisser station in Germany, studying extreme sea states at this location. Investigating this dataset, we find that wind speed and wave height exhibit a negative dependence in the North East Atlantic, contrary to previous findings by Gilroy et al, which suggested a positive dependence. Our results imply that extremal wind speed and wave height share similar spatial patterns in the North East Atlantic, which the copula based method confirms, showing a strong association between the two variables through a heavy-tailed copula. Additionally, we find that extremal wind speed and wave height exhibit a spatial pattern characterized by lower values near coastal areas and higher values in more offshore regions. Our findings show that employing a model accounting for wind speed and wave height extremes reduces mean squared error and scale estimates, which the copula based method heavily relies on, unlike the situation described by Gilroy et al.

Recently, Contrasting pre-trained image and text embeddings through Visual-Language Pre-training has received significant interest due to its capacity to learn transferable visual representations. Nevertheless, its performance is limited by semantic inconsistencies between datasets. To optimize visual-textual alignment for CLIP models on various tasks, we introduce a technique that refines image-text cross-modality learning via VT-CLIP. This process involves utilizing attention-driven mechanisms to direct text features toward informative visual regions, effectively enhancing visual-textual correlation for improved category-based matching. Subsequently, we demonstrate VT-CLIP's efficacy in few-shot classification scenarios on 11 prominent datasets.

To enhance the accuracy of computational models governed by a nonsymmetric linear elliptic equation with variable coefficients, we have developed an advanced shifting framework. This methodology is designed to improve iterative shift-and-boost methods, similar to those utilized in truncated Newton methods, by generating better initial shift estimates. Although initially tailored to symmetric matrices, we now broaden the spectrum to include nonsymmetric matrices, focusing on the Dirichlet-Neumann problem described above. Furthermore, we present adaptive strategies for choosing parameters in the shifting framework and demonstrate the resulting convergence rates. Numerical experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on fundamental applications, including the simulation of incompressible non-Newtonian fluid flow.

We calculate the slices and the slice spectral sequence of integral suspensions of the equivariant Eilenberg-Mac Lane spectra, where the spectra of the form $H\underline{\mathbb{Z}}$ are considered, and the equivariance group in question is the quaternionic group $Q_8$. In the process, we compute the $TPorter$-isomorphisms for all integer values of $n$. These computations reveal that equivariant $p$-local $H\underline{\mathbb{Z}}$-spectra do not possess a homotopy colimit decomposition over the category of finite sets equipped with $Q_8$-actions. To offer an explanation, we note that $Q_8$-sets with a finite dimension are inductive limits of finite sets, but this property does not apply to $H\underline{\mathbb{Z}}$-spectra even after taking the homotopy colimit spectrum. In order to determine $TPorter$-isomorphisms, we employ an equivariant $K(2)$-theory method and establish an equivariant version of the Porter-Conjecture for $H\underline{\mathbb{Z}}$-spectra in the $p$-local setting.

Given a Noetherian local ring with a specific prime characteristic and its primary ideal in terms of an $\mathfrak{m}$-primary parameter, we establish criteria for $F$-rationality based on the tight Hilbert function of that ideal. These criteria make use of a specific polynomial and its coefficient. Additionally, we provide a lower bound for the tight Hilbert function that extends a previous result from Goto and Nakamura, which specifically holds true in equidimensional excellent local rings. If the ring has a specific dimension, we demonstrate the connection between the tight Hilbert function and its lower bound, achieving this condition implies that the ring is $F$-rational. However, this condition does not hold without further constraints, as evident from constructed examples. Based on the ring's properties and test elements, we find formulas to express various coefficients, including the $e_1$, $e_2$, and $e_3$, in a specific polynomial in terms of these parameters, making these coefficients calculable for specific rings. Furthermore, we establish the relationship between $F$-rationality and the coefficients of the tight Hilbert function, as well as the relationship between the coefficients of the tight Hilbert function and the coefficients of the Hilbert-Samuel polynomial, particularly in specific types of local rings.

The application of machine learning in image diagnostics within pathology and radiology is gaining momentum, primarily relying on standardized digital imaging formats such as DICOM. Despite being an industry standard for image distribution, DICOM is more than just an image format; it encompasses specific tags that carry a wide range of metadata, including image characteristics, patient information, and treatment details. The extraction and representation of these metadata can be crucial in the machine learning pipeline, enabling customized models that take the patient's anatomical structure into consideration, among other factors. This article delves into various aspects of incorporating DICOM image metadata into the machine learning process, highlighting the existing challenges, describing approaches to data processing, and examining the benefits of incorporating this information into the machine learning pipeline, although noting that, to date, there is limited research available on this topic.

No evidence exists to support Young's conclusion that Noether's charge related to a symmetry involving the coordinate t is equal to the surface gravity. However, it is found that the charge associated with the symmetry involving the advanced time tau, when combined with a specific stress tensor, results in the Bekenstein-Hawking entropy. Furthermore, using a specific stress tensor, the charges associated with specific symmetries reveal relationships with the gravitational parameters of the Kerr-Newman solution. While these charges do not provide a means to calculate these parameters, they can be used to derive the equations of motion for charges within the Kerr-Newman geometry. Specifically, a method involving a specific stress tensor and a symmetry involving null geodesics allows for the determination of a constant, finite electric potential between a charge and an anticharge.

In recent times, deep learning models have been effectively utilized for categorizing DNA sequences based on various tasks. A major challenge often arises due to the lengthy and variable nature of these DNA sequences. In our current research, a sequence-to-sequence autoencoder model is applied in an unsupervised manner to derive a standardized, fixed-dimensional latent representation for long and variable DNA sequences. The resulting latent representation is then evaluated for a supervised task - splice site classification - both qualitatively and quantitatively. The quantitative assessment was conducted under two distinct conditions. The results demonstrate the efficacy of using these learned representations as features or prior information in related tasks. Moreover, through qualitative analysis, it is observed that the obtained representations contain not only the primary information but also capture the detailed, subtle nuances present within the DNA sequences.

The manner in which the surface of materials is terminated has significant implications for their physical characteristics. Research on V$_2$O$_3$ filmsyeilded first principles calculations which demonstrated that the metal-insulator transition in these films is contingent upon the surface termination. Investigations of transport properties found that the bulk of V$_2$O$_3$ behaves as a metal, yet monolayer and bilayer films exhibited an insulating nature. Through the use of molecular orbitals, it was established that the surface termination dictates the type of band formed at the surface, thereby influencing the transition between metal and insulator states. Furthermore, it was discovered that the surface termination impacts the spin polarization of V orbitals, thereby affecting the transition. Through the application of the Zeeman model and calculation of spin polarization, it was found that surface termination led to the creation of a tri-layer magnetic metal structure, with a spontaneous polarization of ~$1.0\times10^5$ J/T, and a relatively high polarization of ~$1.0\times10^6$ J/T for a monolayer and bilayer films respectively. These findings have significant implications for the use of V$_2$O$_3$ in spintronics and magnetoelectronics technologies, highlighting the importance of surface termination and thickness of films in determining their magnetic properties.

A new, systematic method referred to as the Clebsch canonization has been proposed to convert Lie-Poisson equations into equivalent canonical Hamiltonian systems through a momentum map connection. This process is based on a dual momentum map connection and results in a symplectic representation that depends on the momentum map. It is revealed that the resulting Hamiltonian functions form a Poisson module. Furthermore, the proposed method is beneficial for solving Lie-Poisson equations and can be applied to well-studied systems, such as the Kepler and magnetohydrodynamic systems, to derive new forms of their Hamiltonian structures.

The team has completed a comprehensive analysis of microlensing planets identified by the KMTNet AnomalyFinder in 2018, resulting in 9 newly identified and 8 previously known planets in the sub-polar regions. Out of these 9 new planets, 8 were discovered in the Galactic bulge and 1 in the SPM1 field. Notably, 4 of the newly found planets possess a significant fraction of dark/luminous matter. A crucial aspect of this research lies in the differentiation of true microlensing planets from lens zone analogs, which is achieved through various diagnostics such as radial velocity observations, angular Einstein radii, and anomaly/ejecta fitting formulas. Radial velocity data from the WIRCAML survey supported the planetary nature of several candidates. Furthermore, this study's findings enhance the current microlensing planet mass-ratio dataset and offer future prospects for differentiation.

To address a category of optimal control issues for hyperbolic conservation law systems and their regularization variants across one- and two-dimensional spaces, we develop a generalized theory based on the notion of characteristic coordinates, without assuming specific structures or assumptions about the equations' coefficients. This theory is illustrated by applying it to the Euler equations, specifically applying it to the two-dimensional Euler equations to recover previously existing results and to the one-dimensional Euler equations for a newly identified and useful regularity criterion. It's also shown that the theory can handle complex geometries through the study of the spherically symmetric stellar equations in three-dimensional space. These studies demonstrate the effectiveness of the characteristic approach to strong localizations. By combining the characteristic approach with a homogeneous Besov space framework, we achieve our generalized theory, while the associated numerical schemes and their stability are addressed in a companion paper.

Accurately predicting non-performing loans for individual clients is a key factor for banks to mitigate credit risk and make informed lending decisions. Considering clients typically apply for loans without revealing their financial details, banks must rely on other factors such as income, employment history, and personal background. Recent research, particularly in deep learning for non-performing loans, has largely focused on data from defaulting clients, which doesn't fully capture this hidden credit issue. In this study, we investigate how to classify loans for clients where hidden credit information is a concern, by comparing the effectiveness of different models when given limited data, in a semi-supervised setting, using metrics including accuracy, precision, and loss. Our analysis includes a baseline review of current deep learning approaches, coupled with an evaluation of how to handle biased data, including using balanced metrics, data normalization, and algorithms that adjust for biased data, with our results showing that including unlabelled data points, especially from the client making the application, significantly improves loan classification accuracy when considering application behavior.

The connections between the chromatic symmetric functions of specific Dyck paths, originally discovered by Stanley and later expanded on by Shareshian-Wachs in their $q$-analogue, are crucial in their associations with Hessenberg varieties, diagonal harmonics, and LLT polynomials. Notably, for the $q$-analogue in question, a combinatorial interpretation was proposed by Nzębik, which we demonstrate to be invalid. Nonetheless, its proposed recursive relation can be verified. Additionally, analogous interpretations have been developed for the initially discovered chromatic symmetric function in question.

Deep learning models, specifically Deep Convolutional Neural Networks (DCNNs), are capable of generating robust image representations, but are limited in their ability to account for image pose. The issue arises when similar images with varying orientations have distinct representations, leading to degraded performance in tasks like classification and generation. To mitigate this shortcoming, we have developed Orientation Convolution Networks (OCNs), an extension of DCNNs that incorporates a pose-aware component using orientational self-supervised learning. By leveraging a consistent representation across various orientations, OCNs improve performance on both classification and generation tasks using less data. Our results showcase the effectiveness of OCNs in outperforming state-of-the-art models like DeepSightNet on challenging image recognition tasks. Additionally, OCNs significantly improve image editing tasks, like transfer learning, by accounting for image orientation. Our source code is available at https://github.com/asharakeh/DeepSightNet.

Using a novel relative trace formula, we investigate linear periods on $GL_{2n}$ that are modulated by a character. The key elements in this process involve establishing the relative fundamental lemma and the transfer of orbital integrals. Coupled with the spectral isolation technique pioneered by Beuzart-Plessis--Liu--Zhang--Zhu, we derive comparisons of the elliptic aspects of the involved relative trace formulas, ultimately yielding novel outcomes that extend Waldspurger's theorem to the scenario where n is equal to 1.

We develop a systematic method to study the impact of mass on the pole mass in the case of a heavy quark flavor having a higher mass value than the top quark. Using soft-catalyzed asymptotic expansions in the $\alpha_s$ perturbative series, we perform a renormalization group analysis tailored to heavy quark flavors within the MSbar and SCarm schemes, allowing for a detailed comparison with mass-independent schemes like the on-shell scheme. By applying this new technique to pole mass evolution, we establish that: 1) pole mass systematic renormalization group techniques are valid and universal; 2) pole mass systematic methods eliminate unnecessary systematic uncertainties; 3) pole mass systematic techniques make clear the systematic nature of mass truncation errors; 4) when mass truncation errors are minimized, method choices become irrelevant and do not contribute to total systematic uncertainties. Furthermore, we find that pole mass systematic techniques allow for a significant reduction of total systematic uncertainties to a few GeV, making it around one order of magnitude smaller than current experimental values.

Consider a graph $G$ and a subset $R$ of its vertices $V(G)$.  A specific edge coloring of $G$ with colors from 1 to $t$, where edges connected to vertices in $R$ must have the same color, can be defined as $R$-sequential $t$-coloring.  The challenge consists of determining if such a coloring exists in graphs $K_m \backslash K_n$ and determining the minimum number of colors required, which we'll denote as $\chi_{R}(K_m \backslash K_n)$.  Given a set of integers $S$, we'll show that if $|S|+1 \leq n/m$ and $m+n/m \leq 2$, then $\chi_{R}(K_m \backslash K_n)$ with $R$ consisting of vertices in $G \backslash K_n$ and having connectivity constraint $S$, is $t = |S|+1$.  Furthermore, if $|S|+1 \leq n/m$ and $m+n/m \leq 2$, we'll show that $|R(G \backslash K_n)| = |S|+1$ is the minimum cardinality of $R$ with this property. We establish a precise relationship between L^p to L^q contraction inequalities in weighted Bergman spaces over the unit disk, incorporating typical weight factors and α > 1. This outcome addresses an unresolved issue in reference \cite{JANSON}, with the added consideration of cases where q is greater than or equal to 2, while providing related estimates for 0 < q < 2.

Currently, the most trusted diagnostic tool for COVID-19 is RT-PCR, which takes several days and often yields false results. Computed Tomography (CT) scans can provide valuable assistance in formulating a diagnosis, especially in identifying pulmonary lesions associated with the virus. Due to severe restrictions on scan doses resulting from the low signal-to-noise ratio, ultra-low-dose CT scans often fail to meet diagnostic standards, making their application challenging. To address this issue and minimize the risks associated with COVID-19, researchers combined deep learning with radiological analysis by developing a multi-stage framework for enhancing ultra-low-dose CT scans, which produced high-quality diagnostic images and outperformed competing scans in terms of accuracy, specifically in identifying lung lesions associated with COVID-19. By applying noise reduction techniques and a lung segmentation process, this framework successfully improved image quality and reduced the reliance on noisy data. Consequently, the diagnostic accuracy of ultra-low-dose CT scans increased, enabling healthcare professionals to formulate a diagnosis based on a broader range of data, including those obtained via deeper learning. Which method do you think is more beneficial for enhancing diagnostic accuracy in COVID-19 cases: lung segmentation or three-dimensional CT reconstruction? Justify your answer with your analysis of the data and results provided. How does the accuracy of diagnostic scans performed using the U-Net model compare to that of models performing 3D U-Net and Class Activation Map (CAM) analysis? What potential challenges might researchers face when developing new diagnostic

As numerous satellite constellations in the low-Earth orbit region are scheduled to launch, effectively arranging the space occupied by each satellite in their operational trajectories is essential to prevent collisions and reduce critical encounters. Here, the term "space occupancy" is defined as the area an individual satellite covers during its orbit, taking into account external perturbations and a specified timeframe. Following the discovery of a strong connection between space occupancy in the zonal problem and the principles of frozen orbits and proper eccentricity, frozen-orbit initial conditions in osculating element space were derived and a frozen-orbit polar equation was formulated to define the space occupancy region in an analytically closed form. Further analysis explored minimizing space occupancy in a more general model incorporating various perturbations, such as Gauss-type and Leontovich-Poiseuille, using a single-integrator frozen-orbit approach. To verify the effectiveness and uniqueness of the obtained frozen-orbit solutions, numerical integrations were performed and the results were visualized to facilitate identification of frozen orbits with minimal space occupancy.

To generate top-quality meshes for computational purposes, a significant task involves fair and efficient construction of a quadrilateral mesh with distinct properties. Unlike other basic mesh types, in higher order computing scenarios, quadrilateral elements offer greater advantages due to their compatibility with continuous representations. This research focuses on developing an efficient and fair algorithm to generate a smooth, oriented quadrilateral mesh continuously represented as a Labelling Function. Consequently, the resulting mesh is comprised of varied elements - including triangles - and features primarily quadrilateral elements. In essence, the algorithm aims to yield a mesh with optimal qualities, including few and straightforward boundaries and a seamless layout, all within a specified domain while adhering to constraints such as node placements and field function considerations. Notably, the algorithm incorporates a setup of PDEs that facilitate smooth, oriented mesh formation and includes a seamless and efficient implementation using CGAL data structures and functions for seamless triangulation of certain elements.

Pearson's correlation coefficient is frequently employed as a measure of association in statistical analysis. The strength of evidence for linear correlation is often evaluated using a hypothesis test, resulting in a p-value. Under certain data transformations and assuming normal distribution of a dataset, a t-statistic provides an exact p-value; otherwise, the result is an approximation. The p-value can be estimated by analyzing how a sample correlation coefficient behaves under different permutations of the data. Although such estimates may rely on approximations of distribution moments, an inductive approach in this paper offers a precise formula for expressing sample correlation distribution moments in terms of the dataset's central moments, allowing for the development of novel estimation methods to compute the p-value.

We detail the reasoning behind implementing a quantum S-matrix framework for tackling classical gravitational scattering between two bodies. Furthermore, a method is briefly discussed for computing black hole metrics across multiple spatial dimensions.

We investigate the two- or three-dimensional Navier-Stokes equations in the Biot-Savart framework for external forces within the $L^3(\mathbb{R}^3)$, $L^{\frac{3}{2}}(\mathbb{R}^3)$, or log-space. Our analysis ultimately leads to well-poseness assessments in the specified function spaces, thus filling gaps in prior research and resolving the open Navier-Stokes problem for certain spaces. Moreover, our results establish continuous dependence on the external force for solutions within specific spaces. We also derive continuous dependence estimates for two or three dimensional solutions within specific $L^p(\mathbb{R}^3)$ spaces. Notably, our approach in three dimensions involves novel techniques, including a simplified use of local mean sparsification, a concept introduced by C. De Lellis and J. Schneider in 2020, as well as a novel $A_1$-weighted $BMO$-estimates for the solution $u$ and its vorticity $w=\nabla^\perp p-\text{rot}u$.

Language learning dictionaries can facilitate vocabulary acquisition by supplying words, definitions, and examples. However, conventional dictionaries often struggle to provide sufficient information. A potential solution lies in leveraging generative dictionaries, equipped with a pre-trained neural model, that can generate various examples and descriptions to aid vocabulary building. A novel evaluation framework is introduced to assess the effectiveness of generative dictionaries and gadgets, such as image and audio samples, in improving vocabulary acquisition. Our research reveals that generative dictionaries and samples generate more meaningful content, according to human evaluations, whereas statistical analysis indicates that relevant word associations contribute significantly to this positive impact.

The growing interest in transparent AI has led to an increase in research on explainable recommendation systems. Among these, post-hoc methods have been identified as the most practical solutions for intricate models that operate as "black-boxes." Recent studies have exposed limitations in local surrogate-based post-hoc explanations regarding their inherent reliability, especially in critical applications such as human-centric recommendation tasks. Moreover, an ideal explanation should enhance key aspects of user experience including clarity and trustworthiness, posing additional challenges for current approaches. However, the existing classification methods lack the necessary level of transparency or grounding in human perception laws, thus falling short in addressing these concerns. In light of these issues, we propose a novel framework called PERCEIVE to elevate local surrogates from mere prediction techniques to actionable decision-making tools. Specifically, PERCEIVE incorporates a perception-aware mechanism that incorporates human perception laws and a structured feature representation obtained through disentangled user-item understanding. Comprehensive experiments conducted on multiple public recommendation datasets validate the efficacy of our framework in enhancing the accuracy of post-hoc explanations while aligning better with human perception and user preferences, as evidenced by a significant 69.5% improvement in feature identification rates and a notable increase of 25.2% in human evaluation scores compared to the baseline approach.

Quantum devices based on superconducting properties may be effectively produced
using semiconductor-superconductor hybrids, consisting of materials in close
contact and a well-formed connection. The surface energy levels of materials such as
InAs, which exhibit strong interactions with other layers, can significantly influence
electron movement. This study focuses on the movement of electrons within thin
layers of InAs, situated near the surface, using transport and scanning probe
techniques on samples from two different materials, MoSe2 and WSe2. The surface
texture was found to greatly impact electron movement in samples from one material,
but those from the other material showed little to no impact. This discovery led to
the suggestion that special properties within narrow bands of energy are the cause.
X-ray analysis revealed variations in surface energy levels, correlated with changes
in electron movement. This study further examines how these surface energy levels
change when exposed to various energies of light, showing a significant, abrupt
change in electron movement in samples from one material, but a more gradual,
consistent change in those from the other material. The observed behavior can be
explained by the presence of weakly connected surface energy bands, located close
to the main energy bands. This study provides key insights into the movement of
electrons at the surface of materials, important for the creation of efficient
superconducting semiconductors hybrids.

Research has indicated various forms of adversarially trained learning models that can withstand attacks generated by state-of-the-art differentiable methods. Yet, the trade-offs between model robustness and accuracy remain poorly understood. This study investigates a family of learning models, referred to as local robust classifiers, that utilize multiple 2nm; 0) local membership queries to devise adversarial examples. We establish robust learning algorithms for these classifiers, as well as analyze lower bounds on sample complexity, demonstrating that the trade-offs between robustness and accuracy are significant. This study provides the first theoretical insights into a class of machine learning models, as well as the trade-offs involved in adversarially trained models, empirically confirmed using a specific neural network architecture.

Our previous research significantly sped up Sinkhorn iteration by taking advantage of a kernel matrix's inherent properties, transforming its $O(N^2)$ complexity to $O(N)$ efficiency. This paper delves deeper into kernel matrix characteristics by defining and applying two key concepts, Lower-ColLinear Triangular Matrices and Upper-ColLinear Triangular Matrices, which are characterized by specific equality constraints. We prove that these matrices can perform matrix multiplication, solving linear equations, and calculating inverses in linear time, despite a cubic time inversion in traditional methods. To demonstrate the potential of these findings, we improve our previous research and utilize our findings to implement an efficient Sinkhorn iteration, ultimately contributing to a streamlined and efficient implementation of the Sinkhorn-Knopp process and its variants.

Young stars releasing intense X-ray and UV radiation can drastically alter planetary atmospheres, influencing both mass loss and chemistry. Observing AU Mic, an active 22-million-year-old star hosting two planets inside its debris disk, presents an extraordinary chance to study these impacts directly. AU Mic's planetary atmospheric interactions can be investigated through high-resolution spectroscopy, taking advantage of the low spectral resolution and Earth's atmospheric scattering effects that allow us to detect atmospheric gases at low concentrations. Our cross-correlation analysis of the GIIRS on the Spitzer telescope detected water (H2O) in the circumstellar disk surrounding AU Mic's planets, discovering a previously unseen signal for high-energy water emission. Fitting planetary atmospheres with the NLTE MARF model reveals that both planets feature water in their upper atmospheres, consistent with solar nebula dust grain temperatures predicting water emission at mid-IR wavelengths. Further modeling indicates that planetary mass loss due to strong stellar winds can reproduce the observed water emission pattern, while thermal escape could generate higher emission consistent with upper atmosphere temperatures around 700 K. Our analysis suggests that planetary atmospheric loss is influenced by the surrounding disk, possibly reducing the amount of water lost in the circumstellar disk. These findings provide the initial direct observations of high-energy water emission in planetary atmospheres, inspired by exoplanets within debris disks and their interactions with their host stars.

We develop an innovative approach to describe the friction caused by radiation experienced by particles moving through a medium with mechanical resistance. We introduce an effect where the medium is warped by the motion of charged particles in a way that the Larmor formula accurately describes the energy lost due to radiation. We compare this description to a different model that has been explored in the past and find that they are related by a simple transformation. We also use our description to provide a new understanding of the friction caused by radiation in a universal way, applying it to particles with any form of electric charge and moving through any type of medium with mechanical resistance. We derive a general expression for the friction caused by radiation and show its similarity to the universal friction caused by other types of energy loss mechanisms. We confirm that our derivation of the universal radiation friction applies to any situation where the friction caused by other types of energy loss mechanisms dominates. We also derive a new expression for the friction caused by radiation experienced by particles moving through a plasma and show its relation to the friction caused by other types of energy loss mechanisms in plasmas. We confirm that the universal radiation friction can explain the decrease in rate of spread of radioactive isotopes in the field.

In the context of an unevenly distributed classification problem, most popular classifiers are known to favor larger groups, and the nearest neighbor classifier is not immune to this phenomenon. To address this issue, a revised nearest neighbor classifier has been developed, which incorporates a weighted voting system where class-specific coefficients determine the contribution of individual samples. The proposed classifier aims to mitigate the influence of dominant classes and highlight distinct features specific to individual groups, ultimately leading to a boost in recognition rates and reduction in errors. A comprehensive theoretical framework for the revised classifier has been formulated, showing its capabilities to counterbalance the effects of uneven class distributions and establish a lower boundary for its performance. Moreover, the revised classifier has a wider margin of error compared to other competing methods, and the derived bounds are relatively tight. To further facilitate the application of the revised classifier, a straightforward algorithm for calculating its component weights has been introduced. The supporting theorems for the revised classifier have been proven using a novel technique known as local kernel approximation, which offers additional benefits and applications. To demonstrate the validity of the proposed classifier, a series of classification experiments were conducted using data sets characterized by uneven class distributions. The results show a substantial improvement in recognition rates and reduction in errors for the revised classifier, and the consistency of its performance across a range of data sets implies a wider applicability of the derived theoretical framework.

We employ photometry data from multiple sources to identify extremely luminous quasars across five distinct redshift ranges between z=5.7 and z=8.5 by examining their distribution in color space. Following thorough validation of their identification process, we present a comprehensive set of 17 extremely luminous quasars spanning z=5.7 to z.82. Our research also takes into consideration the evolution of extremely luminous quasar color patterns over time, finding a consistent pattern in color space up to z=8.5 and detecting a significant shift towards bluer colors at z=10.37 and z=12.06. Furthermore, we use our quasar findings to refine and extend the observed luminosity pattern of extremely luminous quasars across z=5.7 to z=8.5 with a double-Schmidt law shape. Our research indicates a significant increase in Extremely Luminous Quasar density by approximately 3-4 times between z=6 and z=8 compared to local measurements. Our research challenges a hypothesis suggesting a significant decrease in Extremely Luminous Quasar density by approximately 2-3 times between z=7.4 and z=8 due to changes in galaxy unionization.

We have successfully observed the charge-tunneling phenomenon occurring between a quantum dot and a superconducting island using a technique that employs radio-frequency sensing. Our approach has allowed us to distinguish between different types of tunneling events, specifically those driven by individual particles as well as by pairs of particles called Cooper pairs. Furthermore, we've found that the quantum dot can be utilized to create a variety of entangled states with these tunneling events, providing a unique method for analyzing the boundaries between different electronic states with reduced signal noise. This method can potentially be used to detect more complex phenomena, such as the exchange of information, and to create novel many-body states in future experiments.

Our research explores the contraction behavior of specific types of shockwaves in systems of equations, particularly those that conserve quantities, in higher-dimensional spaces. We demonstrate the existence of stable sets for these shockwaves and establish the ultimate sets towards which they converge over time. Our findings include the creation of specific systems of equations for which the allowable sets towards which the shockwaves converge are precisely defined.

We explore novel view generation -- the challenge of generating distant, unseen views by virtually navigating a given image -- through a new, promising approach. Our contribution is DiffDreamer, an unsupervised system that synthesizes novel long-distance views by simulating camera movements and training with vast, publicly available image datasets. Our experimental results demonstrate that conditioned diffusion models excel over traditional GAN-based methods, enabling accurate long-distance scene extrapolation. Furthermore, we introduce and evaluate two novel, high-fidelity quantitative metrics for assessing virtual navigation performance in image synthesis.

Many complex systems feature networks where interactions between diverse agents combine simple local rules to create complex emergent behaviors. In various applications, it is crucial to understand the role of random and complex network structures. This research focuses on a specific type of network, known as scale-free networks, featuring a power-law distribution of node connectivity. We investigate the dynamic patterns that emerge from the interaction of random and complex network topologies among a group of agents adhering to a simple decision-making rule. Each agent updates its state by taking an average with neighboring nodes, leading to a state of equilibrium. Through in-depth analysis of the system's properties, as well as numerical simulations, we explore how the unique characteristics of random and complex networks impact the system's behavior.

The dynamics of a liquid film on a fiber heavily depend on how liquids and solids interact at their interface. This interaction influences the rate of film thinning and determines whether the process is governed by gravity or other factors. Previous studies have shown that small changes can significantly impact this thinning process. In this work, we investigate the effect of one such factor, liquid-solid slipping, on the development of perturbations in a cylindrical liquid film. Our research reveals that any discrepancies in how liquids and solids move at their interface lead to faster growth of perturbations during the initial stages of thinning. Consequently, these faster-growing fluctuations eventually take over and dominate the film thinning process. This understanding is then extended to analyze the dynamics of a spherical liquid film and validated through experiments and numerical simulations, which include varying factors to achieve different slip boundary conditions.

We investigate the temporal Lipschitz stability for solutions of the Hunter-Saxton equation, focusing on $\alpha$-dissipative solutions with $\alpha$ a constant in the interval $[0,1]$. We introduce and study the properties of metrics both in the Lagrangian and Eulerian frameworks to determine Lipschitz stability within those systems.

Evaluating scoliosis with ultrasound imaging is particularly difficult for individuals without prior experience. A new approach uses a robotic device to insert and operate an ultrasound probe along the spine, accurately aligning it with the spinous processes first by guiding it to the sacrum, then up the spine. The robotic device can fully automate the imaging process, but for more precise measurements, marks are placed on the skin to guide human interpretation of the images. The combination of robotic scanning and manual image analysis was tested in 42 individuals to assess the accuracy of using manual ScolioGraphy for measuring scoliosis curvature. The results showed good correlation between the ScolioGraphy measurements and clinical spine curvature assessments, suggesting that this approach could provide a reliable and accurate method for scoliosis monitoring.

This paper introduces an innovative method for duration modelling in statistical parametric speech synthesis. Unlike traditional approaches that rely on a single, global mean representation for durations. Our proposed framework utilizes context-aware duration profiles, where the shape is estimated using a median rather than a mean. This enables more effective modelling of varying temporal patterns within a sentence. Additionally, the model now accounts for these patterns in a non-parametric manner. Our research demonstrates that incorporating these profiles into a speech synthesis model yields significant improvements in quality, as measured by the mean opinion score. Moreover, using the median rather than the mean for duration shape estimation contributes to these gains and further enhances the model's adaptability when combined with non-parametric auxiliary features.

Identifying online hate speech is increasingly critical due to its capacity to inflict emotional and psychological harm on minority groups. A recent study from the Global Online Hate Speech Index revealed that hate speech against sexual and gender minorities is particularly prevalent, with an observation that it often goes unreported in survey responses. Given this alarming issue, researchers continue to explore innovative solutions to detect hate speech online, and this study proposes a novel framework to classify hate speech against sexual and gender minorities in Danish language posts from social media platforms, leveraging BERT and Multi-Layer Perceptron models in a mixed bag of tricks configuration. Comparing the performance of different tokenization approaches and training sample sizes, this study found that pre-trained Danish BERT-based models outperform other models in classification tasks, with specific subsets of samples exhibiting exceptional performance. A Multi-Layer Perceptron model with specific dense layers also demonstrated impressive results, emphasizing the importance of tailored training data in accurate hate speech detection. Furthermore, this study analyzed the effect of different data splitting methods and found that random splitting produces consistent results, suggesting that working with multiple algorithms and parameters is an effective strategy to detect hate speech.

Multi-input multi-output (MIMO) networks attempt to improve ensemble performance by training separate subnetworks within a base model and combining their predictions. However, these networks have been found to inefficiently use parameters, hindering their adoption on constrained devices such as smartphones and AR/VR devices. This study suggests that a key issue with current MIMO frameworks lies in their failure to account for interactions between subnetworks, leading to excessive parameter replication and decreased adaptability. We introduce an innovative'silence' mechanism that allows subnetworks to dynamically learn when and how to utilize their parameters, and when not to, thereby preventing unnecessary collaborations and diminishing the size of the shared parameter set. Our proposed approach, dubbed subNet MIMO (sNIMO), demonstrates superior performance relative to traditional MIMO frameworks on widely-used datasets such as CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100, while notably reducing the overall parameter count by as much as 80%.

This study undertakes a comprehensive analysis of existing datasets pertinent to the analysis of historical documents, encompassing a range of tasks such as document image segmentation, ground truth creation, noise removal, visual aesthetic enhancement, text-based identification, sentence or word extraction, and name detection. An in-depth review of 54 prominent datasets has been conducted to facilitate future research endeavors within this domain. The review's primary objectives involve scrutinizing the conventional methods employed in building datasets for document analysis tasks, as well as examining the suitability of deep learning techniques in expanding upon existing datasets. A detailed examination of the suite of tools available for processing document images has also been conducted. The ultimate goal of this review is to facilitate future research directions and offer recommendations for improving existing datasets. An interactive web-based platform has been created to provide access to the datasets under review.

Due to the inherent elasticity in their design, industrial robots that lack advanced precision-enhancing technology are only marginally effective for machining tasks. Besides issues related to structure, temperature, and support bearings, one of the primary causes of performance degradation lies in the motor drive systems. The underlying motor dynamics cause deformation by generating uneven axial forces that result in geometric distortions. By modeling these effects through an adaptive neural network, it becomes possible to devise a correction strategy to mitigate the performance degradation. In this study, a detailed simulation-based analysis of the dynamics of a KUKA Quantec KR300 is provided, revealing the extent of geometric distortion, torque, and acceleration errors it experiences. Furthermore, a numerical correction method is proposed and validated using real-time data from an accompanying sensor to refine the trajectory of the robot's motion. The outcome shows that the correction technique can substantially improve the accuracy of the robot's motion by up to 87% on a machining surface, thereby facilitating the production of high-quality products.

The study of how chronic diseases evolve throughout an individual's lifetime has primarily been examined using a one-way approach, where early life experiences are the primary factors being investigated.  Recent research has revealed the importance of considering persistent individual characteristics, originating from early life exposures, in understanding later life health trajectories.  Three distinct theories provide the framework for characterizing individual life paths - stress trajectory theory, trajectory mix theory, latent trajectory theory, as well as patterns of deviation from normal development - all of which can capture both healthy and diseased states.  Utilizing longitudinal data from the 1953 British Birth Cohort, this research applies various statistical techniques to analyze persistent individual characteristics, originating from early life exposures, in understanding later life health trajectories.  Specifically, latent trajectory models, stress trajectory models, combination distribution models, and patterns of deviation from normal development have been estimated and examined.  Findings reveal that early life experiences not only shape health trajectories, they also persist throughout a person's lifetime.  Specifically, findings reveal that persistent individual characteristics originating from early life experiences explain a substantial portion of variation in later life health outcomes.

One widely accepted method for evaluating electronic integrals in complex molecules involves a modified version of Becke's partitioning scheme, originally designed for functions that decline rapidly over distance. This method employs overlapping grids at each atomic site, effectively dividing the integrand. Although the method has a known bias, a commutator that compensates for this effect has yet to be defined across all molecular configurations. Developing an algorithm that calculates this bias, therefore, has significant implications for ensuring that electronic integrals evaluated via this method remain unbiased. This study develops an algorithm that calculates the molecular bias, confirmed to be accurate through verification with spherical harmonics and cubic crystal structures. This algorithm, in turn, enables evaluation times to remain constant with increasing atomic size in space.

In a graph, a subset of vertices forms a resolving set if, for any two vertices, a single set vertex is positioned at different distances from the two vertices. The problem of finding a resolving set of a specific size has been recognized as a significant challenge in graph theory. Utilizing the concept of contractive metric spaces in functional analysis, the authors develop a new condition to guarantee the existence of large resolving sets in graphs. This condition combines with other methods to identify graphs meeting certain size requirements. The authors also introduce a new class of graphs meeting a specific size requirement, based on a different concept called independent resolving sets.

Domain theory's powerdomains hold significant importance in the semantics of non-deterministic programming languages.  This paper extends powerdomains to directed spaces - a class of spaces that encompass various types, including domains, topological spaces, order structures, and strict partial orders.  Powerdomain-like spaces are defined for directed spaces through structural recursion, and these domains are examined in relation to space types.  This study demonstrates that these domains are inherently possessed by any directed space but exercising the choice in a subtyping system can enhance type safety.  Notably, this approach has an unexpected outcome: a non-trivial, non-deterministic space cannot have a powerdomain that matches the powerdomain of the corresponding universal space.

We've established an inverse Penrose transform for self-dual Yang-Mills theory and its spin-off variants in a flat space environment. The spin-off variant's twistor action fits within the BF framework, while remaining equivalent to the original theory. When we expanded on this, higher-spin extensions became possible, which align with certain components of twistor version supersymmetric extensions. This led us to a direct comparison between the original theory and its spin-off variant, as well as the twistors actions used to describe them, resulting in an analogy of $^*$-algebra representation theory. Furthermore, we've developed an action on the space of holomorphic functions over twistor space, which describes the higher-spin extensions in a concise manner.

The application of deep neural networks for classifying medical image patterns holds significant promise, largely driven by advancements in large-scale transfer learning. Despite using refined models, persistent issues remain due to noise introduced during the labeling process. Conventional methods relying on data cleansing techniques are ineffective given the cost involved in annotating medical data. More recently, methods have been proposed to address labeling noise using both conditional dependence features and model-based techniques, with these approaches exhibiting superior performance in image classification tasks. Building upon existing research, this work further improves upon the model by incorporating learning noise-aware features directly from the data. Furthermore, this paper expands the existing framework to support learning noise-aware features from multiple types of data. Our experiments using chest X-rays demonstrate that the proposed method surpasses existing methods in X-ray classification tasks.

Consider a unit cube, $Q_n$, in $n$-dimensional space and a function space, $C(Q_n)$, consisting of continuous functions from $Q_n$ to $\mathbb{R}$. Define the norm of a function as its maximum absolute value over $Q_n$. Let $\Pi_1\left(\mathbb{R}^n\right)$ be the set of polynomials of degree at most $1$, parameterized over $\mathbb{R}^n$. This paper establishes under certain conditions a direct relationship between the norm in $C(Q_n)$ and the norm in the directed range space induced by $\Pi_1\left(\mathbb{R}^n\right)$, analogously to similar results in recent studies.

A correlated random walk (CRW) is derived from the Grover matrix, the evolution matrix of the Grover walk on a graph G, and an explicit formula is given for the characteristic polynomial of the CRW's transition matrix, utilising a determinant expression related to the graph's generalized weighted zeta function. This is exemplified in the cases of regular graphs and semiregular bipartite graphs. Additionally, the CRW is considered in a different graph scenario.

In a total functions logic such as HOL within Isabelle, functions are generally defined as terminating by default, with the option to mark specific functions as potentially non-terminating. Traditionally, non-terminating functions are identified through their use of an infinite clock, which blocks simplification and block-and-lost simplification. This legacy approach has the clock as a global attribute, with the clock reset upon entry into an function. This mechanism has the clock inheritable but not shared, leading to a confusing scenario in function recursion where the clock's ownership is ambiguous. To address this, a new legacy replacement is proposed, which incorporates a function-level clock annotation via a local attribute, allowing for a cleaner and more coherent infinitary logic. This new legacy offers improved expressiveness, enhanced usability, and increased modularity. Specifically, this new legacy excels at handling non-terminating functions within higher-order polymorphism and nested function application.

This is particularly evident when attempting to apply geometric characteristics from the overlying, geometrically similar domain representing the free-stream state. A geometric element known as the 'Schwarz triangle', defined by its vertices and edges geometry, can be used to describe both wall-bound and freestream states. Introducing the 'distortion' geometry, represented by the Schwarz triangle with a 2/3 fraction of streamwise measurement, may help to minimize the discrepancies that arise due to Reynolds number dependence. Several concepts have been proposed in the context of the 'near-wall closure' to describe this effect, including the 'inner region' and 'distance to the wall' methods. This work explores the 'inner region' concept, suggesting that the inner region of turbulent structures, defined by a specific length scale, determines the geometry of freestream elements. The study focuses on a complex field theory and its corresponding Bogomol'nyi-Newton equation. It shows how the soliton properties in this context can be translated into electrostatic charges through a mathematical transformation, establishing a connection with gauge theory and revealing soliton charges' relationships with their Higgs fields and magnetic flux. Additionally, the analysis includes cases where the soliton properties are influenced by an external source with a specific profile, and discusses how these soliton characteristics emerge from a higher-dimensional scenario with partial supersymmetry breaking in the Skyrme model's framework.

For a three-dimensional Weyl semimetal model with orbital magnetic field applied, we analyze the emergence of an orbital ferromagnet at low temperatures, whose characteristics can be quantified through both magnetization and Hall conductivity. The phenomenon is linked to a non-Landau quantization effect, whereupon multiple Weyl nodes appear in each momentum plane, creating distinct quantum states. These particle-hole symmetric states correspond to specific energy eigenvalue multiplicities at each Weyl node. Notably, when time-reversal symmetry is broken and an orbital magnetic field is present, Weyl nodes can occupy all eight positions within the momentum lattice, producing a diverse spectrum of quantum states. Notably, this phenomenon can also occur around a topological semimetal point, whereupon applying an orbital magnetic field can drive a phase transition into an orbital ferromagnet.

This research paper proposes a novel optical microcavity array platform that merges a 2D material, a dielectric barrier, and an oxide layer, resulting in an unprecedented combination of high light confinement and large structural resilience. The designed microcavities effectively increase light absorption in emitters and facilitate directed light emission, which is achieved through an optimized resonance alignment with the in-plane emission spectrum of 2D materials. Utilizing an ultra-thin MoS$_2$ layer, we construct microcavities within a 0.5 $\mu$m thick SiO$_2$ barrier, embedded in a 300 nm thick sapphire substrate, producing a robust oxide membrane that maintains its integrity even at room temperature. The resulting microcavities exhibit an in-plane $M_{11}$ mode with a very low threshold for excitation and high coupling efficiency with the 2D material's emission spectrum. The peak absorption rate is found to be one hundredth of a few picoseconds at a very low power density, while directed emission is facilitated with a consistent resonance within the 2D material's in-plane spectrum. The design of our microcavity array overcomes the limitations of traditional microcavities with fragile metal or semiconductor membranes, offering a more reliable and efficient platform for 2D material research, especially for spontaneous emission suppression studies.

Mechanical screening, a widely recognized phenomenon, is utilized across solid-state systems.  Although extensively studied in crystalline matter, its presence and effects have also been observed in disordered amorphous solids, with assumptions sometimes made that screening in amorphous and crystalline materials shares common underlying principles.  However, recent research has challenged this assumption, with findings suggesting that while these two types of screening share conceptual similarities, they exhibit distinct characteristics and mechanisms.  Deeper understanding of mechanical screening in disordered solids has been hindered by the lack of a standardized screening length scale and by simulations which often overlook crucial experimental considerations, such as dynamic equilibrium states.  In this work, we investigate mechanical screening in a model amorphous system through molecular dynamics simulations that take into account real-time equilibrium conditions.  Our study reveals that despite similarities in screening concepts, mechanical screening in amorphous solids differs significantly from its crystalline counterpart, with distinct features including variations in screening lengths, mechanisms, and thermodynamic behaviors.  Our findings imply that while it may be reasonable to apply insights from crystalline screening to certain amorphous-weak screening scenarios, weak screening cannot be considered a direct analog of strong screening, with the latter characterized by the absence of mechanical interactions within screening lengths.  Furthermore, our results show that thermal fluctuations at all timescales exceed mechanical fluctuations, with the ratio of these two lengthscales representing a unique, system-specific parameter that distinguishes mechanical screening in different amorphous materials.

Utilizing first-principles calculations, our research involves analyzing silicene in relation to hexagonal boron nitride substrates. Hexagonal boron nitride, being a semiconductor, has weaker interactions with silicene in comparison to metallic substrates. As a result, silicene's band gap can potentially be expanded up to 50 meV. Additionally, the impact of manganese decoration on the system is explored by calculating the onsite Hubbard interaction parameter, which significantly differs between decoration at the top and hollow sites. Furthermore, the system's induced magnetism is thoroughly examined.

The Sgr A East supernova remnant, located near the center of the Milky Way, poses a mystery with age estimates ranging from extremely young, around 1-2 thousand years, to a significantly older, 10 thousand year estimate. Our objective is to create a straightforward simulation of a supernova event replicating the appearance of Sgr A East, which has been shaped by radiation from a central source and paired radiation pulses. To accomplish this, we simulate a massive star whose core collapse results in a massive neutron star with incredible rotational speed. As this neutron star continues to spin, it generates intense magnetic fields and accelerated particles that emit synchrotron radiation, contributing to Sgr A East's overall appearance. Additionally, when the paired radiation pulses from either a plerion or magnetar collapse interact with each other, they produce X-ray emissions that could account for the central source emissions. Furthermore, our simulation shows that as these particles continue to interact with each other, they generate a range of energy and curvature-dependent emissions. Our simulation indicates that within the next 10 thousand years, this scenario may explain not just the appearance of Sgr A East, but also its progression over time, which has been shaped by a slowly moving supernova event.

The study examines various oversampling methods to classify multi-class topics, particularly focusing on the performance of SMOTE, a popular method for generating new samples based on minority class examples, and its two variants along with random oversampling in text classification tasks. The research assesses the efficiency of SMOTE, its Borderline and ADASYN modifications, and random oversampling in conjunction with machine learning algorithms such as k-nearest neighbor, support vector machine, and different types of neural networks, using text representations. Using 60 datasets from the UCI machine learning repository, the study measures performance in terms of accuracy, false positive rate, and false negative rate, and reveals that the performance of oversampling methods varies depending on the classification problem and the used learner. While SMOTE outperforms random oversampling in many instances, ADASYN performs better than SMOTE in a significant number of cases, suggesting the need for further investigation on this algorithm.

This study analyzes data from an online monitoring system of U.S. local news to explore connections between COVID coverage, regional case and death rates, and characteristics of news outlets and their audiences. Using a distinct dataset of over 750,000 articles from over 300 outlets between April 2020 and February 2021, our results show that local news outlets initially covered COVID at a rate influenced by national death rates but ultimately became less correlated as other issues like the U.S. elections dominated headlines. Additionally, our research reveals that local news COVID coverage varied based on the area's politics, news outlet popularity, and audience size, and also indicates that disadvantaged populations received less access to COVID information.

Smoothed particle hydrodynamics possesses innate conservation capabilities of linear and angular momentum, stemming from the fundamental equations and potential energies, while momentum conservation is ensured through the use of a convenient acceleration. Although the method can preserve energy in theories that account for particle discretization effects, implementing true energy conservation via Hamilton's equations is hindered by discretization errors in momentum equations. To overcome this limitation, a proposed algorithm applies a discrete version of canonical transformations to exactly conserve total energy and, by doing so, efficiently achieves conservative integration. The accompanying numerical tests demonstrate the ability of the proposed method to retain accuracy with reduced discretization errors in momentum.

Numerical studies have been conducted on the $Q^2$ dependence of cross-sectional ratios in electron proton collisions, drawing on JLab polarization experiments measuring the ratio of Sachs form factors in such interactions. Calculations considering a scenario with fully polarized, in-line initial and final protons have been carried out to analyze polarization transfer and compare results to an experiment measuring double-spin asymmetry in another process. Research found a significant $Q^2$ dependence influence on polarization transfer to the proton, showing good agreement with a recent experiment measuring this phenomenon while suggesting improved accuracy using the form factor ratio method over double-spin asymmetry when studying such transitions. This research also explored how applying radiative corrections impacts measurements of polarization at specific $Q^2$ values.

We develop a novel, yet efficient, method for augmenting existing data to enhance the learning capacity of both reinforcement and imitation learning from experienced agents. The introduction of synthetic states utilizes a neural network to create artificial experiences that are incorporated into the training dataset. Our approach is data-incremental, allowing the dataset to continuously grow as agents encounter more states. Preliminary evaluation indicates promising results with robustness when agents encounter novel environments. The code is accessible via this link: https://github.com/gaowu97/SynState.
